Thermodynamics • Foundations

Draw the boundary correctly—and the whole problem becomes visible

Thermodynamics begins with a decision: what is the system? Once the system is chosen, every matter and energy transfer must be counted across its boundary.

Boundary-first reasoning

Universe

universe = system + surroundings

Isolated system

matter transfer = 0; energy transfer = 0

Rigid boundary

dV = 0 ⇒ wₚᵥ = 0
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

What thermodynamics studies

A macroscopic framework for energy, equilibrium, direction and limits.

Thermodynamics studies systems through measurable bulk variables and general energy laws. It connects initial and final equilibrium states, the energy exchanged during a change, the direction in which a natural process can proceed, and the limiting efficiency of devices.

Feasibility

Can the proposed change occur under the stated constraints?

Direction

Which direction is thermodynamically favoured?

Equilibrium

What condition is reached when the driving force vanishes?

Extent

How far can a reaction or process proceed before equilibrium?

Concept lens

Macroscopic—not blind to molecules

Classical thermodynamics does not track every molecule. It works with pressure, volume, temperature, composition and other bulk properties. Molecular models may explain the results, but the laws themselves are macroscopic.

Concept Trap

Thermodynamics does not predict rate

A process may be thermodynamically favourable but kinetically slow. Diamond, fuel combustion and many metastable systems demonstrate that direction and speed are different questions.
02

Energetics: Thermodynamics and Thermochemistry

The chapter sequence separates physical-process thermodynamics from chemical-reaction thermochemistry.

Thermodynamics note

General laws, physical processes and direction

solid ⇌ liquid
liquid ⇌ gas
gas expansion
gas compression
heat engines
entropy and free energy

Separate Thermochemistry note

Energy changes accompanying chemical reactions

CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g)
CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

Concept lens

Course architecture

This Thermodynamics sequence develops systems, properties, processes, work, laws, entropy and free-energy criteria. Detailed reaction enthalpies, calorimetry, Hess cycles and bond-enthalpy calculations belong to the separate Thermochemistry note.
03

System, surroundings, boundary and universe

Definitions become powerful only after the selected system is stated explicitly.

System

The selected matter or region of space under investigation.

Surroundings

The relevant remainder that can interact with the system.

Boundary

The real or imagined surface separating the two.

Universe

System plus surroundings for the chosen model.

Concept lens

The same apparatus can define different systems

In a piston-cylinder, the system may be only the gas, the gas plus piston, or the complete insulated assembly. Each choice changes what is counted as crossing the boundary, while the physical law remains unchanged.

Language Discipline

Heat and work are boundary events

A system possesses internal energy, not “stored heat” or “stored work.” Heat and work name modes of energy transfer during a process.
04

Four independent classifications of a boundary

Never infer one boundary property from another.

Concept lens

Rigid does not mean adiabatic

A sealed steel vessel may have fixed volume yet conduct heat readily. Rigidity controls movement; adiabaticity controls heat transfer.

Concept lens

Adiabatic does not mean impermeable

An insulated flow pipe can be adiabatic while matter enters and leaves. Heat transfer and mass transfer are separate questions.
05

Open, closed and isolated systems

Classification is determined by what crosses the chosen boundary during the stated operation.

System or daily-life exampleBest classificationBoundary-based reasoning
Living organism / human bodyOpenFood, water, respiratory gases, waste, heat and work-related energy cross the chosen boundary.
Air in an open roomOpenAir can enter or leave through doors, windows and ventilation; energy also crosses.
Hot tea in an uncovered cupOpenWater vapour and aroma molecules escape while heat is exchanged with the surroundings.
Matter in a sealed containerClosedThe amount of matter is fixed, although heat or work may still cross depending on the walls.
Electrochemical cell with sealed material boundaryClosedMatter can remain confined while electrical work and heat cross the boundary.
Universe in the standard thermodynamic modelIsolatedThere is no external surroundings with which the entire universe can exchange matter or energy.
Pressure cooker before ventingClosedMatter is retained while heat enters from the burner; the model changes once steam escapes.
Pressure cooker during ventingOpenSteam crosses the pressure valve, so both matter and energy can be exchanged.
Boiler operating continuouslyOpenFeed water enters, steam exits, and heat is supplied.
Automobile liquid-cooling circuitModel-dependentThe circulating coolant loop may be treated as closed, while a control volume around the radiator is open to fluid flow.
Chemical reaction in a sealed rigid vesselClosedNo reactant or product crosses the wall, but energy may still cross unless the vessel is adiabatic.
EarthApproximately closed for matterEnergy exchange with the Sun and space is large; matter exchange exists but is often negligible for simplified models.

Concept lens

Real isolated systems are approximations

A thermos flask, insulated calorimeter or cryogenic vessel is isolated only approximately and only over a finite time. The ideal isolated system is a model with exactly zero matter and energy transfer.
06

Adiabatic is not the same as isolated

This distinction produces one of the most common JEE errors.

Adiabatic

q = 0

Rigid

dV = 0 ⇒ wₚᵥ = 0

Isolated

q = 0 and all work modes = 0

Concept lens

Rigid boundary only eliminates pressure–volume work

Electrical, shaft, magnetic, surface or other work may still cross a rigid boundary. State the permitted work modes before concluding that total work is zero.
07

All six chapter true–false traps

Each statement is resolved by returning to the boundary definition.

1.A closed system always has constant volume.

False

Closed means no matter transfer. A sealed gas beneath a movable piston is closed even though its volume changes.

2.If neither heat nor matter crosses the boundary, the system must be isolated.

False

Work may still cross a movable or electrical boundary. Isolation excludes every mode of energy transfer.

3.Every closed system is isolated.

False

A closed system can exchange energy. Isolation is a stronger condition than closure.

4.Every isolated system is also closed.

True

An isolated system cannot exchange matter, so it automatically satisfies the defining condition of a closed system.

5.An adiabatic container fitted with an adiabatic movable piston is isolated.

False

The walls block heat, but piston motion can transfer pressure–volume work.

6.A sealed adiabatic container with a rigid boundary is isolated from heat and pressure–volume work.

True with condition

It blocks matter, heat and boundary movement. The statement assumes no electrical, shaft, radiation or other work mode crosses the boundary.

08

Energy bookkeeping in isolated and rigid systems

Total energy conservation must be separated from changes in individual energy forms.

Isolated composite

Boundary exchange

q = 0; w = 0

Internal kinetic, potential and internal-energy contributions may transform into one another, but the total energy of the complete isolated system remains constant.

Closed rigid vessel

Boundary movement

dV = 0 ⇒ wₚᵥ = 0

Heat may cross, and non-pressure–volume work may also cross unless explicitly excluded. Closed and rigid do not automatically imply isolated.

09

State of a system

The chapter opening closes by introducing the state before properties are developed in Part 02.

The state of a system is its condition described by a sufficient set of thermodynamic variables. At a specified equilibrium state, each state property has a definite value.

Example state labels

State 1: (P₁, V₁, T₁, composition₁) → State 2: (P₂, V₂, T₂, composition₂)

Concept lens

A system has infinitely many possible states

Pressure, volume, temperature and composition can vary continuously over allowed ranges. A process is a path through the space of possible states. Part 02 develops thermodynamic properties, intensive/extensive variables, state functions and path functions.
10

Thermodynamics around you

Original daily-life applications inspired by the real-world physical-chemistry approach.

Bicycle pump

Choosing the air inside the pump as the system exposes a movable boundary. During rapid compression, work enters faster than heat can leave, so the air becomes warm.

Refrigerator

A refrigerator is useful because heat and work cross carefully chosen boundaries. Calling the appliance 'containing heat' confuses a transfer mode with a state property.

Uncovered tea

The tea loses energy as heat and matter as water vapour. The same cup becomes approximately closed if sealed before appreciable evaporation.

Car radiator

A control volume around the radiator is open: coolant and air flow through it while energy is transferred. The complete sealed coolant loop can instead be modelled as closed.

Derivation 1

Distinguishing open, closed and isolated systems from the boundary conditions

Open systemmatter + energy cross the boundary— e.g., a beaker in open air
Closed systemonly energy (heat or work) crosses; no matter transfer— e.g., a sealed, non-rigid balloon
Isolated systemneither energy nor matter crosses— e.g., an ideal Dewar flask
Universeuniverse = system + surroundings— total system; no external boundary

Derivation 2

Boundary classification

Rigid boundaryV = constant → no PdV work possible
Adiabatic boundaryq = 0 → no heat transfer across boundary
Diathermal boundaryheat flows until thermal equilibrium is reached

11

Complete theory, diagrams and worked examples

Twelve original problems; every example and complete solution is displayed below.

◆1. Boundary choice changes the classification

A kettle is boiling. Classify (i) only the liquid remaining inside, (ii) the kettle plus liquid before the lid opens, and (iii) a control volume around the spout during steady steam discharge.

Solution

(i) Open, because vapour leaves the chosen liquid system. (ii) Closed if no matter escapes, though heat enters. (iii) Open because steam flows through the control surface. The physical object is similar, but the chosen system and operating stage differ.

◆2. Rigid but not isolated

A rigid sealed steel vessel is placed in a hot bath. What transfers are possible?

Solution

No matter crosses and pressure–volume work is zero because dV = 0. Heat can cross the diathermal steel wall, so the vessel is closed, not isolated.

◆3. Adiabatic but not isolated

A gas is enclosed by insulated walls and an insulated movable piston. A weight is placed on the piston and the gas is compressed. Is the gas isolated?

Solution

No. The boundary is adiabatic, so q = 0, but work is done on the gas through piston motion. Energy crosses as work.

◆4. Battery as a thermodynamic system

A sealed battery powers a lamp. Matter remains inside the battery. How should the battery be classified?

Solution

Closed with respect to matter, but not isolated because electrical work and heat cross its boundary.

◆5. Earth model

Why is Earth often described as closed rather than isolated?

Solution

Its matter exchange with space is small compared with its mass, but it receives solar radiation and emits thermal radiation. Therefore energy transfer is substantial.

◆6. Can internal energy change in an isolated system?

An isolated vessel contains a falling block, a paddle wheel and a fluid. The block falls and stirs the fluid. Can the fluid temperature rise?

Solution

Yes. Gravitational potential energy can be converted into internal energy within the isolated composite. The total energy of the complete isolated system remains constant.

◆7. Closed rigid vessel and non-PV work

A sealed rigid electrochemical cell drives current through an external resistor. Is all work necessarily zero because the boundary is rigid?

Solution

No. Rigid means pressure–volume boundary work is zero. Electrical work can still cross. Always identify the work mode.

◆8. Open-room air

A student claims that air in a room is closed because the walls are rigid. Identify the error.

Solution

Rigidity concerns volume, not matter permeability. Open doors, windows and ventilation permit mass flow, making the chosen room-air system open.

◆9. Universe statement

Is it scientifically meaningful to call the universe isolated?

Solution

In standard thermodynamic modelling, yes, because the universe has no external surroundings. This is a modelling statement, not a laboratory claim about a container wall.

◆10. System selection in a reaction vessel

A reaction occurs inside a sealed piston-cylinder. Give two legitimate systems and explain how the accounting differs.

Solution

System A may be only the reacting mixture; the moving piston lies in the surroundings and work crosses the boundary. System B may include the mixture and piston; then the external load belongs to the surroundings. Conservation is unchanged, but the bookkeeping boundary differs.

◆11. Multiple-correct boundary problem

For a sealed, thermally conducting piston-cylinder, which descriptions may simultaneously be true: real, movable, impermeable, diathermal?

Solution

All four may be true. Boundary classifications describe independent properties.

◆12. State versus path preview

A gas begins at one equilibrium condition and ends at another. Why are pressure, volume and temperature used to describe the states, while heat and work are not listed as contents of the gas?

Solution

Pressure, volume and temperature can characterize equilibrium states. Heat and work describe energy crossing the boundary during a process; they are not properties stored in the system.

Choose the system → draw the boundary → list every allowed transfer

Thermodynamics • Properties Layer

Phase, scaling and the mathematics of state

A phase tells us where a system is uniform. Scaling separates extensive quantities from intensive ones. Exact differentials reveal which quantities belong to the state itself.

Three master tests

Scaling

X(λn) = λX(n) ⇒ extensive

Intensive

Y(λn) = Y(n)

Exactness

∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

State, equilibrium state and state variables

Part 01 introduced state; this lesson sharpens the meaning before classifying properties.

A thermodynamic state is specified by a sufficient set of macroscopic variables. At equilibrium, those variables have definite, reproducible values and no unbalanced thermal, mechanical, phase or chemical driving force remains inside the system.

State description

state = sufficient independent variables + composition + constraints

Concept lens

Not every listed variable is independent

An equation of state links pressure, volume, temperature and composition. For a fixed amount of ideal gas, specifying any two of P, V and T fixes the third.

Condition Gate

A gradient means non-equilibrium

A system with internal temperature or pressure gradients cannot be described by one global equilibrium temperature or pressure without an approximation.
02

Homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

Classification is based on the number of phases, not merely the number of substances.

A phase is a physically distinct homogeneous region having uniform composition and macroscopic properties throughout. Different phases are separated by an interface across which at least one property changes discontinuously.

SystemComponentsPhasesClassification
Pure liquid water11 liquid phaseHomogeneous
Air after complete mixingmany1 gas phaseHomogeneous
Unsaturated NaCl(aq)21 liquid phaseHomogeneous
Ice + liquid water12 phasesHeterogeneous
Oil + water22 liquid phasesHeterogeneous
Saturated NaCl solution + crystals2liquid + solidHeterogeneous
Fog or mistair + watergas + liquid dropletsHeterogeneous
Graniteseveralseveral solid phasesHeterogeneous
Milk at microscopic scalemulticomponentcontinuous liquid + dispersed dropletsColloidal heterogeneous
Brass alloy, single solid solutionmultiple1 solid phaseHomogeneous

Concept lens

One component can form several phases

Ice and liquid water contain only H₂O, yet they form two phases because solid and liquid regions have different structures and properties.

Concept lens

Several components can form one phase

A completely mixed gas or single solid solution may contain several chemical species but remain one homogeneous phase.
03

Thermodynamic properties

Properties describe the state; heat and work describe transfer during a process.

Thermodynamic properties are measurable or calculable macroscopic quantities used to specify or characterize the state of a system. Pressure, volume, temperature, internal energy, entropy and composition are examples.

Concept lens

Mechanical

Pressure, volume, compressibility and expansion coefficients.

Concept lens

Thermal

Temperature, internal energy, entropy and heat capacities.

Concept lens

Chemical/electrical

Composition, chemical potential, EMF and equilibrium constants.

Language Discipline

Heat and work are not thermodynamic properties

A state has U, H, S and G. It does not contain q or w. Heat and work are process quantities defined only while energy crosses the chosen boundary.
04

Intensive and extensive properties

Use scaling first; the partition test is a practical visualization of the same principle.

Extensive scaling

X(λN) = λX(N)

Intensive scaling

Y(λN) = Y(N)

Concept lens

Partition test requires a uniform equilibrium phase

Divide the system into unequal portions without changing local state. Extensive quantities divide with amount; intensive quantities remain the same. The shortcut fails when the original system has gradients or multiple phases with different local values.

06

Derived intensive properties

A ratio of two linearly extensive quantities is intensive.

Density

ρ = m/V

Molar volume

Vₘ = V/n

Specific volume

v = V/m

Molar internal energy

Uₘ = U/n

Concept lens

“Molar” and “specific” usually convert extensive to intensive

Dividing an additive quantity by amount of substance or mass removes its dependence on total system size. Always check that numerator and denominator scale in the same way.

Trap Detector

Only extensive quantities add directly

Total mass, volume under additive conditions, internal energy and entropy can be summed over subsystems. Temperatures, pressures and densities cannot be added to obtain a total.
07

State functions and path functions

Endpoint functions belong to states; transfer quantities depend on how the process is performed.

QuantityTypeReason
Pressure PState function / propertyDefined for an equilibrium state
Volume VState function / propertyEndpoint value belongs to the state
Temperature TState function / propertyEndpoint value belongs to the state
Internal energy UState functionΔU depends only on states 1 and 2
Enthalpy HState functionDefined from U + PV
Entropy SState functionExact differential dS
Gibbs energy GState functionExact differential dG
Helmholtz energy AState functionExact differential dA
Heat qPath functionAmount transferred depends on process route
Work wPath functionAmount transferred depends on process route

State-function change

ΔX = X₂ − X₁

Closed cycle

∮dX = 0

Concept lens

Notation matters

Exact differentials use dU, dS and dG. Heat and work are often written δq and δw to signal that no state function q or w exists whose ordinary differential they represent.
08

Exact and inexact differentials

The chapter reciprocity idea becomes a practical mathematical test.

General two-variable differential

dF = M(x,y)dx + N(x,y)dy

Exactness condition

(∂M/∂y)ₓ = (∂N/∂x)ᵧ

dF = 2x dx + 2y dy

∂(2x)/∂y = 0 and ∂(2y)/∂x = 0

Exact; F = x² + y² + constant

ω = y dx + x dy

∂y/∂y = 1 and ∂x/∂x = 1

Exact; F = xy + constant

ω = y dx − x dy

∂y/∂y = 1 but ∂(−x)/∂x = −1

Inexact

ω = (2xy + 3)dx + x²dy

∂M/∂y = 2x and ∂N/∂x = 2x

Exact; F = x²y + 3x + constant

Concept lens

Domain condition

Equality of cross partials is the standard local test when the functions are smooth and the domain has no topological obstruction. For JEE-level applications, the stated domain is normally assumed suitable.
09

Ideal-gas pressure as a state function

The proof is recast as an exact-differential demonstration.

Equation of state

P(T,V) = nRT/V

Differential

dP = (nR/V)dT − (nRT/V²)dV

Cross-partial equality

∂(nR/V)/∂V = ∂(−nRT/V²)/∂T = −nR/V²

Concept lens

Why this proves state character

Pressure is a single-valued function of equilibrium state variables. The integral of dP between two states is P₂−P₁ and is independent of the route taken through the T–V plane.
10

Thermodynamics around you

Original daily-life analogies strengthen phase and path reasoning.

Fogged bathroom mirror

The humid air is a gas phase, while condensed droplets form a liquid phase on the mirror. A visually smooth surface can still be multiphase microscopically.

Salad dressing

Oil and aqueous vinegar form two liquid phases. Vigorous shaking creates a temporary dispersion, not necessarily a single thermodynamic phase.

Perfume concentration

Concentration is intensive: doubling both perfume and solvent at the same composition doubles the amount but not the concentration.

Two routes up a hill

Altitude change depends only on endpoints, while walking distance depends on the chosen trail. This mirrors state-function versus path-function thinking.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Proof that internal energy U is a state function

Define state functionf is a state function if ∮ df = 0 for any cyclic path
First LawΔU = q + w for any process between states 1 and 2
Cyclic processΔU_cycle = q_cycle + w_cycle
Joule's resultfor isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0 regardless of path
ConclusionU depends only on state (T, P, V, n) — not on the path taken

Derivation 2

Intensive vs extensive property classification

ExtensiveX_total = Σ X_i (additive over subsystems)— U, H, S, G, V, n, mass
IntensiveX_total = X_i (independent of system size)— T, P, ρ, μ, molar quantities
Ratio ruleextensive / extensive = intensive (e.g., U/n = Um)
11

Complete theory, diagrams, derivations and worked examples

Sixteen original problems spanning phase analysis, scaling, additivity and path dependence.

◆1. Component versus phase

A sealed vessel contains ice and liquid water at equilibrium. How many components and phases are present?

Solution

One component, H₂O, but two phases: solid ice and liquid water. Component count and phase count are different.

◆2. Fog classification

Why is fog heterogeneous even though it may look uniform from far away?

Solution

Fog contains liquid-water droplets dispersed in a gas phase. At the phase scale, liquid–gas interfaces exist throughout.

◆3. Single-phase alloy

Can a solid containing two chemical elements be homogeneous?

Solution

Yes. A single-phase solid solution such as suitable brass can be homogeneous even though it has more than one component.

◆4. Partition-test limitation

A metal rod has a temperature gradient. It is divided into unequal parts. Must temperature be the same in both parts because temperature is intensive?

Solution

No. Intensive means independent of amount for comparable equilibrium states. A non-equilibrium rod can have different local temperatures.

◆5. Ratio of extensive quantities

Show that density is intensive when mass and volume both scale by λ.

Solution

Under scaling, m′ = λm and V′ = λV. Therefore ρ′ = m′/V′ = λm/(λV) = ρ.

◆6. Molar quantity

A system has total internal energy U and amount n. Why is Um = U/n intensive?

Solution

Both U and n scale linearly with system size, so their ratio is invariant under uniform scaling.

◆7. Resistance trap

A wire is cut into two equal lengths. Each half has half the resistance. Does this prove resistance is extensive?

Solution

No. Resistance depends on geometry through R = ρL/A. Combining samples in parallel or changing shape breaks simple thermodynamic additivity.

◆8. Additivity trap

Two equal copper blocks at the same temperature are combined. Which quantities add: mass, entropy, temperature, density?

Solution

Mass and entropy add. Temperature and density remain unchanged; adding intensive values is meaningless.

◆9. Heat and work

A gas reaches the same final state by two routes. Why can q differ even though ΔU is fixed?

Solution

Internal energy is a state function. Heat and work are path-dependent transfers constrained by the first law, so different routes can partition the fixed ΔU differently.

◆10. Closed-cycle state function

A system undergoes a cycle and returns to its initial state. What is ∮dU?

Solution

Zero, because U is a state function and the final state equals the initial state.

◆11. Exactness test

Determine whether ω = (3x² + 2y)dx + (2x + 4y³)dy is exact.

Solution

M = 3x² + 2y and N = 2x + 4y³. ∂M/∂y = 2 and ∂N/∂x = 2, so the form is exact.

◆12. Recover the state function

For the previous exact form, determine F(x,y).

Solution

Integrate M with respect to x: F = x³ + 2xy + g(y). Comparing ∂F/∂y = 2x + g′(y) with N gives g′(y)=4y³, so F=x³+2xy+y⁴+C.

◆13. Ideal-gas pressure

For one mole of an ideal gas, P(T,V)=RT/V. Show that P is a state function.

Solution

P is explicitly a single-valued function of the state variables T and V. Its differential dP=(R/V)dT−(RT/V²)dV is exact because ∂(R/V)/∂V=−R/V² and ∂(−RT/V²)/∂T=−R/V².

◆14. Path integral contrast

For ω = y dx − x dy, compare the integral from (0,0) to (1,1) along y=x and along the broken path (0,0)→(1,0)→(1,1).

Solution

Along y=x, dy=dx and ω=x dx−x dx=0. Along the broken path, the first segment gives 0 and the second gives −∫₀¹dy=−1. Different values prove path dependence.

◆15. Molar entropy of a composite

Two phases have different molar entropies. Can the total-system entropy divided by total moles be treated as the molar entropy of either phase?

Solution

No. It is an overall composition-weighted average for the complete system, not necessarily the local molar entropy of either phase.

◆16. Equilibrium constant classification

Why is K at a fixed temperature intensive even though equilibrium amounts change with system size?

Solution

K depends on temperature and the chosen standard-state convention, not on multiplying every equilibrium amount by the same scale factor.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Count phases → test scaling → test endpoints → test exactness

Phase

uniform macroscopic region

Extensive

Intensive

PART 03 / 30Foundations & the Language of ThermodynamicsState Functions, Path Functions, Exact Differentials, and Mathematical Tests
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYMATHEMATICAL THERMODYNAMICS

Thermodynamics • Function Layer

The destination remembers; the path records the journey

State functions are determined by equilibrium endpoints. Heat and work describe transfers along the chosen route. Exact differentials provide the mathematical test.

Master distinction

State function

Defined at a state; change depends only on endpoints.

Path function

Defined during a process; accumulated value depends on route.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Thermodynamic process and path

A process takes a system from one equilibrium state to another through a chosen sequence of intermediate conditions.

Consider an initial state A and a final state B. Many different processes may connect them: rapid or slow, one-step or multistep, expansion first or heating first. The ordered sequence of intermediate states and interactions is the path.

Concept lens

Endpoints determine state change; route determines transfer

Every path from A to B gives the same change in a state function such as U, but generally different heat q and work w. The First Law links them so that q + w always produces the same ΔU.
02

State function or state variable

A state function has a definite value at each equilibrium state. Its change depends only on the initial and final states—not on the process used to connect them.

Finite change

ΔΦ = ΦB − ΦA

Endpoint integral

∫AB dΦ = ΦB − ΦA
QuantityClassificationReason
Pressure P or pState functionDefinite at an equilibrium state
Volume VState functionDefinite at an equilibrium state
Temperature TState functionDefinite at an equilibrium state
Internal energy UState functionEndpoint change only
Enthalpy HState functionDetailed treatment in Thermochemistry
Entropy SState functionDeveloped later in Thermodynamics
Gibbs energy GState functionDeveloped later in Thermodynamics
Heat qPath functionEnergy crossing due to temperature difference
Work wPath functionOrganised energy transfer across boundary

Concept lens

Notation is a clue, not a proof

Many textbooks use capital symbols for state functions and lower-case symbols for heat and work, but notation alone cannot decide classification. Pressure is often written p, yet it is a state function. The endpoint or exactness test is decisive.

Concept lens

Absolute value versus measurable change

State-function status does not require an experimentally accessible absolute zero. Internal energy U is a state function even though thermodynamics normally measures ΔU rather than an absolute U.
03

Path functions: heat and work

Heat and work are not properties stored inside a system. They describe energy crossing the boundary during a process. A system has internal energy; it does not “contain heat” or “contain work.”

Inexact heat differential

δq

Inexact work differential

δw

Concept lens

Why δ instead of d?

The symbol d is reserved for an exact differential of a state function. The symbol δ reminds us that heat and work do not possess endpoint-only antiderivatives in general.

Concept lens

Important constrained-process nuance

At constant volume with only pressure–volume work, qV = ΔU. At constant pressure with only pressure–volume work, qP = ΔH. Under those specified constraints, the heat between fixed endpoints equals a state-function change. Heat itself does not become a universal state function.
04

Exact and inexact differentials

Let a quantity be expressed using two independent variables x and y:

General differential form

dΦ = M(x,y) dx + N(x,y) dy

On a simply connected region where the derivatives are continuous, the differential is exact if:

Euler reciprocity / exactness criterion

(∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y

STATE FUNCTION

An exact example

dΦ = 2xy dx + (x² + 6y)dy
Here M = 2xy and N = x² + 6y. Both cross derivatives equal 2x. Integrating gives Φ = x²y + 3y² + constant.

PATH DEPENDENT

An inexact example

ω = y dx − x dy
Here ∂M/∂y = 1 but ∂N/∂x = −1. The inequality proves that no ordinary single-valued Φ has dΦ = ω.

Concept lens

Domain warning for advanced mathematics

Equality of cross derivatives is sufficient on a simply connected domain. Singularities or holes can create exceptional cases, but standard JEE thermodynamic domains normally satisfy the needed conditions.
05

Cyclic integral test

In a cyclic process the final state is identical to the initial state. Therefore every state function returns to its starting value:

State function around a cycle

∮ dΦ = 0

For heat and work, the individual cyclic integrals need not vanish:

Heat around a cycle

∮ δq may be non-zero

Work around a cycle

∮ δw may be non-zero

Concept lens

First-Law closure

For a complete cycle, ΔU = 0. Hence ∮δq + ∮δw = 0 using the chemistry sign convention. Net heat absorbed and net work done on the system are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
06

Proof: ideal-gas pressure is a state function

The chapter derivation is expanded into a complete exact-differential proof.

Equation of state

P(V,T) = nRT/V

Total differential

dP = (−nRT/V²)dV + (nR/V)dT

Differentiate the dV coefficient with respect to T

∂/∂T(−nRT/V²) = −nR/V²

Differentiate the dT coefficient with respect to V

∂/∂V(nR/V) = −nR/V²

Concept lens

Conclusion

The cross derivatives are equal. Therefore dP is exact and pressure is a state function. Its value is fixed by the current V, T, n—not by the route used to reach that state.
07

Proof: real-gas pressure is also a state function

van der Waals equation in explicit pressure form

P(V,T) = nRT/(V−nb) − an²/V²

Total differential

dP = [−nRT/(V−nb)² + 2an²/V³]dV + [nR/(V−nb)]dT

First cross derivative

∂/∂T[−nRT/(V−nb)² + 2an²/V³] = −nR/(V−nb)²

Second cross derivative

∂/∂V[nR/(V−nb)] = −nR/(V−nb)²

Concept lens

Equation complexity does not alter state-function character

Ideal and real gases have different equations of state, but pressure remains a state function because it is uniquely determined by the equilibrium state variables.
08

Proof: ideal-gas volume is a state function

Explicit volume form

V(T,P) = nRT/P

Total differential

dV = (nR/P)dT − (nRT/P²)dP

Cross derivative I

∂/∂P(nR/P) = −nR/P²

Cross derivative II

∂/∂T(−nRT/P²) = −nR/P²

The equality confirms that dV is exact. Volume is a state function.

09

Why pressure–volume work is path dependent

Two paths between the same states give different areas on a P–V diagram.

Path I

wI = −P₁(V₂−V₁)

Path II

wII = −P₂(V₂−V₁)

Unless P₁ = P₂, the works differ. Since both paths connect the same A and B but produce different w, work cannot be expressed as wB − wA. A system has no “work value” at a state.

Concept lens

Heat differs in compensation

The internal-energy change ΔU is the same for both paths. Therefore q = ΔU − w differs whenever w differs. Heat and work redistribute the same endpoint energy change.
10

Conservative and non-conservative mechanical work

CONSERVATIVE FORCE

Endpoint-dependent mechanical work

Gravity, ideal spring force and electrostatic force admit potential-energy functions. Their work between fixed endpoints equals minus the change in potential energy.

Wconservative = −ΔEpotential
NON-CONSERVATIVE FORCE

Route-dependent mechanical work

Friction dissipates mechanical energy, and the work depends on travelled distance and path.

∮ δWfriction ≠ 0

Concept lens

Do not confuse conservative-force work with stored work

Even when mechanical work by a conservative force is endpoint dependent, the stored state property is potential energy—not “work contained in the system.”
11

Heat capacity nuance

The general process ratio Cpath = δq/dT can depend on the path. However, the standard equilibrium heat capacities are defined through state functions:

At constant volume

CV = (∂U/∂T)V

At constant pressure

CP = (∂H/∂T)P

Concept lens

Why CP and CV can be properties

U and H are state functions, so their specified partial derivatives are equilibrium properties. Detailed heat-capacity theory remains in the separate Thermochemistry notes.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Derivation of work for isothermal reversible ideal-gas expansion

Define reversibleP_ext = P_gas at every infinitesimal step
Ideal gas lawP = nRT/V
Differential work elementδw_rev = −P_ext dV = −P dV = −(nRT/V) dV
Integrate V₁ → V₂w_rev = −nRT ∫[V₁→V₂] dV/V = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
Equivalent formw_rev = −nRT ln(P₁/P₂) (using P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at const T)
Sign checkexpansion: V₂ > V₁ → ln > 0 → w_rev < 0 (work done BY system)

Derivation 2

Irreversible isothermal expansion against constant external pressure

ConditionP_ext = P_final = constant throughout
Work integralw_irrev = −P_ext ΔV = −P_ext(V₂ − V₁)
Comparison|w_rev| > |w_irrev| for the same initial and final states
Reasonirreversible process loses work to entropy generation in surroundings
12

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — exactness test

For the differential form dΦ = (2xy + 3)dx + (x² + 4y)dy, determine whether Φ is a state function.

Solution

M = 2xy + 3 and N = x² + 4y. Since (∂M/∂y)x = 2x and (∂N/∂x)y = 2x, the form is exact on an ordinary simply connected domain. Hence Φ is a state function. Integration gives Φ = x²y + 3x + 2y² + constant.

◆Concept Application 2 — inexact differential

Test whether ω = y dx − x dy is exact.

Solution

M = y and N = −x. Here ∂M/∂y = 1, while ∂N/∂x = −1. They are unequal, so ω is not exact and its line integral generally depends on the path.

◆Concept Application 3 — ideal-gas pressure

Show mathematically that pressure P = nRT/V is a state function of V and T.

Solution

dP = [−nRT/V²]dV + [nR/V]dT. The cross derivatives are ∂/∂T(−nRT/V²) = −nR/V² and ∂/∂V(nR/V) = −nR/V². They are equal, so dP is exact.

◆Concept Application 4 — real-gas pressure

For a van der Waals gas, P = nRT/(V−nb) − an²/V². Verify that P is a state function of V and T.

Solution

The dV coefficient is −nRT/(V−nb)² + 2an²/V³, and the dT coefficient is nR/(V−nb). Differentiating the first with respect to T and the second with respect to V gives the same result, −nR/(V−nb)². Hence dP is exact.

◆Concept Application 5 — path work

A gas goes from A(P₁,V₁) to B(P₂,V₂). Compare work for path I: isobaric expansion at P₁ followed by isochoric pressure change, and path II: isochoric pressure change followed by isobaric expansion at P₂.

Solution

Using the chemistry convention, wI = −P₁(V₂−V₁) and wII = −P₂(V₂−V₁). If P₁ ≠ P₂, the works differ although the endpoints are identical. Work is therefore a path function.

◆Concept Application 6 — cyclic reasoning

A system completes a cycle. Which statements are necessarily true: ΔU = 0, q = 0, w = 0, and q + w = 0?

Solution

Because U is a state function and the final state equals the initial state, ΔU = 0. From the First Law, q + w = 0 over the full cycle. However, q and w need not individually be zero.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Exact differentials remember endpoints; inexact differentials remember routes

PART 03 COMPLETE

State function

defined at equilibrium states

Path function

defined during a process

Exact test

cross partial derivatives agree

Cycle

∮dΦ = 0 for a state function

Integrated Enrichment

Thermodynamic Processes — Extended Applications

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Reversible work is the theoretical maximum and minimum

For expansion: |w_rev| > |w_irrev| — a reversible engine does the most work. For compression: |w_rev| < |w_irrev| — a reversible compressor requires the least work. Irreversibility always moves toward the unfavourable direction.

Connects → Connects to: second law, Carnot efficiency, Part 14–15.

Adiabatic processes in atmospheric science

Rising air in the troposphere expands adiabatically and cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate (≈9.8 K km⁻¹). When it cools below the dew point, condensation releases latent heat, reducing the rate to the saturated lapse rate (≈5–6 K km⁻¹).

Connects → Connects to: Cp, Cv, adiabatic index γ.

Free expansion: the purest test of the ideal-gas model

In Joule's free expansion, a gas expands into a vacuum (w = 0, q = 0, ΔU = 0). For a real gas, ΔT ≠ 0 because intermolecular potential energy changes. For an ideal gas, ΔT = 0 exactly.

Connects → Connects to: Joule coefficient, Joule–Thomson, Part 25.

PART 04 / 30Foundations & the Language of ThermodynamicsThermodynamic Processes, Reversibility, Equilibrium, and Graph Intelligence
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYPROCESS ANIMATION EDITION

Thermodynamics • Process Layer

A process is a path through state space

Isothermal, isobaric, isochoric and adiabatic processes impose different constraints. Reversibility asks a deeper question: can an infinitesimal change retrace the path while restoring both the system and the surroundings?

Three questions for every process

Constraint

Which state variable is fixed?

Boundary

Can heat, work, or matter cross?

Reversibility

Are all gradients infinitesimal and dissipations absent?

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Thermodynamic process

A process changes the system from an initial equilibrium state to a final equilibrium state.

A thermodynamic process is described by the path followed in state space and by the boundary interactions that occur along that path. The same endpoints can be connected by different constraints, producing different heat and work even though every state-function change remains the same.

Concept lens

A named process specifies a constraint—not a complete heat–work answer

“Isothermal” tells us that temperature remains constant. It does not by itself tell us whether the process is reversible, whether expansion occurs into vacuum, or how much work is performed. Those details require the path and surroundings.
02

Isothermal, isobaric and isochoric processes

ISOTHERM

Isothermal process

T = constant
dT = 0 and ΔT = 0

Temperature remains constant throughout the process. Heat may enter or leave to compensate for work or other energy changes.

Examples

  • ◆Very slow gas expansion while in contact with a large thermal reservoir
  • ◆Idealised compression using a conducting cylinder immersed in a constant-temperature bath

ISOBAR

Isobaric process

P = constant
dP = 0 and ΔP = 0

Pressure remains constant while temperature and volume may change. Constant atmospheric pressure is a common approximation, but openness is not required.

Examples

  • ◆Heating a gas beneath a freely moving weighted piston
  • ◆Boiling water in an open vessel at approximately constant atmospheric pressure
  • ◆Melting wax exposed to a nearly constant external pressure

ISOCHORE

Isochoric process

V = constant
dV = 0 and ΔV = 0

Volume remains constant. For a rigid closed vessel, pressure and temperature may change while pressure–volume boundary work is zero.

Examples

  • ◆Heating gas in a rigid sealed steel vessel
  • ◆Cooling a fixed quantity of gas in a rigid bulb

Isothermal control

Adiabatic isolation

Concept lens

Isothermal does not mean adiabatic

Isothermal control often requires heat transfer. Adiabatic isolation prohibits heat transfer and therefore commonly allows temperature to change. A process can be both isothermal and adiabatic only in special cases, such as ideal-gas free expansion with ΔU = 0, not as a general identity.
03

Adiabatic process

Defining condition

q = 0

An adiabatic process occurs through a boundary that permits no heat transfer during the process. Energy may still cross as work, and the system temperature may change.

Concept lens

Reversible adiabatic

The system remains arbitrarily close to equilibrium and no entropy is generated. For a closed simple compressible system, the process is isentropic.

Concept lens

Irreversible adiabatic

Heat transfer remains zero, but friction, free expansion, finite pressure differences or viscosity can generate entropy. Adiabatic therefore does not automatically mean isentropic.

Preview relation

PVγ = constant

This relation applies to a reversible adiabatic change of an ideal gas with appropriate heat-capacity assumptions. Its complete derivation will appear in the process-calculation module.

04

Cyclic process

A cyclic process returns the system to its initial state after two or more legs. Every state function therefore has zero net change over the full cycle:

State-function closure

ΔP = ΔV = ΔT = ΔU = ΔH = ΔS = ΔG = 0

Heat and work are path functions and can have non-zero net values. On a pressure–volume graph, the magnitude of net pressure–volume work equals the enclosed area.

Chemistry sign convention: clockwise

wcycle < 0

Chemistry sign convention: anticlockwise

wcycle > 0

Concept lens

Cycle does not mean q = w = 0

Only state-function changes vanish. With ΔUcycle = 0, the First Law gives qcycle = −wcycle.
05

Isoenthalpic and isentropic processes

ISENTHALPIC

Isoenthalpic process

H = constant
dH = 0 and ΔH = 0

Enthalpy remains constant. Throttling through a porous plug or valve is the standard engineering model, discussed fully with Joule–Thomson behaviour in the appropriate advanced section.

Examples

  • ◆Steady throttling through an insulated valve under negligible kinetic and potential energy changes

ISENTROPE

Isentropic process

S = constant
dS = 0 and ΔS = 0

Entropy remains constant. A reversible adiabatic process of a closed simple system is isentropic, but a generic adiabatic process need not be.

Examples

  • ◆Ideal reversible adiabatic compression in a frictionless piston
  • ◆Idealised turbine or compressor stage with negligible entropy generation

Concept lens

A cyclic process is not generally isentropic at every instant

The total entropy change of the system over a complete cycle is zero because the final state equals the initial state. Individual legs may nevertheless have non-zero entropy changes. “Net ΔS = 0” is not the same as “S remains constant throughout.”
06

Reversible and irreversible processes

Reversibility is a limiting ideal defined by complete restoration of system and surroundings.

REVERSIBLE LIMIT
  • • Driving and opposing forces differ infinitesimally.
  • • The direction can be reversed by an infinitesimal change.
  • • System passes through a continuous sequence of equilibrium states.
  • • No friction, viscosity, finite temperature gradient or other dissipation.
  • • Produces maximum expansion work or requires minimum compression work between fixed states.
  • • Takes an idealised infinite time in the strict limit.
IRREVERSIBLE REALITY
  • • Finite driving force produces a definite rate.
  • • Reversing one external control does not restore all surroundings.
  • • Intermediate pressure, temperature or composition may be non-uniform.
  • • Friction, mixing, free expansion, diffusion and heat flow across finite ΔT generate entropy.
  • • Gives less expansion work than the reversible limit for fixed endpoints.
  • • All real finite-rate processes are irreversible to some degree.

Concept lens

The reversibility test includes the surroundings

A movie played backward is not sufficient. After the reverse process, there must be no net change anywhere: not in the system, weights, reservoirs, atmosphere or any other part of the surroundings.
07

Quasi-static process

A quasi-static process proceeds slowly enough that the system remains arbitrarily close to internal equilibrium. Pressure, temperature and other state variables remain meaningful throughout the path.

Mechanical quasi-static limit

|P − Pext| → 0

Concept lens

Necessary for mechanical reversibility

A reversible piston process must be quasi-static so that no finite pressure imbalance develops.

Concept lens

Not sufficient for reversibility

A piston can move extremely slowly while friction converts work into internal energy. Such a process is quasi-static but irreversible.

During a strongly irreversible process, the equilibrium equation of state can be used reliably at the initial and final equilibrium states. A single uniform bulk pressure or temperature may not exist throughout the intermediate non-equilibrium state.

08

Thermodynamic equilibrium

A system is in complete thermodynamic equilibrium only when every relevant spontaneous macroscopic change has ceased. Thermal, mechanical and material equilibrium must coexist.

uniform temperature

Thermal equilibrium

T

no internal heat flow

balanced pressure and forces

Mechanical equilibrium

P

no unbalanced macroscopic motion

no net phase conversion

Phase equilibrium

μᵅ = μᵝ

no net transfer between phases

no net reaction progress

Chemical equilibrium

A = 0

composition no longer changes with time

Concept lens

Material equilibrium has two parts

Phase equilibrium requires no net transfer between phases. Chemical equilibrium requires no net reaction progress. A system may satisfy one without satisfying the other.

Concept lens

Equilibrium with surroundings versus internal equilibrium

A system can be internally uniform yet not be in equilibrium with its surroundings. A gas under a piston may have uniform internal pressure while P differs slightly from Pext and the piston moves quasi-statically.
09

Scientific statements corrected for Advanced concept accuracy

StatementVerdictScientifically correct form
“A reversible process means state variables do not change.”IncorrectState variables generally change continuously during a reversible process; they remain well-defined at every stage.
“Every quasi-static process is reversible.”IncorrectQuasi-static motion is necessary but not sufficient. Friction, viscosity, electrical resistance, or finite thermal gradients destroy reversibility.
“Every adiabatic process is isentropic.”IncorrectOnly a reversible adiabatic process is isentropic for a closed simple system.
“Every isobaric process is an open-system process.”IncorrectA closed weighted-piston system can also undergo a constant-pressure process.
“A reversible process simply runs backward.”IncompleteThe reverse must restore both system and surroundings with no net change anywhere.
“An irreversible path consists of no states.”RefineIts initial and final equilibrium states are defined, but intermediate bulk variables may be non-uniform and a single equilibrium path may not exist.
10

Graph intelligence from the chapter sequence

Convert process labels between P–V, T–V and P–T representations.

P–V plane

Isobar: horizontal. Isochore: vertical. Ideal-gas isotherm: rectangular hyperbola.

T–V plane

Isotherm: horizontal. Isochore: vertical. Ideal-gas isobar: straight line through the origin in kelvin variables.

P–T plane

Isobar: horizontal. Isotherm: vertical. Ideal-gas isochore: straight line through the origin in kelvin variables.

Concept lens

Conversion algorithm

For each leg, write the invariant first. Then use PV = nRT only when the system is an ideal gas in equilibrium. Translate the invariant into the requested axes before sketching direction arrows.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Zeroth Law and the definition of temperature

StatementIf A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is also in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
ConsequenceThere exists a property called temperature T such that T_A = T_C and T_B = T_C imply T_A = T_B.
Empirical scaleT/K = 273.15 + θ/°C (by definition for ideal-gas scale)
Thermometer basisany measurable property that changes monotonically with T can define an empirical temperature scale

Derivation 2

Conditions for mechanical and thermal equilibrium

Mechanical equilibriumP_system = P_surroundings (no unbalanced pressure forces)
Thermal equilibriumT_system = T_surroundings (no net heat flow)
Chemical equilibriumμᵢ,system = μᵢ,surroundings for all species i
Thermodynamic equilibriumall three conditions satisfied simultaneously
11

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Graph Intelligence 1 — T–V to P–V conversion

For one mole of an ideal gas, A→B is isobaric on a T–V graph, B→C is isochoric, and C→A is isothermal. Describe the corresponding P–V paths.

Solution

A→B becomes a horizontal line on P–V because pressure is constant. B→C becomes a vertical line because volume is constant. C→A lies on an isotherm PV = constant. The exact orientation depends on the labelled endpoint values.

◆Graph Intelligence 2 — six-step cycle

A→B is isobaric expansion, B→C reversible adiabatic expansion, C→D isochoric cooling, D→E isobaric compression, E→F reversible adiabatic compression, and F→A isochoric heating. Identify which legs have zero PV work.

Solution

The isochoric legs C→D and F→A have dV = 0, hence pressure–volume work is zero. All expansion or compression legs may involve non-zero PV work.

◆Concept Application 1 — isothermal versus adiabatic

An ideal gas begins from the same state and expands reversibly to the same larger volume by an isothermal path and an adiabatic path. Which final pressure is larger?

Solution

The isothermal final pressure is larger. During adiabatic expansion the gas cools, so pressure falls more rapidly; the reversible adiabat is steeper than the isotherm on a P–V graph.

◆Concept Application 2 — isentropic trap

Is every adiabatic process isentropic?

Solution

No. An adiabatic reversible process is isentropic. An adiabatic irreversible process produces entropy internally, so the system entropy generally increases even though q = 0.

◆Concept Application 3 — quasi-static with friction

A piston moves extremely slowly but rubs against the cylinder wall. Is the process reversible?

Solution

No. Slow motion may keep the gas close to internal equilibrium, making the process quasi-static, but friction produces entropy and requires a finite force imbalance. Reversing the external conditions does not retrace both system and surroundings exactly.

◆Concept Application 4 — equilibrium subsets

A container has uniform temperature and pressure, but a reaction continues slowly. Is the system in thermodynamic equilibrium?

Solution

No. It has thermal and mechanical equilibrium but lacks chemical equilibrium. Complete thermodynamic equilibrium requires every relevant equilibrium condition simultaneously.

◆Concept Application 5 — cycle signs

A gas traverses a clockwise closed loop on a P–V diagram. What are the signs of net work and net heat using the chemistry convention ΔU = q + w?

Solution

The gas does net work, so wcycle is negative. Since ΔUcycle = 0, qcycle = −wcycle is positive: the gas absorbs net heat over the cycle.

◆Concept Application 6 — constant pressure is not automatically open

Must every isobaric process occur in an open system?

Solution

No. A closed gas beneath a freely moving weighted piston can expand or compress at constant external pressure without any mass transfer. Open vessels often realise approximately constant atmospheric pressure, but openness is not the defining condition.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Constraint names the process; dissipation decides reversibility

T constant

Isochoric

V constant

Adiabatic

q = 0

Reversible

no entropy production in the ideal limit

PART 05 / 30Foundations & the Language of ThermodynamicsPartial-Derivative Tools and Thermodynamic Response Coefficients
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYRESPONSE COEFFICIENTS

Thermodynamics • Response Layer

How strongly does a system respond?

Thermodynamic response coefficients convert qualitative ideas—expansion, compression, pressure rise— into measurable constrained derivatives.

Read every coefficient in words

α

fractional volume change per kelvin at constant pressure

κT

fractional compression per pascal at constant temperature

(∂P/∂T)V

pressure rise per kelvin at fixed volume

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Partial derivatives as constrained slopes

The subscript tells us which variable is held fixed.

For a fixed-composition single-phase system, any two independent variables may be used to describe the state. If volume is written as V(T,P), then a temperature change and a pressure change influence volume in different constrained directions.

Temperature slope at constant pressure

(∂V/∂T)P

Pressure slope at constant temperature

(∂V/∂P)T

Concept lens

The subscript is part of the quantity

(∂V/∂T)P and (∂V/∂T)S are different response functions. Never suppress the constraint in a thermodynamic derivative.
02

Advanced concept derivative toolkit

Reciprocal rule

(∂x/∂y)z = 1 / (∂y/∂x)z

Reverse the dependent and independent variables while holding the same third variable fixed.

Cyclic rule

(∂x/∂y)z (∂y/∂z)x (∂z/∂x)y = −1

For three mutually related state variables, the cyclic product carries a minus sign.

Chain rule

(∂x/∂y)z = (∂x/∂u)z (∂u/∂y)z

Insert an intermediate variable only when the same constraint is respected throughout.

Total differential

dx = (∂x/∂y)z dy + (∂x/∂z)y dz

Combines independent infinitesimal changes in two variables.

Concept lens

Cyclic rule with P, V and T

The relation (∂P/∂T)V(∂T/∂V)P(∂V/∂P)T = −1 connects directly measurable slopes and generates the coefficient identity used later.
03

Coefficient of isobaric thermal expansion

How much the system expands when heated at constant pressure.

Volume expansion coefficient

α
K⁻¹
α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)P

If α = 2×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, a 1 K rise at constant pressure produces approximately a 2×10⁻⁴ fractional increase in volume.

Typical sign: usually positive; can be negative over special ranges

Small finite temperature interval

ΔV ≈ αVΔT

Fractional form

ΔV/V ≈ αΔT

Concept lens

Linear versus volume expansion

For an isotropic solid, the volume expansion coefficient is approximately three times the linear expansion coefficient for small strains: αV ≈ 3αL.

Concept lens

Water anomaly

Liquid water contracts when heated from 0°C toward 4°C at ordinary pressure, so its effective α is negative over part of this range. Above the density maximum, ordinary positive expansion resumes.
04

Isothermal compressibility

How much volume decreases when pressure rises at constant temperature.

Isothermal compressibility

κT
Pa⁻¹
κT = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)T

The minus sign converts the normally negative slope (∂V/∂P)T into a positive material response coefficient.

Typical sign: positive for mechanically stable ordinary matter

Small finite pressure interval

ΔV ≈ −κTVΔP

Bulk modulus

BT = 1/κT

Concept lens

Gases, liquids and solids

Gases are highly compressible, liquids much less so, and solids generally least compressible. “Incompressible liquid” is a useful approximation, not an exact physical truth.

Concept lens

Mechanical stability

Stable matter normally satisfies (∂V/∂P)T < 0, hence κT > 0. A negative isothermal compressibility would signal instability under ordinary equilibrium conditions.
05

Thermal pressure coefficient

How pressure changes with temperature when volume is fixed.

Unnormalised thermal pressure coefficient

(∂P/∂T)V
Pa K⁻¹
(∂P/∂T)V

In a rigid vessel, heating increases molecular momentum transfer to the walls and therefore raises pressure.

Typical sign: usually positive

Normalised pressure coefficient

β
K⁻¹
β = (1/P)(∂P/∂T)V

Some books use β or another symbol for the normalised pressure response. Always state the convention before using it.

Typical sign: usually positive

Concept lens

Notation warning

Different books use β, γ or other symbols for pressure coefficients, and β is also used elsewhere for thermal expansion or reciprocal temperature. Definitions—not symbols—must control the solution.
06

Relationship among α, κT and thermal pressure response

Begin with the cyclic derivative identity for P, V and T:

Cyclic relation

(∂V/∂T)P(∂T/∂P)V(∂P/∂V)T = −1

Using the reciprocal rule and the definitions of α and κT:

Key relation

(∂P/∂T)V = α/κT

Normalised form

β = α/(PκT)

Concept lens

Dimensional check

α/κT has dimensions K⁻¹ ÷ Pa⁻¹ = Pa K⁻¹, exactly matching (∂P/∂T)V.
07

Master differential for volume

Thermal expansion and mechanical compression combine in one equation.

For V = V(T,P),

Total differential

dV = (∂V/∂T)PdT + (∂V/∂P)TdP

Substitute the coefficient definitions:

Response-coefficient form

dV = αVdT − κTVdP

Fractional differential

dV/V = αdT − κTdP

Small finite change

ΔV/V ≈ αΔT − κTΔP

Concept lens

Competing effects

Heating tends to expand ordinary matter, while pressure tends to compress it. A process can be designed so the two contributions cancel and volume remains constant.
08

Density response

For fixed mass, ρ = m/V. Therefore:

Differential density response

dρ/ρ = −dV/V = −αdT + κTdP

Concept lens

Heating at constant pressure

When α > 0, density decreases as temperature increases.

Concept lens

Compression at constant temperature

When κT > 0, density increases as pressure increases.
09

Ideal-gas values

Ideal-gas equation

V = nRT/P

Expansion coefficient

α = 1/T

Compressibility

κT = 1/P

Thermal pressure slope

(∂P/∂T)V = P/T

Normalised pressure coefficient

β = 1/T

Concept lens

Use absolute temperature

The relations α = 1/T and β = 1/T require T in kelvin. Celsius temperature is not admissible in these ratios.
10

Real-gas coefficient strategy

Use implicit differentiation instead of solving the equation of state for volume.

General equation of state

F(P,V,T) = 0

At constant pressure

(∂V/∂T)P = −(∂F/∂T)V,P / (∂F/∂V)T,P

At constant temperature

(∂V/∂P)T = −(∂F/∂P)V,T / (∂F/∂V)P,T

van der Waals pressure form

P = nRT/(V−nb) − an²/V²

Concept lens

Why implicit differentiation is powerful

Real-gas equations may be cubic in volume. The response coefficients can still be obtained directly from derivative ratios without explicitly solving the cubic equation.
11

Few-second coefficient animations

Thermal expansion

Isothermal compression

Thermal pressure

12

Thermodynamics around you

Railway tracks and bridges

Expansion joints prevent thermal stress when solids expand during hot weather. The relevant response is quantified by a thermal expansion coefficient.

Deep-sea instruments

Large external pressure slightly reduces the volume of liquids and solids and strongly affects trapped gases. Compressibility determines the magnitude.

Rigid aerosol can in sunlight

When volume is approximately fixed, heating raises pressure. The thermal pressure coefficient quantifies the sensitivity.

Mercury thermometer

The liquid volume changes more strongly with temperature than the glass envelope, producing a measurable column rise.

13

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Omitting the minus sign in κTWrongFor ordinary matter, increasing pressure decreases volume. The minus sign makes κT positive.
Calling (∂P/∂T)V and (1/P)(∂P/∂T)V the same coefficientAmbiguousState the convention. The first has unit Pa K⁻¹; the normalised coefficient has unit K⁻¹.
Using Celsius temperature in α = 1/T for an ideal gasWrongThermodynamic temperature must be in kelvin.
Treating α and κT as constants over every rangeWrongThey generally depend on temperature, pressure, composition, and phase.
Assuming every substance has α > 0WrongNegative thermal expansion can occur over limited ranges.
Writing dV/V = αdT + κTdPWrong signCompression lowers volume, so the pressure term is −κTdP.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Chain rule and cyclic relation for partial derivatives

Two-variable functionz = f(x, y): dz = (∂z/∂x)_y dx + (∂z/∂y)_x dy
At constant z0 = (∂z/∂x)_y dx + (∂z/∂y)_x dy
Divide by dx at constant z(∂x/∂y)_z = −(∂z/∂x)_y⁻¹ · (∂z/∂y)_x
Cyclic relation(∂x/∂y)_z · (∂y/∂z)_x · (∂z/∂x)_y = −1
Application to PVT(∂P/∂V)_T · (∂V/∂T)_P · (∂T/∂P)_V = −1

Derivation 2

Exact differential test (Euler reciprocity)

Exact formdz = M(x,y) dx + N(x,y) dy is exact if (∂M/∂y)_x = (∂N/∂x)_y
First Law checkdU = T dS − P dV: test (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V ✓
Inexact differentialsδq and δw individually are NOT exact — they depend on path
Combinationbut dU = δq + δw IS exact — it is path-independent
14

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — ideal-gas coefficients

For an ideal gas, obtain α, κT, (∂P/∂T)V, and the normalised pressure coefficient β = (1/P)(∂P/∂T)V.

Solution

From V = nRT/P, α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)P = 1/T and κT = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)T = 1/P. Also P = nRT/V gives (∂P/∂T)V = P/T. Therefore β = 1/T.

◆Concept Application 2 — relation among coefficients

Prove that (∂P/∂T)V = α/κT.

Solution

Use the cyclic relation (∂V/∂T)P(∂T/∂P)V(∂P/∂V)T = −1. Replace (∂V/∂T)P by αV and (∂V/∂P)T by −κTV, then use reciprocal derivatives. The result is (∂P/∂T)V = α/κT.

◆Concept Application 3 — small simultaneous changes

A material has α = 2.0×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and κT = 4.0×10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹. Estimate ΔV/V for ΔT = +25 K and ΔP = +5.0 MPa.

Solution

Use ΔV/V ≈ αΔT − κTΔP. The thermal contribution is 5.0×10⁻³. The compression contribution is 2.0×10⁻³. Hence ΔV/V ≈ 3.0×10⁻³, a net increase of 0.30%.

◆Concept Application 4 — density response

For a fixed mass, derive the differential change in density with T and P.

Solution

Since ρ = m/V and m is fixed, dρ/ρ = −dV/V. Substituting dV/V = αdT − κTdP gives dρ/ρ = −αdT + κTdP.

◆Concept Application 5 — van der Waals α

For P = nRT/(V−nb) − an²/V², write α in derivative form without solving explicitly for V.

Solution

At constant P, dP = (∂P/∂T)V dT + (∂P/∂V)T dV = 0. Thus (∂V/∂T)P = −(∂P/∂T)V/(∂P/∂V)T. Therefore α = −(1/V)[nR/(V−nb)]/[−nRT/(V−nb)² + 2an²/V³].

◆Concept Application 6 — coefficient dimensions

Determine the SI dimensions of α, κT, and (∂P/∂T)V.

Solution

α has unit K⁻¹. κT has unit Pa⁻¹. The unnormalised thermal pressure derivative (∂P/∂T)V has unit Pa K⁻¹. The normalised pressure coefficient β has unit K⁻¹.

◆Concept Application 7 — incompressible approximation

What does κT → 0 imply, and why must it be treated as an approximation rather than an exact property of real matter?

Solution

It implies negligible fractional volume change with pressure. Real solids and liquids still compress slightly, so κT is small but not exactly zero. Exact zero compressibility would require infinite bulk modulus.

◆Concept Application 8 — negative thermal expansion

Can α be negative? Interpret physically.

Solution

Yes. Negative α means volume decreases when temperature rises at constant pressure over the specified range. This occurs in special materials and in liquid water over part of the 0–4°C interval because structural rearrangement dominates ordinary thermal expansion.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Response coefficients are constrained fractional slopes

α

thermal expansion at constant P

κT

compression at constant T

α/κT

pressure rise per kelvin at constant V

dV/V

αdT − κT dP

PART 06 / 30Foundations & the Language of ThermodynamicsInternal Energy, Molecular Energy Modes, and Ideal/Real-Gas Dependence
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYMOLECULAR ENERGY EDITION

Thermodynamics • Energy Layer

Internal energy is the microscopic energy ledger

A system may translate, rise, fall or accelerate as a whole. Internal energy records something different: the sum of microscopic kinetic and potential energies within the selected matter.

Master separation

Inside the molecular ledger

translation, rotation, vibration, interaction and electronic energy

Outside U

motion and external potential energy of the system as a whole

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Total energy and internal energy

The chosen frame of reference separates bulk motion from microscopic energy.

The total energy assigned to a system can be separated into internal energy, macroscopic kinetic energy and potential energy associated with external fields such as gravity.

Energy decomposition

E = U + KEmacroscopic + PEexternal

Concept lens

Why a gas in an aeroplane does not gain U merely because the aeroplane moves

Relative to the ground, the entire vessel has macroscopic kinetic energy. Internal energy is evaluated in a frame moving with the vessel, so uniform centre-of-mass motion is not counted inside U.

Concept lens

Ordinary thermodynamic simplification

For a stationary system with no changing external-field contribution, macroscopic kinetic and external potential-energy changes vanish. The energy change of interest is then ΔE = ΔU.
02

What internal energy contains

U is the sum of microscopic kinetic and microscopic potential energies.

Microscopic energy inventory

U = Utrans + Urot + Uvib + Uinter + Uelec + Unuc + …

Mode 1

Translational

motion of molecular centres of mass

present in gases, liquids and solids

Mode 2

Rotational

rotation of molecules about molecular axes

important for molecules

Mode 3

Vibrational

bond stretching and bending

temperature-dependent quantum excitation

Mode 4

Intermolecular potential

attraction and repulsion among particles

absent in the ideal-gas model

Mode 5

Electronic

electronic configurations and bonding

changes strongly in reactions or excitation

Mode 6

Nuclear

energy associated with nuclei

normally unchanged in chemical thermodynamics

Concept lens

Chemical thermodynamics rarely changes nuclear energy

Nuclear contributions are part of the full microscopic inventory, but ordinary chemical and physical processes leave nuclei unchanged. They therefore cancel from most ΔU calculations.
03

Internal energy is an extensive state function

State-function change

ΔU = Ufinal − Uinitial

Extensivity

U(λn,T,V scaled consistently) = λU(n,T,V)

Internal energy has a definite value for each equilibrium state, although thermodynamics normally cannot determine an absolute zero of U experimentally. What is measurable and useful is the difference ΔU.

Concept lens

Reverse process

If ΔU(A→B) = +X, then ΔU(B→A) = −X.

Concept lens

Molar internal energy

U is extensive, but Um = U/n is intensive.
04

Factors affecting internal energy

Amount of matter

U ∝ n

Internal energy is extensive. Doubling an identical system doubles U.

Physical state

Usolid, Uliquid, Ugas differ

Different structures and intermolecular separations produce different microscopic energies.

Temperature

higher T usually raises U

Thermal excitation increases accessible translational, rotational and vibrational energy.

Volume or pressure

important for real gases

Changing separation alters intermolecular potential energy even at fixed temperature.

Composition

U = U(T,V,{ni})

Changing chemical identity or amount changes the microscopic energy inventory.

External fields

electric / magnetic coupling

Polarisation or magnetisation can add field-dependent contributions when relevant.

Concept lens

State versus process

Amount, state, temperature, volume, pressure and composition determine U through the equilibrium state. Heat and work determine how energy crosses the boundary during a process, but are not arguments that define a stored equilibrium property.
05

Ideal gas: Joule’s law

For a fixed-composition ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature.

In the ideal-gas model, intermolecular attraction and repulsion are neglected except for perfectly elastic collisions. Therefore the interaction potential-energy contribution does not vary with volume.

Joule’s law

Uideal gas = U(T)

Equivalent derivative

(∂U/∂V)T = 0

General differential for ideal gas

dU = (∂U/∂T)VdT

Concept lens

Isothermal ideal-gas process

ΔT = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0, regardless of whether the path is reversible, irreversible or free expansion.

Concept lens

Not only monatomic gases

The relation U = U(T) applies to any ideal gas of fixed composition. The specific function of temperature depends on active molecular degrees of freedom.

The familiar expression U = (3/2)nRT applies to a monatomic ideal gas in the classical temperature range. It must not be used blindly for diatomic or polyatomic gases.

06

Real gas: temperature and volume both matter

Intermolecular separation changes microscopic potential energy.

General dependence

Ureal gas = U(T,V) or equivalently U(T,P)

Total differential

dU = (∂U/∂T)VdT + (∂U/∂V)TdV

Concept lens

Isothermal does not guarantee ΔU = 0 for a real gas

When temperature is fixed but volume changes, intermolecular potential energy can change. Thus the second term in dU may remain non-zero.
07

Advanced concept identity for volume dependence

A measurable pressure derivative reveals how U changes with volume.

General closed simple system identity

(∂U/∂V)T = T(∂P/∂T)V − P

van der Waals equation

P = nRT/(V−nb) − an²/V²

Evaluate the derivative

T(∂P/∂T)V − P = an²/V²

At constant temperature

dU = (an²/V²)dV

Integrated volume dependence

U(T,V) = f(T) − an²/V

Concept lens

Physical meaning

Attractive intermolecular potential energy is negative. Increasing volume weakens the attraction and makes the potential energy less negative, so U rises during isothermal expansion of a van der Waals gas.

Concept lens

Hard-sphere insight

A gas obeying P(V−nb) = nRT has excluded-volume nonideality but no attractive-energy term. For this model, T(∂P/∂T)V − P = 0, so U still depends only on T.
08

Internal energy versus temperature

At constant volume, the temperature slope of internal energy defines the constant-volume heat-capacity property:

Slope of U against T

(∂U/∂T)V = CV

Therefore, for a fixed-composition ideal gas:

Finite temperature change

ΔU = ∫T₁T₂ CV(T)dT

Concept lens

Boundary with Thermochemistry notes

This relation is retained because it is essential for internal-energy calculations. Detailed heat-capacity theory, molecular activation and calorimetry remain in the separate Thermochemistry note set.
09

Thermodynamics around you

Ice cream cools the mouth

Energy leaves the warmer mouth and enters the colder ice cream. The mouth’s internal energy falls while the ice cream warms and melts.

Bicycle pump becomes warm

Work done on the trapped gas raises its internal energy. Rapid compression leaves little time for the energy to escape as heat.

Water warms at a waterfall base

Gravitational potential energy lost during descent ultimately appears partly as microscopic internal energy through turbulence and dissipation.

A moving gas cylinder

Placing a sealed gas cylinder in a moving vehicle changes the cylinder’s macroscopic kinetic energy, but not its internal energy merely because of uniform translational motion.

10

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Internal energy is the kinetic energy of the whole moving system.IncorrectMacroscopic centre-of-mass kinetic energy is excluded from U.
The absolute internal energy can be measured directly.IncorrectThermodynamics normally determines differences ΔU, not a unique absolute U.
For every gas, isothermal means ΔU = 0.IncorrectThis is guaranteed for an ideal gas of fixed composition, not for a general real gas.
Potential energy is zero for every ideal-gas molecule.RefineIntermolecular potential energy is taken as zero in the ideal-gas model; internal molecular and electronic energies may still exist.
Internal energy contains heat.IncorrectHeat is energy in transit across the boundary. After transfer, the system possesses internal energy.
If a system is stationary, its total energy must be zero.IncorrectStationarity only removes macroscopic kinetic energy; internal energy remains.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

First Law derivation for a closed system

Empirical statementEnergy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted.
Formal statementΔU = q + w (chemistry sign convention: q > 0 absorbed, w > 0 done ON system)
Differential formdU = δq + δw
For PV work onlyδw = −P_ext dV
Reversible limitδw_rev = −P dV → dU = δq_rev − P dV
Combined with entropyδq_rev = T dS → dU = T dS − P dV (fundamental relation)

Derivation 2

Isothermal expansion of ideal gas: ΔU = 0

Joule's experimentfree expansion into vacuum: w = 0, q = 0 → ΔU = 0
Joule coefficient(∂U/∂V)_T = 0 for an ideal gas (no intermolecular forces)
Proof from kinetic theoryU = U_kinetic only = (f/2)nRT → U depends only on T
Consequenceany isothermal process on ideal gas: ΔU = 0 → q = −w
11

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — frame-of-reference trap

A sealed vessel containing gas is carried from rest to a train moving at constant speed. Does the gas internal energy necessarily increase?

Solution

No. The macroscopic kinetic energy of the vessel–gas system changes relative to the ground, but internal energy is measured relative to the system’s centre-of-mass frame. Uniform translation alone does not change U.

◆Concept Application 2 — reverse path

A fixed amount of a substance changes from state A to state B with ΔU = +6.4 kJ. What is ΔU for the exact reverse change?

Solution

Because U is a state function, ΔU(B→A) = UA − UB = −6.4 kJ.

◆Concept Application 3 — ideal-gas isothermal change

Two moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally from 4.0 L to 12.0 L. Find ΔU without calculating q or w.

Solution

For a fixed-composition ideal gas, U depends only on T. Since the process is isothermal, ΔT = 0 and therefore ΔU = 0.

◆Concept Application 4 — real-gas isothermal change

For a van der Waals gas, derive ΔU when n moles expand isothermally from V₁ to V₂.

Solution

Using U(T,V) = f(T) − an²/V, ΔU = an²(1/V₁ − 1/V₂). For expansion V₂ > V₁, ΔU is positive.

◆Concept Application 5 — hard-sphere model

A non-ideal gas obeys P(V−nb) = nRT but has no attractive term. Show whether U depends on V at fixed T.

Solution

Here (∂P/∂T)V = nR/(V−nb), so T(∂P/∂T)V − P = 0. Therefore (∂U/∂V)T = 0 and U = U(T), despite excluded-volume nonideality.

◆Concept Application 6 — total versus internal energy

A thermally insulated rigid box falls freely. During the fall, how do the total energy components change relative to Earth?

Solution

External gravitational potential energy decreases and macroscopic kinetic energy increases. In ideal free fall without dissipation, internal energy remains essentially unchanged. On impact, macroscopic kinetic energy can convert into internal energy.

◆Concept Application 7 — differential form

For a real gas U = U(T,V), write the most general infinitesimal change and identify the ideal-gas simplification.

Solution

dU = (∂U/∂T)V dT + (∂U/∂V)T dV. For an ideal gas, the second derivative is zero, so dU = (∂U/∂T)V dT.

◆Concept Application 8 — extensivity

Two identical non-interacting gas samples at the same T and V per sample are combined. What happens to total U and molar U?

Solution

Total U doubles because internal energy is extensive. Molar internal energy Um = U/n remains unchanged because it is intensive.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Ideal-gas U remembers temperature; real-gas U can remember separation

PART 06 COMPLETE

U

microscopic kinetic + potential energies

State function

ΔU = Uf − Ui

Ideal gas

U = U(T)

Real gas

U = U(T,V) in general
