PART 07 / 30Work, Heat & the First LawThermodynamic Work, Sign Conventions, and Pressure–Volume Work
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYWORK & SIGN CONVENTION

Thermodynamics • Transfer Layer

Work is energy transferred through organised motion

Pressure moving a piston, voltage moving charge, tension stretching a surface and gravity lifting a mass are different expressions of one thermodynamic pattern: an intensity factor acting through a capacity change.

Chemistry convention

Work done on system

w > 0

Work done by system

w < 0

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Thermodynamic meaning of work

Work is a mode of energy transfer, not a property possessed by a state.

Thermodynamic work is energy transferred across the boundary when a generalised force produces a coordinated displacement. In pressure–volume work, a piston moves coherently; in electrical work, charge moves through an electrical potential difference.

Concept lens

Work is transitory

Work exists only while a process occurs. State A and state B have energies, but neither state contains a quantity called “work.”

Concept lens

Work is path dependent

Different external-pressure histories between the same endpoint states can transfer different amounts of work.

Concept lens

Microscopic distinction from heat

Work transfers energy through coordinated motion. Heat transfers energy because of a temperature difference through disordered microscopic interactions. Both alter energy, but by different boundary mechanisms.
02

Generalised force–displacement structure

Every common work mode pairs an intensity factor with a capacity change.

General pattern

δw = intensity factor × differential capacity factor

Pressure–volume work

Intensity factor:external pressure Pext
Capacity factor:volume change dV
δw = −Pext dV

gas moving a piston

Electrical work

Intensity factor:electrical potential φ
Capacity factor:charge transfer dq
δw = φ dq

charging a cell or capacitor

Gravitational work

Intensity factor:gravitational field / mg
Capacity factor:height change dh
δw = mg dh

raising a mass

Surface work

Intensity factor:surface tension γ
Capacity factor:surface-area change dA
δw = γ dA

stretching a liquid film

Elastic work

Intensity factor:tension or force F
Capacity factor:extension dx
δw = F dx

stretching a spring or polymer

Magnetic work

Intensity factor:magnetic field
Capacity factor:magnetisation change
convention-dependent

magnetising matter

Concept lens

Sign convention belongs to the chosen definition

The algebraic sign of each generalised work term depends on how the generalised force and displacement are defined. For chemistry pressure–volume work, the locked convention is δw = −PextdV.
03

Pressure–volume work: piston derivation

Consider gas beneath a frictionless piston of area A. The surroundings exert an external pressure Pext, producing force Fext = PextA. If the piston moves by dx, the volume changes by dV = A dx.

Infinitesimal pressure–volume work

δw = −PextdV

Finite general path

w = −∫VᵢV𝒇 Pext(V)dV

Concept lens

Why external pressure appears

Work measures the energy transferred against the mechanical resistance supplied by the surroundings. Therefore actual boundary work uses Pext, not automatically the internal gas pressure.
04

Chemistry and physics sign conventions

Chemistry commonly writes the First Law as ΔU = q + w, so work received by the system is positive. Many physics texts instead define Wby as work done by the system and write ΔU = q − Wby. The physical process is identical; only the accounting symbol changes.

CaseVolume relationΔVChemistry wMeaning
ExpansionVf > ViΔV > 0w < 0Energy leaves the system as work
CompressionVf < ViΔV < 0w > 0Energy enters the system as work
Rigid boundaryVf = ViΔV = 0wPV = 0No pressure–volume boundary displacement
Free expansion into vacuumPext = 0ΔV > 0wPV = 0No resisting external pressure

Chemistry convention

won = −∫PextdV

Physics-style work by gas

Wby = +∫PextdV = −won

Concept lens

Never mix equations from opposite conventions

Before solving, identify whether the symbol represents work on the system or work by the system. A correct magnitude with the wrong convention produces a wrong First-Law result.
05

Constant external pressure

Finite pressure–volume work

w = −Pext(Vf − Vi) = −PextΔV

The magnitude equals the rectangular area under the constant external-pressure line on a P–V graph.

Concept lens

Expansion

ΔV > 0 ⇒ w < 0. The gas transfers energy to the surroundings.

Concept lens

Compression

ΔV < 0 ⇒ w > 0. The surroundings transfer energy to the gas.

Concept lens

Rigid boundary

ΔV = 0 ⇒ wPV = 0, even if pressure changes strongly.
06

Variable external pressure and graphical work

Finite-step process

w = −Σ Pext,kΔVk

Continuous external-pressure path

w = −∫ Pext(V)dV

Concept lens

Signed area

The geometric area under a Pext–V curve is positive. Chemistry expansion work is the negative of that area because dV is positive while the leading sign is negative.
07

Reversible and irreversible pressure–volume work

REVERSIBLE LIMIT

During expansion, Pext is infinitesimally below the gas pressure; during compression, infinitesimally above it. At every step, Pext approaches P.

wrev = −∫ P dV
IRREVERSIBLE PATH

A finite pressure difference drives the process. Work must be calculated from the actual external pressure history, which may be constant, stepwise or time-dependent.

wirr = −∫ PextdV

Concept lens

Maximum-work principle for fixed endpoints

Reversible expansion gives the maximum magnitude of work delivered by the system. Reversible compression requires the minimum magnitude of work input. This is a limiting comparison, not a claim that real machines operate reversibly.
08

Free expansion

Vacuum boundary

Pext = 0

Pressure–volume work

wPV = −∫0·dV = 0

Concept lens

Large volume change can still give zero work

Work requires resistance. In expansion into vacuum, no surroundings are displaced against pressure, so pressure–volume work is zero even though the gas spreads into a larger volume.
09

Work units and conversions

Work unitConversion logicSI value
1 Pa m³1 N m1 J
1 bar L10⁵ Pa × 10⁻³ m³100 J
1 L atm101325 Pa × 10⁻³ m³101.325 J
1 calthermochemical calorie4.184 J

Concept lens

Dimensional proof

Pressure × volume = (force/area) × volume = force × length = energy.
10

Total work versus pressure–volume work

The relation −∫PextdV describes only mechanical boundary work caused by volume displacement. The total work may also contain electrical, surface, elastic, gravitational or other non-PV terms.

General energy-transfer decomposition

δwtotal = δwPV + δwelectrical + δwsurface + δwother

Concept lens

Rigid electrochemical cell

A rigid cell has dV = 0 and therefore no PV work, but it can still deliver electrical work to an external circuit.
11

Thermodynamics around you

Bicycle pump

Your hand performs compression work on the trapped gas. Rapid pumping raises internal energy and warms the barrel.

Air leaving a tyre

The expanding gas pushes atmospheric air aside. Energy transfer as work contributes to cooling during rapid discharge.

Charging a battery

Electrical potential drives organised charge transfer across the system boundary: a non-PV work mode.

Soap-film frame

Pulling a movable wire increases surface area against surface tension, transferring energy as surface work.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Work is stored inside a system.IncorrectWork is a boundary transfer during a process. Energy, not work, is associated with a state.
Use the gas pressure in w = −PΔV for every process.IncorrectActual boundary work is determined by Pext. Pint may replace it only in the reversible limit.
Expansion work is positive in chemistry.IncorrectWith ΔU = q + w, expansion gives w < 0 because the system transfers energy to the surroundings.
If ΔV = 0, every kind of work is zero.IncorrectOnly PV work is forced to zero. Electrical, surface, elastic or other non-PV work may remain.
A large internal pressure guarantees large work.IncorrectFree expansion into vacuum has Pext = 0 and therefore zero PV work despite finite gas pressure.
Pressure multiplied by volume has no energy dimension.IncorrectPa·m³ = N·m = J.
Work is intensive because pressure is intensive.IncorrectThe volume displacement is extensive; total work scales with system size for similar paths.
Reversible expansion happens at exactly equal pressure with no driving force.RefineIt is the limiting process with an infinitesimal pressure difference; exact equality would produce no directional motion.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Work done by a gas against varying external pressure

General expressionw = −∫[V₁→V₂] P_ext dV
Free expansionP_ext = 0 → w = 0
Against constant P_extw = −P_ext(V₂ − V₁) = −P_ext ΔV
Reversible isothermalP_ext = P = nRT/V → w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
Maximum work theorem|w_max| = |w_rev| ≥ |w_actual| for any real expansion
Physical meaningreversible work is the upper bound; irreversibility destroys useful work

Derivation 2

Derivation of enthalpy from the First Law at constant pressure

First LawΔU = q_p + w = q_p − P_ext ΔV
At constant PP_ext = P = constant → ΔU = q_p − PΔV
Rearrangeq_p = ΔU + PΔV = ΔU + Δ(PV) (since P constant)
Define HH = U + PV → ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV)
Resultq_p = ΔH (heat at constant pressure equals enthalpy change)
NoteH is a state function; q_p is a path function that equals ΔH only when P is constant
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — constant external pressure

A gas expands from 2.5 L to 7.0 L against a constant external pressure of 1.20 bar. Calculate the chemistry-sign work in joules.

Solution

ΔV = 4.5 L. Hence w = −PextΔV = −(1.20 bar)(4.5 L) = −5.4 bar L = −540 J.

◆Concept Application 2 — compression sign

A gas is compressed from 8.0 L to 3.0 L against 2.0 atm. Determine w in litre-atmosphere and joule.

Solution

ΔV = −5.0 L. Thus w = −(2.0 atm)(−5.0 L) = +10.0 L atm = +1013.25 J. Positive work means energy enters the gas through compression.

◆Concept Application 3 — free expansion

An ideal gas expands into an evacuated chamber from 4 L to 12 L. Find pressure–volume work.

Solution

The opposing external pressure is zero. Therefore wPV = −PextΔV = 0, even though the gas volume increases.

◆Concept Application 4 — two-step expansion

A gas expands from 1.0 L to 3.0 L against 3.0 bar, then from 3.0 L to 5.0 L against 1.0 bar. Find total w.

Solution

w1 = −3.0(2.0) = −6.0 bar L and w2 = −1.0(2.0) = −2.0 bar L. Total w = −8.0 bar L = −800 J.

◆Concept Application 5 — linear external-pressure path

During expansion from V₁ to V₂, external pressure decreases linearly from P₁ to P₂. Obtain w.

Solution

The area under a linear Pext–V path is average pressure times volume change. Thus w = −[(P₁ + P₂)/2](V₂ − V₁).

◆Concept Application 6 — piston and lifted mass

A piston lifts a 12 kg load upward by 0.20 m. Neglect friction. What is the work on the gas due solely to this load during expansion?

Solution

The surroundings gain gravitational potential energy mgh = 12×9.8×0.20 = 23.52 J. The gas loses this energy as work, so chemistry-sign work on the gas is w = −23.52 J.

◆Concept Application 7 — rigid vessel

A reaction in a rigid sealed vessel raises the pressure from 1 bar to 20 bar. Is pressure–volume work necessarily non-zero?

Solution

No. The vessel is rigid, so dV = 0 and wPV = −∫Pext dV = 0. Pressure change alone does not create PV work.

◆Concept Application 8 — system versus surroundings

For a frictionless process, the system has w = −350 J. What is the corresponding work assigned to the surroundings?

Solution

With consistent boundaries and no dissipative storage at the interface, wsurroundings = +350 J. Energy lost by one side as work is gained by the other.

◆Concept Application 9 — reversible ranking

The same gas expands between fixed equilibrium endpoints by free expansion, one-step expansion, many-step expansion and reversible expansion. Rank the magnitude of work done by the gas.

Solution

For expansion, |wby gas| is smallest for free expansion (zero), increases through one-step and multistep paths, and reaches the maximum in the reversible limit.

◆Concept Application 10 — non-PV work

A closed rigid electrochemical cell supplies 500 J of electrical energy to a circuit. Can total work be non-zero although ΔV = 0?

Solution

Yes. Rigid volume makes only PV work zero. Electrical work is a distinct non-PV mode, so the cell can transfer 500 J as electrical work.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

External resistance and boundary displacement determine pressure–volume work

PART 07 COMPLETE

Expansion

ΔV > 0, w < 0

Compression

ΔV < 0, w > 0

Constant Pext

w = −PextΔV

Reversible

w = −∫P dV

PART 08 / 30Work, Heat & the First LawZeroth Law, First Law, and Energy-Balance Architecture
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYLAWS & ENERGY BALANCE

Thermodynamics • Conservation Layer

Temperature makes comparison possible; energy conservation closes the balance

The Zeroth Law gives operational meaning to temperature. The First Law states that heat and work can alter internal energy, but cannot create or destroy the total energy of system plus surroundings.

Locked chemistry convention

Heat enters system

q > 0

Work done on system

w > 0

Energy balance

ΔU = q + w

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics

The logical foundation of temperature comparison and thermometry.

Formal statement

If A is in thermal equilibrium with C and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium.

Concept lens

Temperature is the common property

The law guarantees that a scalar property—temperature—has the same value for systems in mutual thermal equilibrium. This makes thermometers possible.

Concept lens

Why it is called the Zeroth Law

It was articulated after the First and Second Laws, but logically precedes them. The name “zeroth” places it before the First Law in conceptual order.

Concept lens

Thermal equilibrium is dynamic at the microscopic scale

Equal temperatures mean no net heat transfer. Microscopic energy exchanges may still occur in both directions with equal average rates.
02

Thermometer as the third system

A thermometer does not directly reveal an abstract temperature. It uses a calibrated thermometric property—such as liquid-column length, electrical resistance or thermoelectric voltage—that settles to a reproducible value after thermal equilibrium.

Liquid thermometer

Thermometric property: liquid volume or column length.

Resistance thermometer

Thermometric property: electrical resistance.

Gas thermometer

Thermometric property: gas pressure or volume under controlled conditions.

Concept lens

A reading must be allowed to settle

Before equilibrium, the thermometer perturbs the object and its own thermometric property is still changing. A premature reading is not the object’s equilibrium temperature.
03

First Law of Thermodynamics

A conservation principle connecting internal energy, heat and work.

In any physical or chemical process, energy may move between the system and surroundings or transform from one form to another. The total energy of the combined system and surroundings remains constant.

Universe-level conservation

ΔEsystem + ΔEsurroundings = 0

Equivalent statement for an isolated universe

ΔEuniverse = 0

Concept lens

The First Law is more precise than “energy of the system is constant”

A non-isolated system can gain or lose energy. What remains constant is the total energy of system plus surroundings.
04

Deriving ΔU = q + w

Closed system, negligible bulk kinetic and potential-energy changes, chemistry sign convention.

Let the system begin with internal energy U1. Suppose it absorbs heat q and receives work w from its surroundings. The final internal energy is:

Energy ledger

U2 = U1 + q + w

Finite First-Law form

ΔU = U2 − U1 = q + w

Differential form

dU = δq + δw

Concept lens

Exact plus inexact differentials

dU is exact because U is a state function. δq and δw are inexact because their individual values depend on the path. Their sum is constrained to produce the endpoint quantity dU.

Concept lens

Scope of this compact equation

The form ΔU = q + w applies directly to a closed system when changes in macroscopic kinetic and external potential energy are negligible. Open systems require energy carried by matter; moving systems may require additional kinetic and potential-energy terms.
05

Only pressure–volume work

Pressure–volume work

δw = −PextdV

First Law with PV work only

dU = δq − PextdV

Rearranged heat expression

δq = dU + PextdV

Concept lens

Reversible limit

For a reversible process, Pext approaches the system pressure P at every stage, giving dU = δqrev − P dV.
06

Heat and work are equivalent routes to ΔU

An insulated water sample can be warmed by mechanical paddle work or electrical resistance work. Equal energy input can produce the same final temperature and the same internal-energy change, even though the transfer mechanism differs.

Concept lens

Equivalent in energy accounting, not identical microscopically

Heat and work are both measured in joules and can produce the same ΔU, but they represent different modes of transfer. Work is organised; heat is driven by temperature difference.
07

Complete special-case map

Pure heat transfer

w = 0

ΔU = q

Requires no work of any kind, not merely zero PV work.

Adiabatic closed process

q = 0

ΔU = w

Internal energy changes entirely through work transfer.

Rigid closed vessel

dV = 0

wPV = 0

Electrical or other non-PV work may still occur.

Rigid vessel, only PV work allowed

w = 0

ΔU = qV

This is the standard constant-volume relation.

Isolated system

q = 0, w = 0

ΔU = 0

Energy may redistribute internally while total system energy remains fixed.

Cyclic process

final state = initial state

ΔUcycle = 0, qcycle = −wcycle

q and w need not individually vanish.

Isothermal ideal gas

ΔT = 0 and U = U(T)

ΔU = 0, therefore q = −w

Not a universal statement for real gases.

Free expansion of ideal gas in isolation

Pext = 0, q = 0

w = 0, ΔU = 0, ΔT = 0

The process is irreversible despite no temperature change.

08

System–surroundings sign ledger

Transfer viewed from systemSystemSurroundingsCombined change from transfer
Heat entering system+qsys−qsys0
Work done on system+wsys−wsys0
Heat leaving system−qsys+qsys0
Work done by system−wsys+wsys0

Concept lens

Internal consistency check

Every transfer appears with equal magnitude and opposite sign when the boundary is viewed from the other side. This is why system-plus-surroundings energy change from internal transfer is zero.
09

Sign decision tree

Heat q

Heat enters system

q > 0

Heat leaves system

q < 0

Work w

Work done on system

w > 0

Work done by system

w < 0

Fast mental check

ΔU positive means the system finishes with more internal energy than it started.
10

Closed, isolated and open-system energy balances

CLOSED SYSTEM

No matter crosses. Energy may cross as heat or work.

ΔU = q + w
ISOLATED SYSTEM

Neither matter nor energy crosses the external boundary.

q = 0, w = 0, ΔE = 0
OPEN SYSTEM

Matter carries internal, flow, kinetic and potential energy through the boundary.

include mass-flow energy

Concept lens

Why there is no single one-line formula for every situation

The conservation law is universal, but the mathematical balance depends on the selected system, permitted transfers, reference frame, steady or unsteady operation, and whether matter crosses the boundary.
11

What the First Law cannot tell us

It can determine

  • • energy conservation;
  • • relation among ΔU, q and w;
  • • missing energy-transfer terms;
  • • impossibility of a first-kind perpetual-motion machine.

It cannot determine alone

  • • direction of spontaneous change;
  • • maximum conversion of heat into work;
  • • irreversibility;
  • • equilibrium criterion.

Concept lens

The Second Law is still needed

Energy conservation permits many hypothetical processes that nature does not perform spontaneously. Direction and irreversibility require entropy and the Second Law.
12

Thermodynamics around you

Clinical thermometer

A thermometer acts as the third system. A stable reading means thermal equilibrium has been reached.

Bicycle pump

Rapid compression transfers work into the gas. With little time for heat loss, internal energy and temperature rise.

Electric kettle

Electrical work is converted into internal energy of the heating element and water, followed by heat transfer within the device.

Hydroelectric station

Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic, mechanical and electrical energy; losses appear as internal energy, while total energy is conserved.

13

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
The First Law predicts whether a process is spontaneous.IncorrectIt enforces energy conservation but does not determine direction or spontaneity.
ΔU = q + w is the complete formula for every open system.IncorrectMass flow carries energy and requires additional terms in an open-system balance.
If ΔU = 0, then q = 0 and w = 0 separately.IncorrectOnly their sum must vanish; q and w can be non-zero and opposite.
An isolated system cannot undergo any internal change.IncorrectInternal conversions can occur while total energy remains constant.
The Zeroth Law says heat always flows from hot to cold.IncorrectThe Zeroth Law establishes transitivity of thermal equilibrium and the basis of temperature measurement.
At constant volume, total work is always zero.IncorrectOnly PV work is zero. Electrical, shaft or other work may remain.
Heat absorbed always increases internal energy by the same amount.IncorrectPart of the absorbed energy may leave as work; ΔU = q + w.
Energy is conserved separately for the system.IncorrectA non-isolated system may gain or lose energy. Conservation applies to system plus surroundings.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Hess's Law from the state-function nature of enthalpy

State function propertyΔH depends only on initial and final states, not on path
Consequenceany sequence of reactions with the same net change gives the same ΔH
Formal statementΔH_rxn = Σ ΔH°_f(products) − Σ ΔH°_f(reactants)
Algebraic manipulationreactions can be reversed (change sign) and scaled (multiply ΔH)
ExampleC(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g): ΔH°_f = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹
CombinationΔH°_rxn = ΔH°_f[CO₂] − ΔH°_f[C,graphite] − ΔH°_f[O₂] = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹

Derivation 2

Relation between ΔH and ΔU for gas-phase reactions

DefinitionΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV)
Ideal gasPV = nRT → Δ(PV) = Δn_g RT
ResultΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT
Δn_g definitionΔn_g = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants
When Δn_g = 0ΔH = ΔU (e.g., H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0)
14

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — direct First-Law balance

A closed system absorbs 420 J of heat and does 160 J of work on the surroundings. Find ΔU using the chemistry convention.

Solution

q = +420 J. Work done by the system means w = −160 J. Therefore ΔU = q + w = 420 − 160 = +260 J.

◆Concept Application 2 — adiabatic compression

During adiabatic compression, 850 J of work is done on a gas. Find q and ΔU.

Solution

Adiabatic means q = 0. Work done on the gas gives w = +850 J. Hence ΔU = +850 J.

◆Concept Application 3 — rigid vessel

A rigid closed vessel receives 1.40 kJ of heat. No electrical, shaft or other non-PV work occurs. Find ΔU.

Solution

Rigid volume gives wPV = 0, and all other work modes are absent, so w = 0. Therefore ΔU = q = +1.40 kJ.

◆Concept Application 4 — cyclic device

Over one complete cycle, a device does 2.5 kJ of net work on the surroundings. Determine ΔUcycle and qcycle.

Solution

For a cycle, ΔUcycle = 0. Work done by the device gives wcycle = −2.5 kJ. Thus qcycle = +2.5 kJ.

◆Concept Application 5 — heat rejected and work input

A system releases 300 J of heat while 500 J of work is done on it. Find ΔU.

Solution

Heat released gives q = −300 J; work done on the system gives w = +500 J. Therefore ΔU = +200 J.

◆Concept Application 6 — two paths, same endpoints

Path I between A and B has q1 = +900 J and w1 = −250 J. Path II has w2 = +150 J. Find ΔU and q2.

Solution

For path I, ΔU = 900 − 250 = +650 J. The same endpoints require the same ΔU. Thus q2 = ΔU − w2 = 650 − 150 = +500 J.

◆Concept Application 7 — isolated internal conversion

Inside an isolated box, a falling mass stirs a liquid and finally comes to rest. Which energy changes can occur?

Solution

Heat and work do not cross the external boundary, so total energy of the box is constant. Gravitational potential energy of the mass decreases and is converted into kinetic and then internal energy of the contents.

◆Concept Application 8 — open-system caveat

Can ΔU = q + w be applied without modification to a steady-flow turbine through which matter continuously passes?

Solution

Not as the complete steady-flow balance. Matter carries energy across the boundary, commonly represented through enthalpy plus kinetic and potential energy terms. The simple closed-system form omits this mass-flow energy.

◆Concept Application 9 — isothermal ideal gas

An ideal gas absorbs 720 J of heat during an isothermal expansion. Find w and ΔU.

Solution

For an ideal gas, isothermal means ΔU = 0. Hence 0 = q + w, so w = −720 J.

◆Concept Application 10 — thermometer logic

Thermometer C gives the same stable reading when separately placed in contact with bodies A and B. What can be concluded?

Solution

A and C are in thermal equilibrium, and B and C are in thermal equilibrium. By the Zeroth Law, A and B have the same temperature and would be in thermal equilibrium if placed in suitable thermal contact.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Thermal equilibrium defines temperature; energy conservation defines the First-Law balance

thermal equilibrium is transitive

First Law

Isolated

Cycle

Isothermal Ideal-Gas Processes

Constant temperature fixes ideal-gas internal energy, but heat and work remain strongly path dependent.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Ideal-gas energy at constant temperature

Joule law

U = U(T)

Isothermal ideal gas

ΔU = 0

First Law

q = −w

Concept lens

Critical distinction

Isothermal does not mean no heat transfer. Heat may enter or leave while the temperature remains constant.
02

Reversible isothermal expansion

Mechanical equilibrium

Pext = P − dP

Work integral

wrev = −∫V₁V₂ P dV

Ideal-gas substitution

wrev = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁)

Pressure form

wrev = −nRT ln(P₁/P₂)
03

Irreversible one-step expansion

Constant external pressure

wirr = −Pext(V₂−V₁)

Concept lens

Final mechanical equilibrium

In a one-step expansion ending at equilibrium, the chosen constant external pressure commonly equals the final gas pressure.
04

Free expansion

Vacuum

Pext = 0

Work

w = 0

Insulated ideal gas

q = 0, ΔU = 0, ΔT = 0

Concept lens

Irreversible despite zero work

The gas expands spontaneously into available volume and cannot retrace the path through an infinitesimal pressure difference.
05

Multistep approach to reversibility

Replacing one large pressure drop by many smaller pressure drops increases the magnitude of expansion work. In the limiting case of infinitely many infinitesimal steps, the path becomes reversible.

Expansion ranking

|wrev| > |wmultistep| > |wone-step| > 0

Compression ranking

reversible compression requires minimum work input

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Bond enthalpy and its use in estimating ΔH_rxn

DefinitionBond enthalpy = mean enthalpy required to break 1 mol of X–Y bonds in gaseous molecules
Signbond breaking: endothermic (positive ΔH); bond forming: exothermic (negative ΔH)
Estimation formulaΔH°_rxn ≈ Σ D(bonds broken) − Σ D(bonds formed)
All species must be gaseousmust include phase-change enthalpies if reactants or products are not gas
Limitationbond enthalpies are averages; actual bond strengths vary with molecular environment
ExampleH₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g): ΔH = D(H–H) + D(Cl–Cl) − 2D(H–Cl) = 436 + 242 − 2(431) = −184 kJ mol⁻¹

Derivation 2

Born–Haber cycle for lattice enthalpy

TargetNa(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s) ΔH°_f = −411 kJ mol⁻¹
Step 1: atomisation NaNa(s) → Na(g) ΔH°_sub = +108 kJ mol⁻¹
Step 2: dissociation Cl₂½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g) ½D(Cl₂) = +121 kJ mol⁻¹
Step 3: ionisation NaNa(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ IE₁ = +496 kJ mol⁻¹
Step 4: electron affinity ClCl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) EA = −349 kJ mol⁻¹
Step 5: lattice enthalpyNa⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s) U_L = ΔH°_f − (108 + 121 + 496 − 349) = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ mol⁻¹
07

Complete worked examples and applications

Reversible work

Derive the reversible isothermal work of an ideal gas.

wrev = −∫P dV = −nRT∫dV/V = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁).

Pressure form

Express reversible isothermal work using pressures.

Because P1V1=P2V2, wrev=−nRT ln(P₁/P₂).

Free expansion

Find q, w, ΔU and ΔT for ideal-gas free expansion in an insulated container.

Pext=0 gives w=0; q=0; hence ΔU=0 and, for an ideal gas, ΔT=0.

Work ranking

Rank work magnitude for reversible, multistep, one-step and free expansion.

|wrev| > |wmultistep| > |wone-step| > |wfree|=0.

Compression ranking

Which path requires the least work input for isothermal compression?

The reversible path requires the minimum work input magnitude.

Integrated Enrichment

Bond Enthalpy and Ionic Lattice — Extended Understanding

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Why mean bond enthalpies are averages

The C–H bond enthalpy in CH₄ (413 kJ mol⁻¹) differs from that in C₂H₆ or benzene because the electronic environment changes with molecular structure. Tabulated mean bond enthalpies average over many compounds; they give estimates, not exact ΔH values.

Connects → Connects to: molecular orbital theory, chemical bonding.

Madelung constant and the Kapustinskii equation

The lattice enthalpy magnitude is approximately U_L ≈ A M z⁺z⁻ e²/(4πε₀r₀), where A is the Avogadro number, M is the Madelung constant (1.748 for NaCl), and r₀ is the interionic distance. Kapustinskii simplified this as U_L ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ ν |z⁺z⁻| / (r⁺ + r⁻) kJ mol⁻¹.

Connects → Connects to: ionic bonding, crystal structure.

6

Insulated free expansion

1

ΔU = q + w = 0.

4

For an ideal gas U depends only on T, so ΔT = 0.

5

The process is nevertheless irreversible.

Practice questions with visible answers

Question 1

Why is reversible expansion work greatest in magnitude?

Answer: The external pressure remains infinitesimally below the gas pressure, so each volume increment occurs against the largest pressure compatible with expansion.

Question 2

Does isothermal mean adiabatic?

Answer: No. Isothermal fixes temperature; adiabatic fixes q = 0. A reversible isothermal ideal-gas expansion requires heat input.

Question 3

Why is free expansion irreversible although w = 0?

Answer: It occurs through a finite pressure imbalance into a vacuum. The system and surroundings cannot both be restored without intervention.

Question 4

What happens as the number of finite pressure steps increases?

Answer: The staircase approaches the reversible isotherm and the magnitude of expansion work increases toward the reversible limit.

Question 5

Which pressure is used for irreversible boundary work?

Answer: The external pressure exerted by the surroundings.

Question 6

Can a real gas change temperature during insulated free expansion?

Answer: Yes. Intermolecular potential energy can change even when total internal energy remains constant.

Final work ranking

wrev < wmultistep < wone-step < wfree = 0

|wrev| > |wmultistep| > |wone-step| > |wfree|

PART 10 / 30Work, Heat & the First LawReversible and Irreversible Adiabatic Ideal-Gas Processes
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYADIABATIC PROCESS ENGINE

Thermodynamics • Ideal-Gas Process Layer

No heat crosses—so work writes the temperature history

In an adiabatic process, the boundary blocks heat transfer. Expansion spends internal energy and cools the gas; compression stores work as internal energy and warms it.

Adiabatic core

Boundary condition

q = 0

First Law

ΔU = w

Reversible ideal gas

PV^γ = constant

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Adiabatic expansion and compression

Adiabatic is a heat-transfer condition, not a constant-temperature condition.

Defining condition

q = 0

Closed-system First Law

ΔU = w

Fixed-composition ideal gas

ΔU = w = nCV,m(T₂−T₁)

Minimal ideal-gas enthalpy result

ΔH = nCP,m(T₂−T₁)

Concept lens

Expansion

The gas performs work, so w < 0. Internal energy decreases and an ideal gas generally cools.

Concept lens

Compression

The surroundings perform work on the gas, so w > 0. Internal energy and temperature rise.
02

Heat-capacity ratio γ

Only the minimum heat-capacity framework needed for process equations.

Ideal-gas relation

CP,m − CV,m = R

Adiabatic index

γ = CP,m/CV,m

Solve for Cv,m

CV,m = R/(γ−1)

Solve for Cp,m

CP,m = γR/(γ−1)

Monatomic ideal gas

Cv,m = 3R/2
Cp,m = 5R/2
γ = 5/3

classical translational degrees of freedom

Diatomic ideal gas

Cv,m ≈ 5R/2
Cp,m ≈ 7R/2
γ ≈ 7/5

moderate-temperature rotational contribution; vibration neglected

General ideal gas

Cp,m − Cv,m = R
γ = Cp,m/Cv,m
Cv,m = R/(γ−1)

heat capacities may vary with temperature

Concept lens

Temperature dependence

CP,m, CV,m and γ can vary with temperature. The simple Poisson equations assume they are effectively constant over the process range.
03

Derivation of the reversible adiabatic relation

Every step, assumption and substitution made explicit.

1. Adiabatic First Law

q = 0 ⇒ dU = δw

For reversible pressure–volume work, δw = −P dV.

2. Ideal-gas internal energy

nCv,m dT = −P dV

Use dU = nCv,m dT for a fixed amount of ideal gas.

3. Substitute the equation of state

nCv,m dT = −(nRT/V)dV

Replace P by nRT/V.

4. Separate variables

dT/T = −(R/Cv,m)(dV/V)

For an ideal gas, R/Cv,m = γ − 1.

5. Integrate

ln(T₂/T₁) = −(γ−1)ln(V₂/V₁)

Assume Cv,m and Cp,m are effectively constant over the temperature range.

6. Exponentiate

T₁V₁^(γ−1) = T₂V₂^(γ−1)

This is the temperature–volume Poisson relation.

Concept lens

Required assumptions

Closed system; fixed composition; ideal-gas equation; only pressure–volume work; reversible mechanical path; q = 0; and heat capacities treated as constant over the interval.
04

Poisson relations

Temperature–volume

TVγ−1 = constant

Pressure–volume

PVγ = constant

Temperature–pressure

TγP1−γ = constant

Endpoint TV form

T₂/T₁ = (V₁/V₂)γ−1

Endpoint PV form

P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)γ

Endpoint TP form

T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)(γ−1)/γ

Concept lens

Validity boundary

These equations are not definitions of every adiabatic process. They are path equations for a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process under the stated heat-capacity approximation.
05

Reversible adiabatic work

Temperature form

wrev = nCV,m(T₂−T₁)

Using γ

wrev = nR(T₂−T₁)/(γ−1)

Endpoint PV form

wrev = (P₂V₂−P₁V₁)/(γ−1)

Concept lens

Expansion sign

Reversible adiabatic expansion has T₂ < T₁, so every work form gives w < 0 in the chemistry convention.
06

Adiabatic versus isothermal curves

Isothermal P–V slope

(dP/dV)T = −P/V

Adiabatic P–V slope

(dP/dV)ad,rev = −γP/V

Concept lens

Why the adiabat is steeper

Isothermal expansion receives heat to maintain temperature. Adiabatic expansion receives no heat, so pressure falls both because volume rises and because temperature drops.

Concept lens

Work comparison needs endpoint clarity

From the same initial state to the same larger final volume, the reversible isothermal path has greater expansion-work magnitude because its pressure remains higher. The final temperatures, and therefore final states, are different.
07

Irreversible adiabatic process

Use the actual external pressure, not Poisson relations.

Constant external pressure

nCV,m(T₂−T₁) = −Pext(V₂−V₁)

General endpoint strategy

combine the First Law with P₁V₁ = nRT₁ and P₂V₂ = nRT₂

Concept lens

Same initial state and same final volume

Reversible expansion performs the greatest work and therefore produces the lowest final temperature. A one-step expansion cools less. Ideal-gas free expansion performs no work and does not cool.
08

Adiabatic free expansion

Boundary conditions

q = 0 and Pext = 0

Energy balance

w = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0

Concept lens

Ideal gas

U = U(T), so ΔU = 0 gives ΔT = 0. The process is both adiabatic and isothermal, but irreversible.

Concept lens

Real gas

U depends on T and V. Temperature may fall or rise while ΔU remains zero; attraction-dominated gases commonly cool.
09

Retained chapter examples

Retained example 1

Two-mole monatomic gas: three adiabatic routes

COMPLETE ROUTE COMPARISON

Two moles of an ideal monatomic gas expand adiabatically from 5.0 L at 127°C to 40.0 L. Calculate q, ΔU, w and the minimal ideal-gas ΔH result for: (i) reversible expansion; (ii) expansion against constant Pext = 0.10 atm; and (iii) free expansion.

Initial temperature

T₁ = 400 K

Monatomic heat capacities

Cv,m = 3R/2, Cp,m = 5R/2

Adiabatic heat

q = 0

Route (i): reversible

Final temperature

T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 400(5/40)^(2/3) = 100 K

Internal-energy change and work

ΔU = w = nCv,m(T₂−T₁) = −7.48 kJ

Minimal ideal-gas enthalpy result

ΔH = nCp,m(T₂−T₁) = −12.47 kJ

Route (ii): constant external pressure

Work

w = −Pext(V₂−V₁) = −(0.10)(35.0) L atm ≈ −0.355 kJ

Internal-energy change

ΔU = w ≈ −0.355 kJ

Final temperature

T₂ = T₁ + ΔU/(nCv,m) ≈ 385.8 K

Minimal ideal-gas enthalpy result

ΔH = γΔU ≈ −0.591 kJ

Scientific completion: because the stated final volume is fixed at 40 L while the external pressure is only 0.10 atm, the process must be stopped mechanically at that volume. Otherwise the listed endpoint is not the final mechanical-equilibrium state.

Route (iii): free expansion

Boundary transfers

q = 0 and w = 0

Ideal-gas state changes

ΔU = 0, ΔT = 0, ΔH = 0

Concept lens

Temperature ranking for the same final volume

T2,rev = 100 K is far below T2,one-step ≈ 385.8 K, while ideal-gas free expansion leaves T unchanged at 400 K. Greater expansion work causes a larger internal-energy decrease.

Retained example 2

Final temperature in one-step adiabatic expansion

IMPLICIT ENDPOINT SOLUTION

Five moles of an ideal monatomic gas expand adiabatically from 12 atm at 27°C against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. The final equilibrium pressure is 1 atm. Calculate T₂, q, ΔU, w and the minimal ideal-gas ΔH result.

Adiabatic First Law

q = 0 and nCv,m(T₂−T₁) = −Pext(V₂−V₁)

Use endpoint ideal-gas volumes

V₁ = nRT₁/P₁ and V₂ = nRT₂/P₂

Substitute Pext = P₂ = 1 atm and Cv,m = 3R/2

(3/2)(T₂−300) = −(T₂−300/12)

Final temperature

T₂ = 190 K

Heat

q = 0

Work and ΔU

w = ΔU ≈ −6.86 kJ

Minimal ΔH result

ΔH ≈ −11.43 kJ

Concept lens

Why T₂ is not found from TV^(γ−1) = constant

That Poisson relation applies only to a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas path. This is a one-step irreversible expansion, so the First Law and actual external pressure must be used.
10

Process-result matrix

ProcessHeatWork/internal energyTemperature behaviourEquation note
Reversible adiabatic expansionq = 0w = ΔU < 0T falls most for fixed final volumePV^γ = constant
Reversible adiabatic compressionq = 0w = ΔU > 0T risesPoisson relations valid
One-step adiabatic expansionq = 0w = −PextΔVT falls less than reversible for same ΔVPoisson relations invalid
One-step adiabatic compressionq = 0w = −PextΔV > 0T rises more than reversible for same ΔVPoisson relations invalid
Ideal-gas adiabatic free expansionq = 0w = 0ΔU = 0 and ΔT = 0irreversible
11

Thermodynamics around you

Bicycle pump warms

Rapid compression leaves little time for heat to escape. Positive work raises the gas internal energy and temperature.

Aerosol spray feels cold

Rapid expansion and evaporation remove energy from the remaining fluid. The combined process is not a perfect textbook adiabat, but adiabatic cooling is part of the effect.

Cloud formation

Rising air encounters lower pressure, expands and cools approximately adiabatically. Cooling promotes condensation when saturation is reached.

Diesel ignition

Rapid compression raises air temperature enough for injected fuel to ignite. Real cylinders include losses, but adiabatic compression gives the core model.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Adiabatic means temperature remains constant.IncorrectAdiabatic means q = 0. Temperature generally changes when work changes internal energy.
Every adiabatic process obeys PV^γ = constant.IncorrectThe relation is restricted to a reversible ideal-gas path with suitable heat-capacity assumptions.
Every adiabatic process is isentropic.IncorrectOnly a reversible adiabatic process is isentropic for the stated closed simple system.
Reversible adiabatic expansion is less steep than an isotherm.IncorrectIts P–V slope magnitude is γP/V, larger than the isothermal magnitude P/V.
Free expansion has zero work, so it is reversible.IncorrectIt is driven by a finite pressure imbalance and is strongly irreversible.
A one-step adiabatic path can use Poisson relations at every stage.IncorrectOnly initial and final equilibrium states are well-defined; use the First Law with Pext.
For the same final volume, irreversible expansion cools more than reversible expansion.IncorrectIt performs less work and therefore cools less; its final temperature is higher.
The classical value γ = 7/5 is exact for every diatomic gas at every temperature.IncorrectVibrational excitation and non-ideal effects can change heat capacities and γ.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Derivation of Cp − Cv = R for an ideal gas

Start from H = U + PV(∂H/∂T)_P = (∂U/∂T)_P + P(∂V/∂T)_P
Cp definitionCp = (∂H/∂T)_P
Expand (∂U/∂T)_P(∂U/∂T)_P = (∂U/∂T)_V + (∂U/∂V)_T (∂V/∂T)_P
Ideal gas: (∂U/∂V)_T = 0(∂U/∂T)_P = Cv (for ideal gas only)
Ideal gas: PV = nRT(∂V/∂T)_P = nR/P
SubstituteCp = Cv + P · (nR/P) = Cv + nR
Per moleCp,m − Cv,m = R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Derivation 2

Kirchhoff's equation — temperature dependence of ΔH

Differentiate ΔH°_rxn w.r.t. Td(ΔH°)/dT = Σ νᵢ Cp,m,i = ΔCp
Kirchhoff's equationΔH°(T₂) = ΔH°(T₁) + ∫[T₁→T₂] ΔCp dT
If ΔCp ≈ constantΔH°(T₂) ≈ ΔH°(T₁) + ΔCp(T₂ − T₁)
General Cp = a + bT + cT²ΔH° = ΔH°(T₁) + Δa(T₂−T₁) + ½Δb(T₂²−T₁²) + ⅓Δc(T₂³−T₁³)
Sign of ΔCpΔCp > 0 → ΔH increases with T; ΔCp < 0 → ΔH decreases with T
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — volume doubling

One mole of a monatomic ideal gas at 360 K expands reversibly and adiabatically until its volume doubles. Find T₂.

Solution

For γ = 5/3, T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 360(1/2)^(2/3) ≈ 226.8 K.

◆Concept Application 2 — pressure ratio

A diatomic ideal gas with γ = 1.40 expands reversibly and adiabatically from 8.0 bar to 1.0 bar at an initial temperature of 420 K. Find T₂.

Solution

Use T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((γ−1)/γ). Thus T₂ = 420(1/8)^(0.4/1.4) ≈ 231.9 K.

◆Concept Application 3 — work from temperatures

Three moles of an ideal gas with γ = 1.30 cool from 500 K to 350 K adiabatically. Calculate w.

Solution

Cv,m = R/(γ−1) = R/0.30. Therefore w = ΔU = nCv,mΔT = 3(R/0.30)(−150) ≈ −12.47 kJ.

◆Concept Application 4 — work from endpoint PV values

For a reversible adiabatic process with γ = 1.40, P₁V₁ = 10.0 kJ and P₂V₂ = 7.2 kJ. Find chemistry-sign work.

Solution

w = (P₂V₂−P₁V₁)/(γ−1) = (7.2−10.0)/0.40 = −7.0 kJ.

◆Concept Application 5 — slope comparison

At the same point on a P–V graph, compare the slopes of an ideal-gas isotherm and reversible adiabat.

Solution

Isothermal slope is (dP/dV)T = −P/V. Adiabatic slope is (dP/dV)S = −γP/V. Since γ > 1, the adiabat is steeper in magnitude.

◆Concept Application 6 — same final volume

From the same initial state, an ideal gas expands adiabatically to a fixed final volume by a reversible path and by a one-step path. Which has the higher final temperature?

Solution

The one-step irreversible expansion has the higher final temperature because it delivers less work. The reversible path loses more internal energy and cools more.

◆Concept Application 7 — adiabatic versus isentropic

An insulated gas expands through a finite pressure difference. Is ΔS necessarily zero?

Solution

No. q = 0, but irreversibility produces entropy. Only a reversible adiabatic process is isentropic for the stated closed simple system.

◆Concept Application 8 — free expansion of a real gas

A real gas freely expands in an insulated container. What is fixed, and what may change?

Solution

q = 0, w = 0 and therefore ΔU = 0. Because U may depend on T and V, temperature may change. An attraction-dominated gas often cools during expansion.

◆Concept Application 9 — derive pressure relation

Starting from TV^(γ−1) = constant and PV = nRT, derive PV^γ = constant.

Solution

Write T = PV/(nR). Then TV^(γ−1) = [PV/(nR)]V^(γ−1) = PV^γ/(nR). Since nR is constant, PV^γ is constant.

◆Concept Application 10 — derive temperature–pressure relation

Derive a relation involving only T and P for a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process.

Solution

Eliminate V using V = nRT/P in TV^(γ−1) = constant. This gives T^γP^(1−γ) = constant, or T P^((1−γ)/γ) = constant.

◆Concept Application 11 — one-step final temperature equation

An ideal gas expands adiabatically against constant Pext to a final equilibrium pressure P₂ = Pext. Write the equation that determines T₂ from P₁, T₁, n and Cv,m.

Solution

Use nCv,m(T₂−T₁) = −P₂[nRT₂/P₂ − nRT₁/P₁]. This implicit linear equation can be solved directly for T₂.

◆Concept Application 12 — validity audit

A student applies PV^γ = constant to an abrupt piston expansion. Identify the error.

Solution

PV^γ = constant requires a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas path with suitable heat-capacity assumptions. An abrupt expansion is irreversible, so intermediate equilibrium pressure is not defined and the Poisson relation is invalid.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

q = 0 for every adiabat; Poisson relations only for the reversible ideal-gas path

PART 10 COMPLETE

First Law

ΔU = w

Reversible ideal gas

PV^γ = constant

Expansion

T falls and w < 0

Free ideal-gas expansion

q = w = ΔU = ΔT = 0

Integrated Enrichment

Heat Capacities and Kirchhoff — Deeper Analysis

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Ratio γ = Cp/Cv and speed of sound

The speed of sound in an ideal gas is c = √(γRT/M). For air (γ ≈ 1.4, M = 29 g mol⁻¹) at 298 K: c = √(1.4 × 8.314 × 298/0.029) = 346 m s⁻¹. Adiabatic compressibility, not isothermal, governs sound propagation.

Connects → Connects to: adiabatic processes, Part 3.

Equipartition theorem and Cv for polyatomic gases

Each quadratic energy mode contributes ½R to Cv,m. Monatomic: 3 translational → Cv,m = 3/2 R. Diatomic: 3 trans + 2 rot → 5/2 R. Polyatomic nonlinear: 3 trans + 3 rot → 3R (minimum, vibrational modes frozen at room T). At high T, vibrational modes activate, raising Cv,m.

Connects → Connects to: statistical mechanics, equipartition.

SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYPOLYTROPIC PROCESS MAP

Thermodynamics • Generalised Ideal-Gas Path

One exponent connects isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and isochoric limits

The polytropic law \(PV^x=\text{constant}\) creates a unified family of reversible ideal-gas paths. The index \(x\) controls curve shape, temperature change, work and even the effective heat capacity.

Master equation set

PVx = constant
TVx−1 = constant
Cm = CV,m + R/(1−x)
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Meaning of a polytropic process

A compact process model joining several familiar reversible ideal-gas paths.

Defining path equation

PVx = K

The constant \(x\) is the polytropic index. Different values of\(x\) generate different pressure–volume paths. The model is especially useful when a real compression or expansion exchanges some heat but is neither perfectly isothermal nor perfectly adiabatic.

Concept lens

A path model, not a universal law of state

An ideal gas does not possess a fixed polytropic index. The value belongs to the chosen process and may be obtained from the endpoint data or fitted to a measured path.
02

Derivation of the ideal-gas path relations

1. Define the path

PVˣ = K

x is the polytropic index and remains constant along the chosen reversible path.

2. Combine with ideal gas

P = nRT/V

Substitution gives nRTV^(x−1) = K.

3. Temperature–volume relation

TV^(x−1) = constant

For x > 1, expansion cools the gas. For x < 1, expansion heats it.

4. Work integral

w = −∫ K V^(−x)dV

Use the chemistry sign convention and a reversible pressure path.

5. Result for x ≠ 1

w = (P₂V₂−P₁V₁)/(x−1)

Using PV = nRT, this also becomes nR(T₂−T₁)/(x−1).

6. Special case x = 1

w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁)

The algebraic x ≠ 1 expression has a removable limiting form that becomes the isothermal logarithm.

Pressure–temperature relation

TxP1−x = constant

V–T endpoint form

T₂/T₁ = (V₁/V₂)x−1

P–V endpoint form

P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)x

P–T endpoint form

T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)(x−1)/x
03

Work done in a reversible polytropic process

The logarithmic isothermal result appears as the special x = 1 limit.

For x ≠ 1

w = (P₂V₂−P₁V₁)/(x−1)

Equivalent temperature form

w = nR(T₂−T₁)/(x−1)

For x = 1

w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁)

Concept lens

Expansion sign check

For an expansion with \(x>1\), temperature falls and \(T_2-T_1<0\), so the temperature-form work is negative.

Concept lens

Why direct substitution at x = 1 fails

Both \(T_2-T_1\) and \(x-1\) approach zero. The ratio is indeterminate; its correct limiting value is the finite logarithmic isothermal work.
04

Energy changes

Internal-energy change

ΔU = nCV,m(T₂−T₁)

Minimal ideal-gas enthalpy result

ΔH = nCP,m(T₂−T₁)

Heat along the path

q = ΔU − w = nCm(T₂−T₁)

Concept lens

Thermodynamics–Thermochemistry boundary

Only the process-essential \(C_V\), \(C_P\), \(\Delta U\) and minimal \(\Delta H\) relations are used here. Full heat-capacity theory remains in the separate Thermochemistry notes.
05

Effective molar heat capacity

The chapter derivation completed step by step.

For a reversible path, the First Law gives:

First Law

δq = dU + P dV

Use dU and define Cm

nCmdT = nCV,mdT + P dV

Differentiate \(TV^{x-1}=\text{constant}\):

Polytropic differential relation

P dV = nR dT/(1−x)

Effective heat capacity

Cm = CV,m + R/(1−x)

Equivalent form

Cm = (CP,m−xCV,m)/(1−x)

Concept lens

Negative path heat capacity is not instability

\(C_m\) is the process ratio \(\delta q/(n\,dT)\), not an equilibrium stability property like \(C_V\). It can be negative when heat enters while temperature falls.
06

Limiting cases

x = 0

Isobaric

P = constant

Cₘ = Cₚ

Expansion requires heating for an ideal gas.

x = 1

Isothermal

PV = constant

|Cₘ| → ∞

Finite heat may be transferred while dT = 0.

x = γ

Reversible adiabatic

PV^γ = constant

Cₘ = 0

No heat transfer; work alone changes U.

x → ∞

Isochoric limit

V ≈ constant

Cₘ → Cᵥ

PV work tends to zero.

07

Heat-flow and temperature regimes during expansion

x < 1

T rises

q > 0 for expansion

Cₘ > Cᵥ; at x = 0, Cₘ = Cₚ

x = 1

T constant

q = −w > 0

effective heat capacity diverges

1 < x < γ

T falls

q > 0 although T falls

Cₘ < 0

x = γ

T falls

q = 0

Cₘ = 0

x > γ

T falls

q < 0

0 < Cₘ < Cᵥ

Concept lens

The surprising 1 < x < γ region

The gas cools because it does substantial work, yet heat still enters. The work output exceeds the heat input, and the difference comes from the decrease in internal energy.

09

Original complete worked example

Original Synergic Bond worked example

Complete energy audit of a polytropic expansion

FULL DERIVATION

Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas at 400 K expand reversibly according to PV1.20 = constant until the volume doubles. Calculate T₂, w, ΔU, q and the minimal ideal-gas ΔH result.

Temperature relation

T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(x−1) = 400(1/2)^0.20 ≈ 348.2 K

Work

w = nR(T₂−T₁)/(x−1) ≈ −4.31 kJ

Internal-energy change

ΔU = n(3R/2)(T₂−T₁) ≈ −1.29 kJ

Heat

q = ΔU − w ≈ +3.02 kJ

Minimal ideal-gas enthalpy result

ΔH = n(5R/2)(T₂−T₁) ≈ −2.15 kJ

Concept lens

Why heat enters even though temperature falls

For 1 < x < γ, the gas performs more work than the decrease in internal energy alone can supply. Heat enters while the gas still cools. This is the physical meaning of a negative effective heat capacity for the path.
10

Thermodynamics around you

Real compressor modelling

A compression process with partial heat removal often lies between isothermal and adiabatic behaviour and is approximated by a fitted polytropic index.

Multistage compression

Intercooling moves each stage closer to isothermal compression, reducing required work compared with one strongly adiabatic stage.

Reciprocating engines

Expansion and compression data are often fitted by PV^x = constant to represent heat leakage, combustion effects and non-idealities in a compact engineering model.

Atmospheric air parcels

Dry reversible adiabatic motion corresponds to x = γ, while heat exchange, condensation and mixing shift the effective path away from that value.

11

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Every process can be represented exactly by one constant polytropic index.IncorrectPV^x = constant is a process model. A real path may require a variable local exponent.
x = γ for every adiabatic process.IncorrectThat equality belongs to a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process under the stated assumptions.
Negative effective heat capacity means the gas is thermodynamically unstable.IncorrectHere it is a path ratio δq/(n dT), not the equilibrium Cv or Cp stability property.
x = 1 gives zero work because ΔT = 0.IncorrectThe temperature-form work becomes indeterminate; its correct limit is logarithmic and generally non-zero.
The x → ∞ limit means infinite pressure.IncorrectIt describes a path whose fractional volume change tends to zero for finite endpoint pressure ratios.
For 1 < x < γ, cooling proves heat leaves.IncorrectHeat enters while the gas performs still more work, so internal energy and temperature decrease.
Cm is always between Cv and Cp.IncorrectIt may be negative, zero, divergent, or exceed Cp depending on x.
Polytropic work always uses constant external pressure.IncorrectFor a reversible polytropic path, system pressure follows P = K/V^x and varies continuously.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

C_cal from calibrationC_cal = q_known / ΔT_measured

12

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — identify x

An ideal gas follows a reversible path for which pressure becomes one-fourth when volume doubles. Find the polytropic index.

Solution

From P1V1^x = P2V2^x, P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^x. Thus 1/4 = (1/2)^x, giving x = 2.

◆Concept Application 2 — final temperature

One mole of ideal gas expands polytropically with x = 1.30 from 300 K until its volume triples. Find T₂.

Solution

T₂/T₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(x−1) = (1/3)^0.30. Hence T₂ ≈ 215.8 K.

◆Concept Application 3 — work from temperatures

Three moles of ideal gas undergo x = 1.25 polytropic expansion from 500 K to 400 K. Calculate chemistry-sign work.

Solution

w = nR(T₂−T₁)/(x−1) = 3×8.314×(−100)/0.25 ≈ −9.98 kJ.

◆Concept Application 4 — effective heat capacity

For a monatomic ideal gas, calculate Cm for x = 1.20.

Solution

Cv,m = 3R/2. Cm = Cv,m + R/(1−x) = 1.5R − 5R = −3.5R.

◆Concept Application 5 — adiabatic index recovery

Show that Cm becomes zero when x = γ.

Solution

Cm = Cv,m + R/(1−γ). Since R = (γ−1)Cv,m, the second term is −Cv,m. Therefore Cm = 0.

◆Concept Application 6 — isobaric recovery

Show that x = 0 gives the constant-pressure heat capacity.

Solution

Cm = Cv,m + R/(1−0) = Cv,m + R = Cp,m.

◆Concept Application 7 — isochoric limit

Explain mathematically why x → ∞ approaches an isochoric process.

Solution

For finite pressure ratios, V₂/V₁ = (P₁/P₂)^(1/x) tends to 1 as x → ∞. Hence volume change tends to zero and Cm tends to Cv,m.

◆Concept Application 8 — negative heat capacity

For 1 < x < γ, why is the effective path heat capacity negative?

Solution

Expansion gives dT < 0 but q > 0. Since δq = nCm dT, positive heat divided by negative temperature change requires Cm < 0.

◆Concept Application 9 — heat-flow sign for x > γ

During expansion with x > γ, determine the signs of ΔT, w, ΔU and q.

Solution

Expansion gives ΔT < 0, w < 0 and ΔU < 0. Here 0 < Cm < Cv,m, so q = nCmΔT < 0: heat leaves while the gas also does work.

◆Concept Application 10 — x = 1 limit

Why can the formula w = nRΔT/(x−1) not be used by direct substitution at x = 1?

Solution

At x = 1, ΔT also tends to zero, producing an indeterminate 0/0 form. The correct limit yields the logarithmic isothermal work, not zero.

◆Concept Application 11 — endpoint work form

A reversible polytropic process has x = 1.5, P1V1 = 10 kJ and P2V2 = 7 kJ. Find w.

Solution

w = (P2V2−P1V1)/(x−1) = (7−10)/0.5 = −6 kJ.

◆Concept Application 12 — pressure–temperature form

Derive the T–P relation for a polytropic ideal-gas process.

Solution

Eliminate V from PV^x = constant using V = nRT/P. This gives T^xP^(1−x) = constant, or T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((x−1)/x).

◆Concept Application 13 — infer process from Cm

An ideal gas has Cv,m = 2.5R and follows a path with Cm = −2.5R. Find x.

Solution

−2.5R = 2.5R + R/(1−x). Thus 1/(1−x) = −5, so 1−x = −0.2 and x = 1.2.

◆Concept Application 14 — process ranking

From the same initial state to the same larger volume, rank final pressure for x = 0, 1, 1.2 and γ = 1.4.

Solution

P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^x. For V₂ > V₁, larger x gives smaller final pressure. Therefore P(x=0) > P(x=1) > P(x=1.2) > P(x=1.4).

Synergic Bond rapid recall

The index x controls path shape, work, temperature response and effective heat capacity

PART 11 COMPLETE

x = 0

isobaric; Cm = Cp

x = 1

isothermal; logarithmic work

x = γ

reversible adiabatic; Cm = 0

x → ∞

isochoric limit; Cm → Cv

PART 12 / 30Work, Heat & the First LawCyclic Ideal-Gas Processes and Integrated Energy Accounting
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYCYCLE ENERGY ACCOUNTING

Thermodynamics • Integrated Process Layer

A cycle forgets every state change—but remembers its heat and work

When the system returns to its starting state, every state function closes. The path still encloses an area, and that area records net pressure–volume work.

Cycle closure

ΔUcycle = 0
wcycle = −∮P dV
qcycle = −wcycle
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Definition of a cyclic process

A sequence of two or more processes that returns the system to its initial thermodynamic state.

State closure

final state = initial state

A cycle may contain isochoric, isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic, polytropic or other legs. Because the final state equals the initial state, every state function returns to its original value.

State functions

ΔU = ΔH = ΔS = ΔG = 0 over the cycle

Path functions

qcycle and wcycle may be non-zero

Concept lens

Cycle does not mean nothing happened

The system can absorb heat, reject heat, perform work and receive work during different legs. Only its final thermodynamic state matches the initial state.
02

Net work as signed P–V area

Expansion and compression contributions compete over the complete loop.

Chemistry-sign pressure–volume work

wcycle = −∮PextdV

Concept lens

Clockwise loop

Expansion occurs at a higher average pressure than compression. The gas delivers net work:\(w_{\text{cycle}}<0\).

Concept lens

Anticlockwise loop

Compression occurs at a higher average pressure than expansion. The surroundings deliver net work:\(w_{\text{cycle}}>0\).

Concept lens

Only P–V area has direct work meaning

The enclosed area on \(T\)-\(V\), \(P\)-\(T\) or other graphs is not directly pressure–volume work. Work requires integration of pressure with respect to volume.
03

First-Law closure of a cycle

First Law over the complete loop

0 = ΔUcycle = qcycle + wcycle

Heat–work balance

qcycle = −wcycle

Concept lens

Clockwise heat sign

Since clockwise \(w_{\text{cycle}}<0\), the system must absorb net heat:\(q_{\text{cycle}}>0\).

Concept lens

Anticlockwise heat sign

Since anticlockwise \(w_{\text{cycle}}>0\), the system must reject net heat:\(q_{\text{cycle}}<0\).
04

Six-step cycle audit method

1. Reconstruct every state

PV = nRT

Complete the state table before calculating any leg quantity.

2. Name each leg

isochoric / isobaric / isothermal / adiabatic / polytropic

The process label decides the correct work and heat relations.

3. Calculate ΔU first

ΔU = nCv,mΔT

For an ideal gas, internal-energy change depends only on endpoint temperatures.

4. Calculate work from the path

w = −∫Pext dV

Use zero, rectangle, logarithm, adiabat or polytropic relation as appropriate.

5. Obtain heat

q = ΔU − w

This is often safer than memorising separate heat formulas.

6. Close the cycle

ΣΔU = 0 and Σq = −Σw

The closure test catches arithmetic and sign errors.

05

Common P–V area cases

Rectangular cycle

|wcycle| = (Phigh−Plow)(Vhigh−Vlow)

Direction supplies the sign. Clockwise is negative in chemistry notation.

Curved cycle

wcycle = −∮P dV

Subtract the compression area from the expansion area or integrate leg by leg.

No enclosed area

wcycle = 0

Outward and return paths coincide, so net PV work vanishes.

Non-PV work present

wtotal ≠ wPV alone

The P–V area gives only net pressure–volume work.

06

Retained three-state cycle example

Retained chapter cycle example

One mole of a monatomic ideal gas through states 1, 2 and 3

FULL STATE & ENERGY TABLE

One mole of a monatomic ideal gas executes a reversible cycle: state 1 → state 2 at constant volume, state 2 → state 3 isothermally, and state 3 → state 1 at constant pressure. Complete the state table and evaluate q, w, ΔU and the minimal ideal-gas ΔH result for every leg and for the cycle.

Step 1 — reconstruct the three states

StatePressureVolumeTemperatureRole

State 1

State 2

(P₂,V₂,T₂) = (2 atm, 22.4 L, 546 K)

State 3

(P₃,V₃,T₃) = (1 atm, 44.8 L, 546 K)

Step 2 — leg-by-leg calculations

Leg A: 1 → 2

Isochoric work

wA = 0

Internal-energy change

ΔUA = (3/2)R(546−273) = (3/2)R(273)

Heat

qA = ΔUA

Minimal ΔH

ΔHA = (5/2)R(273)

Leg B: 2 → 3

Isothermal state changes

ΔUB = 0 and ΔHB = 0

Reversible work

Heat

Physical meaning

heat absorbed = work delivered

Leg C: 3 → 1

Isobaric work

wC = −P(V₁−V₃) = +R(273)

Internal-energy change

ΔUC = (3/2)R(273−546) = −(3/2)R(273)

Heat

qC = ΔUC − wC = −(5/2)R(273)

Minimal ΔH

ΔHC = −(5/2)R(273)

Step 3 — close the complete cycle

LegProcessqwΔUMinimal ΔH
A: 1 → 2Isochoric heating+(3/2)R(273)0+(3/2)R(273)+(5/2)R(273)
B: 2 → 3Reversible isothermal expansion+546R ln 2−546R ln 200

Net chemistry work

wcycle = 273R(1−2ln2) ≈ −0.877 kJ

Net heat absorbed

qcycle = 273R(2ln2−1) ≈ +0.877 kJ

Concept lens

Graph-area verification

The cycle is clockwise. The curved high-pressure expansion leg encloses more area than the low-pressure compression leg. Hence the gas delivers net work, chemistry-sign \(w_{\text{cycle}}<0\), and absorbs equal net heat.
07

State and path consistency checks

State closure

Sum every \(\Delta U\), \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta S\) or other state-function change. Each total must be zero.

Graph sign

Confirm whether the loop is clockwise or anticlockwise before assigning the chemistry work sign.

First-Law closure

Check that \(\Sigma q + \Sigma w = 0\). Any residual signals an arithmetic or sign error.

08

Non-PV work in a cycle

The P–V loop gives only net pressure–volume work. A cycle may also include electrical, shaft, surface, elastic or magnetic work.

Complete work accounting

wtotal,cycle = wPV,cycle + wnon-PV,cycle

Concept lens

Electrochemical cycle

A battery can return approximately to its initial thermodynamic state while electrical work crosses the boundary. Its work cannot be read from a P–V area.
09

Cycle work, power and efficiency are different

Work per cycle

Magnitude of the signed P–V area, plus any non-PV work.

Power

Work per cycle multiplied by the number of cycles per unit time.

Efficiency

Useful work divided by the relevant energy input; developed fully with heat engines later.

10

Thermodynamics around you

Petrol and diesel engines

A working gas repeatedly compresses, heats, expands and rejects energy. The P–V loop area represents indicated mechanical work per cycle.

Refrigerator compressor loop

The refrigeration system consumes net work, corresponding to an anticlockwise orientation in an idealised pressure–volume representation of the working fluid.

Stirling-style engine

Alternating isothermal and constant-volume idealisations produce a closed loop whose area is net work, while regenerators recycle part of the heat internally.

Battery charge–discharge cycle

A cell can return approximately to its initial state after charge and discharge while electrical work and heat cross the boundary. Its useful work is not represented by P–V area alone.

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Every quantity is zero over a cycle.IncorrectOnly state-function changes vanish. Net heat and work may be non-zero.
Clockwise P–V cycle means positive chemistry work.IncorrectClockwise means net work is done by the gas, so chemistry-sign wcycle is negative.
Area on any thermodynamic graph equals work.IncorrectDirect mechanical work area belongs specifically to a P–V graph.
ΔScycle = 0 proves the cycle is reversible.IncorrectEntropy is a state function; a system can return to its initial entropy after irreversible legs.
The P–V area gives all work modes.IncorrectIt gives only pressure–volume work. Electrical, surface or shaft work must be added separately.
An isochoric leg cannot exchange energy.IncorrectPV work is zero, but heat or non-PV work can change internal energy.
A larger cycle area always means higher efficiency.IncorrectArea gives work per cycle. Efficiency also depends on heat input and the full cycle design.
A larger cycle area always means larger power.IncorrectPower depends on work per cycle multiplied by cycle frequency.

12

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — rectangular clockwise cycle

A gas executes a clockwise rectangle between pressures 1 bar and 4 bar and volumes 2 L and 7 L. Find chemistry-sign net PV work.

Solution

Area = (4−1)(7−2) = 15 bar L = 1500 J. Clockwise means the gas delivers net work, so wcycle = −1500 J.

◆Concept Application 2 — anticlockwise reversal

The same rectangular path is traversed anticlockwise. Find wcycle and qcycle.

Solution

wcycle = +1500 J. Since ΔUcycle = 0, qcycle = −1500 J.

◆Concept Application 3 — triangular cycle

A clockwise triangular cycle has base ΔV = 4 L and pressure height ΔP = 3 bar. Calculate net work.

Solution

Enclosed area = (1/2)ΔPΔV = 6 bar L = 600 J. Clockwise gives wcycle = −600 J.

◆Concept Application 4 — state closure

Over a complete cycle, a system absorbs 2.8 kJ of heat. Find ΔUcycle and chemistry-sign wcycle.

Solution

ΔUcycle = 0. Therefore wcycle = −qcycle = −2.8 kJ.

◆Concept Application 5 — one missing leg

For a three-leg cycle, w1 = 0.4 kJ, w2 = −1.7 kJ and net heat absorbed is 0.9 kJ. Find w3.

Solution

For the cycle, qtotal + wtotal = 0, so wtotal = −0.9 kJ. Hence 0.4−1.7+w3 = −0.9, giving w3 = +0.4 kJ.

◆Concept Application 6 — two isochoric legs

A cycle contains two isochoric legs and two curved expansion/compression legs. Which legs contribute directly to PV work?

Solution

The isochoric legs have dV = 0 and contribute zero PV work. Only the legs with changing volume contribute to the P–V area.

◆Concept Application 7 — T–V diagram warning

Can the enclosed area on a T–V cycle diagram be identified directly as work?

Solution

No. Pressure–volume work is ∫P dV. Area on a T–V graph has units K·volume and is not work unless converted using an equation of state and integrated appropriately.

◆Concept Application 8 — entropy over a cycle

Is the system entropy change over a complete cycle always zero? Does that prove every leg is reversible?

Solution

The system returns to its initial state, so ΔScycle = 0 because entropy is a state function. This does not prove reversibility; entropy can be produced in irreversible legs and exported to surroundings.

◆Concept Application 9 — work from two paths

A gas expands from V₁ to V₂ along a high-pressure curve and returns along a lower-pressure curve. Determine the cycle direction and work sign.

Solution

Expansion occurs at higher pressure than compression, so the loop is clockwise. The gas delivers net work and chemistry-sign wcycle is negative.

◆Concept Application 10 — electrical cycle

A cyclic electrochemical device returns to its initial thermodynamic state while delivering 600 J electrical work and receiving no PV work. What net heat is required?

Solution

Total chemistry work is w = −600 J. Since ΔUcycle = 0, qcycle = +600 J.

◆Concept Application 11 — ideal-gas leg identification

On a P–V graph, a vertical leg doubles pressure at fixed volume. For an ideal gas, what happens to temperature and PV work?

Solution

At fixed volume, T is proportional to P, so temperature doubles. PV work is zero because dV = 0.

◆Concept Application 12 — high-temperature isotherm

Two isotherms connect the same volume limits. Which one gives the larger reversible expansion-work magnitude?

Solution

The higher-temperature isotherm has higher pressure at every volume. Since |w| = nRT ln(V₂/V₁), the higher-temperature path gives larger magnitude.

◆Concept Application 13 — consistency audit

A proposed cycle table gives ΣΔU = +200 J and ΣΔH = 0. What is wrong?

Solution

A genuine complete cycle returns to the same state, so every state-function change, including ΔU and ΔH, must sum to zero. At least one leg value or sign is incorrect.

◆Concept Application 14 — area and power

Does a larger P–V cycle area automatically imply greater power output?

Solution

It implies greater work per cycle. Power also depends on cycle frequency or duration. A large-area cycle run very slowly can have low power.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

State functions close; the P–V loop area survives as net work

PART 13 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyLimitations of the First Law, Natural Direction, and Spontaneity
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYDIRECTION & SPONTANEITY

Thermodynamics • Direction Layer

Energy conservation tells what balances—not what nature chooses

The First Law audits energy perfectly, yet remains silent about natural direction. Spontaneity, irreversibility and heat-engine limits require a new principle.

Two independent questions

First Law

Does the energy balance close?

Second Law

Which direction is naturally permitted?

Kinetics

How fast does the allowed change occur?

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Limitations of the First Law

Conservation is essential, but direction requires additional information.

No natural direction

The First Law accepts both a process and its exact reverse if both satisfy energy conservation.

No spontaneity test

It cannot decide whether diffusion, mixing, heat flow or a reaction will occur on its own.

No irreversibility measure

Energy conservation alone does not quantify lost work or entropy production.

No heat-engine ceiling

It cannot explain why a cyclic engine cannot convert all heat from one reservoir into work.

No refrigerator direction rule

It does not forbid heat transfer from cold to hot unless the work requirement is supplied by the Second Law.

Exothermicity is insufficient

Heat release alone cannot determine spontaneity; temperature and entropy effects also matter.

Rate remains unknown

A thermodynamically allowed process may be extremely slow because of a kinetic barrier.

Classical mass-energy scope

The ordinary chemical First-Law form does not explicitly include nuclear mass-to-energy conversion; a relativistic energy balance is needed.

Concept lens

Modern correction to the nuclear statement

Energy conservation remains valid in nuclear processes. The limitation is that the ordinary fixed-mass chemical form does not explicitly include measurable rest-mass conversion, radiation and matter-flow terms.
02

Natural direction and thermodynamic asymmetry

Many energy-conserving reverse processes are never observed spontaneously.

Concept lens

Work can become heat completely

Friction, electrical resistance and viscous dissipation can convert organised work entirely into microscopic internal energy.

Concept lens

Heat cannot become work completely in a cycle

No cyclic engine can extract heat from a single reservoir and transform all of it into work. Some heat must be rejected.

Concept lens

Ordered versus disordered transfer—careful wording

Work is energy transfer through coordinated macroscopic motion. Heat is energy transfer driven by a temperature difference through disordered microscopic interactions. Energy itself is not a material substance labelled “ordered” or “disordered”; the distinction concerns transfer mode and accessibility for producing work.
03

Spontaneous and non-spontaneous processes

Spontaneous means naturally directed under the specified constraints—not necessarily fast.

Operational definition

spontaneous change = proceeds without continuous external driving once permitted
Process typeNatural directionNon-spontaneous reverseDriving imbalance
Heat flowhot → coldcold → hot without worktemperature difference
Gas expansioninto available lower-pressure spacespontaneous reconcentrationpressure/volume constraint
Diffusionhigh concentration → low concentrationself-separationchemical-potential difference
Mechanical motionunbalanced force → balanceobject climbs without energy inputforce imbalance
Phase changetoward stable phase at stated T,Ptoward unstable phasefree-energy difference
Chemical reactiontoward equilibrium compositionaway from equilibrium without couplingreaction affinity

Concept lens

Constraint removal matters

A compressed gas does not expand while a rigid partition remains intact. Once the constraint is removed, expansion into available lower-pressure space becomes spontaneous.

Concept lens

The reverse can occur when driven

Gas separation, uphill pumping and electrolysis are non-spontaneous in isolation but occur when coupled to external work or another sufficiently favourable process.
04

Thermodynamic favourability versus kinetic accessibility

A process may have a preferred direction yet remain trapped behind an activation barrier.

FrameworkMain questionFocusOutput
ThermodynamicsIs the change favourable under the stated conditions?Initial and final equilibrium statesDirection and equilibrium
KineticsHow fast does it occur and by what mechanism?Reaction pathway and activation barrierRate and mechanism
CatalystDoes not change equilibrium or overall thermodynamic driving forceLowers activation barrierSpeeds forward and reverse routes

Concept lens

Initiation is not continuous driving

A spark can initiate combustion by helping the first molecules cross an activation barrier. Once established, the reaction can continue because of its own thermodynamic and kinetic feedback; the spark does not supply the entire reaction energy.

Concept lens

Catalysts do not change equilibrium

A catalyst lowers activation barriers for forward and reverse routes. It accelerates approach to equilibrium but does not alter the equilibrium state or overall thermodynamic driving force.
05

Equilibrium as the destination of spontaneous change

A spontaneous process moves in the direction that reduces the relevant thermodynamic driving imbalance. As equilibrium is approached, the macroscopic driving force decreases and finally becomes zero.

Thermal

Temperature differences disappear.

Mechanical

Unbalanced pressures and forces vanish.

Chemical

No net reaction progress remains.

Phase

No net transfer between stable coexisting phases.

Concept lens

Dynamic equilibrium

Equilibrium does not mean molecular motion stops. Forward and reverse microscopic events can continue at equal average rates.
06

Perpetual-motion machines and the missing law

PMM OF THE FIRST KIND

Creates work without equivalent energy input

This violates energy conservation. It is forbidden directly by the First Law.

Impossible claim

Wout > energy input
PMM OF THE SECOND KIND

Obeys energy balance but violates natural direction

Examples include a cyclic engine converting all heat from one reservoir into work, or a refrigerator moving heat from cold to hot without work.

Energy balance may still hold

q = −w, yet the process remains impossible

Concept lens

Refrigerator statement

A cyclic device cannot have the sole effect of transferring heat from a colder body to a hotter body. External work or an equivalent compensating change is required.
07

Exothermicity is not a spontaneity criterion

Exothermic but non-spontaneous

Freezing releases heat, yet liquid water does not spontaneously freeze above its melting temperature at the stated pressure.

Endothermic but spontaneous

Ice melts spontaneously above its melting temperature even though melting absorbs heat.

Concept lens

What is missing?

Direction depends on both energy and entropy under the specified constraints. The formal criteria are developed in the Second-Law, entropy and free-energy modules.
08

Retained five-route ideal-gas comparison

Retained chapter comparison

One initial state, one final pressure, five different paths

irreversible free expansion into vacuum
