Concept lens

Path ranking from the same initial state

The example shows why the First Law alone is not a direction law. It can calculate the energy balance for every admissible path, but a separate criterion is needed to decide which unconstrained path nature will select.
09

Why the Second Law is required

Need 1

Direction

hot → cold, diffusion, expansion and reaction progress

Need 2

Irreversibility

why real processes cannot be exactly undone

Need 3

Conversion limit

why heat cannot be fully converted into cyclic work

Need 4

Equilibrium criterion

where spontaneous change stops

Preview

spontaneous change in an isolated universe ⇒ entropy of the universe increases
10

Thermodynamics around you

Hot tea cools

Energy conservation can describe the heat lost and gained, but the Second Law identifies hot-to-cold as the spontaneous direction.

Perfume spreads through a room

Diffusion proceeds toward a more uniform concentration. Spontaneous re-concentration is not observed without separation work.

Petrol requires ignition

Combustion may be thermodynamically favourable yet require a spark because the reaction pathway has an activation barrier.

Refrigerator needs electricity

Moving heat from a colder interior to a warmer room requires work. The First Law determines the balance; the Second Law explains the necessity.

11

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
A spontaneous process must be rapid.IncorrectSpontaneity concerns direction, not rate. A favourable process can be extremely slow.
Every exothermic process is spontaneous.IncorrectHeat release alone is insufficient; temperature and entropy effects matter.
An activation spark supplies the thermodynamic driving force.IncorrectIt helps cross a kinetic barrier but does not determine the equilibrium direction.
The First Law forbids heat flow from cold to hot.IncorrectEnergy conservation permits the balance. The Second Law requires work input for the transfer.
Work and heat are perfectly symmetric forms of transfer.IncorrectThey are equal in energy units but differ in natural convertibility and entropy implications.
Equilibrium means all microscopic motion stops.IncorrectMicroscopic events continue, but there is no net macroscopic change.
A PMM-II violates energy conservation.IncorrectIt may satisfy the First Law while violating the Second Law’s direction restriction.
A non-spontaneous process can never occur.IncorrectIt can occur when driven by external work or coupled to a more favourable process.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Boltzmann's entropy formula — derivation outline

Define microstateone specific quantum-mechanical configuration of all particles
Macrostate Ωnumber of microstates compatible with the observed macroscopic state
Boltzmann postulateS = k_B ln Ω (k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)
Additivity checktwo independent systems: Ω_total = Ω_A · Ω_B → S_total = k_B ln(Ω_A Ω_B) = S_A + S_B ✓
Maximum entropyequilibrium corresponds to the macrostate with the maximum number of microstates
Link to disordermore disordered configurations have larger Ω → larger S

Derivation 2

Spontaneity from the entropy of the universe

Second Lawfor any spontaneous process: ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr ≥ 0
ΔS_surrΔS_surr = −q_sys / T (at constant T)
At constant T,PΔS_univ = ΔS_sys − ΔH_sys/T = −ΔG_sys/T
SpontaneousΔG_sys < 0 ↔ ΔS_univ > 0
EquilibriumΔG_sys = 0 ↔ ΔS_univ = 0
12

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — conservation versus direction

Heat Q flows from a 300 K body to a 400 K body with no other effect. Does this violate the First Law?

Solution

Energy conservation can still be satisfied because the heat lost by one body equals the heat gained by the other. The impossibility is a Second-Law issue: the proposed direction is opposite to spontaneous heat flow.

◆Concept Application 2 — exothermicity trap

Water freezing releases heat. Must freezing therefore be spontaneous at every temperature?

Solution

No. Above the melting temperature at the stated pressure, liquid water is the stable phase and freezing is non-spontaneous despite being exothermic.

◆Concept Application 3 — endothermic spontaneity

Give a thermodynamic reason why an endothermic process may still be spontaneous.

Solution

Spontaneity depends on the complete driving criterion, not heat alone. A sufficiently favourable entropy contribution can outweigh positive enthalpy at the specified temperature.

◆Concept Application 4 — activation barrier

A fuel–air mixture can remain unchanged until a spark is supplied. Does the spark make combustion thermodynamically favourable?

Solution

No. The spark helps the system cross the kinetic activation barrier. It does not create the overall thermodynamic driving force or change the final equilibrium criterion.

◆Concept Application 5 — diffusion reverse

Two gases mix after a partition is removed. Could energy conservation alone forbid their spontaneous re-separation?

Solution

No. A hypothetical re-separation could conserve energy. The reason it does not occur spontaneously is directional and entropic, requiring the Second Law.

◆Concept Application 6 — refrigerator

A refrigerator transfers 500 J from a cold space and rejects 700 J to the room. Determine the required work input.

Solution

Energy conservation gives Winput = 700−500 = 200 J. The First Law gives the magnitude; the Second Law explains why non-zero work is required.

◆Concept Application 7 — PMM-I

A machine claims to deliver 10 kJ work per cycle while receiving only 6 kJ total energy. Identify the violated law.

Solution

It violates the First Law because 4 kJ of energy appears without an equivalent decrease elsewhere.

◆Concept Application 8 — PMM-II

A cyclic engine absorbs 1000 J from a single reservoir and converts it entirely to work. Energy is conserved. Why is it impossible?

Solution

It violates the Kelvin–Planck form of the Second Law. A cyclic heat engine must reject some heat to a lower-temperature sink.

◆Concept Application 9 — spontaneity and speed

Diamond conversion to graphite is thermodynamically favourable under ordinary conditions but extremely slow. What does this demonstrate?

Solution

Thermodynamic favourability and kinetic rate are different questions. A large activation barrier can make a favourable change imperceptibly slow.

◆Concept Application 10 — equilibrium destination

What happens to the thermodynamic driving force as a spontaneous process approaches equilibrium?

Solution

The macroscopic driving force decreases and becomes zero at equilibrium. Forward and reverse microscopic events may continue at equal average rates.

◆Concept Application 11 — work-to-heat conversion

A paddle wheel supplies 4 kJ work to an insulated liquid. Can all 4 kJ appear as increased internal energy?

Solution

Yes. With q = 0 and negligible other energy changes, ΔU = w = +4 kJ. Complete conversion of work into disordered internal energy is allowed.

◆Concept Application 12 — heat-to-work asymmetry

Why is the reverse claim—complete cyclic conversion of heat from one reservoir into work—not equivalent?

Solution

It would require a Second-Law-forbidden PMM-II. Energy conservation alone permits the arithmetic, but natural direction and entropy impose an additional restriction.

◆Concept Application 13 — classical nuclear caveat

Why is ΔU = q + w for a fixed-mass chemical system insufficient for a nuclear reactor energy audit?

Solution

Nuclear processes can change rest mass measurably. A complete balance must include mass–energy conversion, radiation, matter flow, and other energy terms.

◆Concept Application 14 — coupled non-spontaneous process

Can a non-spontaneous process occur in nature?

Solution

Yes, when coupled to a sufficiently favourable process or driven by external work. The combined process must satisfy the overall thermodynamic direction criterion.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

The First Law closes the energy ledger; the Second Law chooses the natural direction

Kinetics

PART 14 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyHeat Engines, Carnot Cycle, Carnot Theorem, and Working-Fluid Independence
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYCARNOT ENGINE EDITION

Thermodynamics • Heat-Engine Layer

Maximum efficiency is fixed by temperature—not by clever working fluid

A heat engine must absorb heat from a hot source, reject part to a cold sink, and convert only the remainder into work. The reversible Carnot cycle establishes the absolute efficiency ceiling.

Carnot limit

Wout = QH − QC
η = Wout/QH
ηCarnot = 1 − TC/TH
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Thermal reservoirs, source and sink

Ideal bodies whose temperature remains effectively constant during heat exchange.

A thermal reservoir has such a large effective heat capacity that receiving or releasing the cycle heat does not measurably alter its temperature. The high-temperature reservoir is the source; the low-temperature reservoir is the sink.

Concept lens

Hot source

Supplies the absorbed heat magnitude \(Q_H\) at temperature \(T_H\).

Concept lens

Working system

Executes a cycle and returns to its initial state.

Concept lens

Cold sink

Receives the rejected heat magnitude \(Q_C\) at temperature \(T_C\).

Concept lens

Temperature order

A heat engine requires \(T_H>T_C>0\).
02

Heat engine and efficiency

A continuously operating engine must work cyclically.

Energy conservation per cycle

QH = Wout + QC

Thermal efficiency

η = Wout/QH = 1 − QC/QH

Concept lens

Magnitude convention

\(Q_H\), \(Q_C\), and \(W_{\text{out}}\) are positive magnitudes in engine language. In chemistry sign notation, net work on the engine is negative because the engine delivers work to the surroundings.

Concept lens

Why an engine needs a sink

The Second Law forbids cyclic conversion of all heat drawn from one reservoir into work. Some heat must be rejected.
03

Carnot cycle

A theoretical reversible cycle designed to achieve the maximum possible efficiency.

A fixed quantity of working substance executes four reversible processes: two isothermal and two adiabatic.

Concept lens

1 → 2

Reversible isothermal expansion at \(T_H\); heat \(Q_H\) enters and the gas performs work.

Concept lens

2 → 3

Reversible adiabatic expansion; \(q=0\) and temperature falls from \(T_H\) to \(T_C\).

Concept lens

3 → 4

Reversible isothermal compression at \(T_C\); heat \(Q_C\) is rejected.

Concept lens

4 → 1

Reversible adiabatic compression; \(q=0\) and temperature rises back to \(T_H\).
04

Carnot cycle on P–V and T–S diagrams

Concept lens

P–V interpretation

The clockwise enclosed area equals net work output. Expansion occurs at higher pressure than compression.

Concept lens

T–S interpretation

For a reversible process, \(\delta q_{\mathrm{rev}}=T\,dS\). The two isotherms form the horizontal sides and the reversible adiabats are vertical because entropy remains constant.
05

Derivation of Carnot efficiency

The chapter ideal-gas derivation reconstructed with explicit signs and magnitudes.

Leg 1 → 2

QH = nRTH ln(V₂/V₁)

Reversible isothermal expansion at the hot-reservoir temperature.

Leg 2 → 3

q23 = 0

Reversible adiabatic expansion lowers the gas temperature from TH to TC.

Leg 3 → 4

QC = nRTC ln(V3/V4)

QC is the positive magnitude of heat rejected during reversible isothermal compression.

Leg 4 → 1

q41 = 0

Reversible adiabatic compression raises the temperature from TC back to TH.

Adiabatic geometry

V₂/V₁ = V3/V4

This follows by dividing the two reversible-adiabatic endpoint relations.

Heat ratio

QC/QH = TC/TH

The logarithmic volume ratios are identical and cancel.

Work output

Wout = QH − QC

Heat ratio

QC/QH = TC/TH

Carnot efficiency

ηCarnot = 1 − TC/TH

Concept lens

Absolute temperatures only

The temperature ratio is meaningful only on an absolute scale. Always use kelvin.
06

Why 100% efficiency is impossible

Condition for η = 1 at finite TH

TC = 0 K

Alternative limiting idealisation

TH → ∞ for finite TC

Concept lens

Both are unattainable operating limits

Absolute zero cannot be reached, and an infinite-temperature source is not a physical reservoir. Therefore every real or reversible finite-temperature engine has \(\eta<1\).
07

How source and sink temperatures affect efficiency

Differential sensitivities

∂η/∂TH = TC/TH2, ∂η/∂TC = −1/TH

Concept lens

Equal kelvin changes are not equally powerful

Because \(T_C/T_H<1\), lowering \(T_C\) by one kelvin changes efficiency more than raising \(T_H\) by one kelvin.

Concept lens

Engineering caution

A colder sink may raise the theoretical ceiling, but producing that sink can require additional equipment and energy.
08

Carnot theorem

Maximum efficiency

No engine operating between the same two reservoir temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible engine.

Universal reversible value

All reversible engines between the same TH and TC have the same efficiency.

Working-fluid independence

Efficiency depends only on reservoir temperatures, not on whether the working substance is an ideal gas, real gas, liquid–vapour system or another reversible medium.

Irreversibility penalty

Friction, finite temperature differences, turbulence and uncontrolled expansion reduce actual efficiency below the Carnot value.

Concept lens

Maximum work logic

Reversible expansion produces the maximum possible work, while reversible compression requires the minimum work input. Their combination gives the largest possible net cycle work for the given heat input and reservoir temperatures.

Concept lens

Contradiction proof idea

If one reversible engine were more efficient than another between the same reservoirs, the better engine could drive the other backward and create a forbidden net effect. Hence all reversible engines must share the same efficiency.
09

Retained van der Waals working-fluid proof

Retained chapter proof

A van der Waals working gas gives the same Carnot efficiency

WORKING-FLUID INDEPENDENCE

Let the working gas obey\((P+a n^2/V^2)(V-nb)=nRT\), with heat capacity \(C_{V,m}\) treated as constant. The four cycle legs remain reversible.

Reversible isothermal entropy change

ΔS = nR ln[(V₂−nb)/(V₁−nb)]

Heat absorbed at TH

QH = nRTH ln[(V₂−nb)/(V₁−nb)]

Heat rejected magnitude at TC

QC = nRTC ln[(V₃−nb)/(V₄−nb)]

Reversible adiabatic relation

T(V−nb)R/CV,m = constant

Upper adiabat

TH(V₂−nb)R/CV,m = TC(V₃−nb)R/CV,m

Lower adiabat

TC(V₄−nb)R/CV,m = TH(V₁−nb)R/CV,m

Divide the adiabatic relations

(V₂−nb)/(V₁−nb) = (V₃−nb)/(V₄−nb)

Heat ratio and efficiency

QC/QH = TC/TH ⇒ η = 1−TC/TH

Concept lens

Where did the attraction parameter a go?

The attraction term affects individual work and internal-energy changes on particular legs, but the reversible isothermal heat is \(T\Delta S\), and the cyclic efficiency depends on the heat ratio. The final temperature-only result is independent of both \(a\) and \(b\).
10

Reversible versus real engines

Engine typeKey featuresEfficiencyMeaning
Reversible/CarnotNo friction; infinitesimal thermal and mechanical gradientsη = 1−TC/THmaximum theoretical efficiency
Internally reversible but finite heat transferMechanical idealisation but heat crosses finite ΔTbelow Carnotexternal irreversibility remains
Real engineFriction, turbulence, finite rates, leakagewell below Carnotfinite power and practical losses
Single-reservoir 100% converterQH converted entirely to W in a cycleη = 1 claimedimpossible by Second Law

Concept lens

Efficiency versus power

Carnot operation maximises efficiency but requires infinitesimal temperature and pressure differences. The ideal cycle therefore takes infinite time and has zero limiting power.
11

Thermodynamics around you

Steam power station

Fuel or nuclear heat supplies a hot source, turbines produce work, and cooling towers or rivers act as the low-temperature sink.

Car engine radiator

The engine cannot convert all combustion energy into work. Waste heat must be rejected through exhaust and cooling systems.

Ocean thermal power

A small temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water produces a very low Carnot ceiling.

Cryogenic sink advantage

A colder sink can raise the theoretical efficiency, but creating and maintaining that sink may itself require substantial energy.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
A heat engine converts all absorbed heat into work.IncorrectA cyclic engine must reject some heat to a lower-temperature sink.
Carnot efficiency uses Celsius temperatures.IncorrectTH and TC must be absolute temperatures in kelvin.
A reversible engine can have 100% efficiency at ordinary temperatures.Incorrectη = 1 requires TC = 0 K or the limiting idealisation TH → ∞.
Changing the working fluid changes Carnot efficiency.IncorrectFor a reversible cycle between fixed reservoirs, efficiency depends only on TH and TC.
Carnot engine has maximum power.IncorrectIt has maximum efficiency. The reversible limit operates infinitely slowly and has zero limiting power.
The adiabatic legs transfer heat because temperature changes.IncorrectTheir temperature changes arise from work; q = 0.
All reversible engines are equally efficient regardless of reservoir temperatures.IncorrectEquality applies only when they operate between the same TH and TC.
A real engine may exceed Carnot efficiency by using a better design.IncorrectDesign can reduce losses but cannot surpass the reversible temperature limit.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Carnot cycle — step-by-step derivation

Step 1: Isothermal expansion at T_hq_h = −w₁ = nRT_h ln(V₂/V₁) > 0
Step 2: Adiabatic expansion T_h → T_cq = 0; w₂ = Cv(T_c − T_h) < 0; work done by gas
Step 3: Isothermal compression at T_cq_c = −w₃ = nRT_c ln(V₄/V₃) < 0 (heat released)
Step 4: Adiabatic compression T_c → T_hq = 0; w₄ = Cv(T_h − T_c) > 0
Net workw_net = w₁ + w₂ + w₃ + w₄ = −(q_h + q_c)
Adiabat relationT_h V₂^{γ−1} = T_c V₃^{γ−1} and T_h V₁^{γ−1} = T_c V₄^{γ−1}
ThereforeV₂/V₁ = V₃/V₄
Efficiencyη = w_by/q_h = 1 + q_c/q_h = 1 − T_c/T_h
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — direct Carnot efficiency

A reversible engine operates between 600 K and 300 K. Calculate its efficiency.

Solution

η = 1 − TC/TH = 1 − 300/600 = 0.50, or 50%.

◆Concept Application 2 — heat rejection

The engine in the previous problem absorbs 8.0 kJ per cycle. Find work output and heat rejected.

Solution

Wout = ηQH = 0.50×8.0 = 4.0 kJ. Therefore QC = QH−Wout = 4.0 kJ.

◆Concept Application 3 — unknown source temperature

A Carnot engine has efficiency 40% and rejects heat to a 300 K sink. Find TH.

Solution

0.40 = 1−300/TH, so TH = 300/0.60 = 500 K.

◆Concept Application 4 — unknown sink temperature

A reversible engine operates at 70% efficiency with TH = 1000 K. Find TC.

Solution

TC = TH(1−η) = 1000×0.30 = 300 K.

◆Concept Application 5 — compare temperature changes

For TH = 600 K and TC = 300 K, compare the efficiency gain from raising TH by 10 K with lowering TC by 10 K.

Solution

Original η = 0.5000. Raising TH to 610 K gives η ≈ 0.5082, gain 0.0082. Lowering TC to 290 K gives η ≈ 0.5167, gain 0.0167. Lowering the sink has the larger effect.

◆Concept Application 6 — impossible claim

An engine between 500 K and 300 K claims 50% efficiency. Assess the claim.

Solution

Carnot maximum is 1−300/500 = 0.40. A 50% engine would exceed the reversible maximum and is impossible.

◆Concept Application 7 — reversible heat ratio

A reversible engine absorbs 12 kJ at 800 K and rejects heat at 400 K. Find QC.

Solution

For a reversible engine, QC/QH = TC/TH = 400/800 = 1/2. Hence QC = 6 kJ.

◆Concept Application 8 — 100% efficiency

Why can a finite-temperature Carnot engine not reach 100% efficiency?

Solution

η = 1−TC/TH. With finite TH and positive TC, the ratio TC/TH is non-zero. Reaching η = 1 would require TC = 0 K or the limiting idealisation TH→∞.

◆Concept Application 9 — working-fluid change

An ideal-gas Carnot engine is replaced by a reversible liquid–vapour working substance between the same reservoirs. What happens to efficiency?

Solution

Nothing. Carnot theorem fixes the efficiency solely through TH and TC, provided the complete cycle is reversible.

◆Concept Application 10 — adiabatic volume ratio

Show that the two isothermal volume ratios in an ideal-gas Carnot cycle are equal.

Solution

Use THV2^(γ−1)=TCV3^(γ−1) and TCV4^(γ−1)=THV1^(γ−1). Division gives (V₂/V₁)^(γ−1)=(V3/V4)^(γ−1), so V₂/V₁=V3/V4.

◆Concept Application 11 — T–S rectangle

A reversible Carnot cycle has entropy width ΔS = 20 J K⁻¹ between 500 K and 300 K. Find QH, QC and Wout.

Solution

QH = THΔS = 10.0 kJ. QC = TCΔS = 6.0 kJ. Wout = (TH−TC)ΔS = 4.0 kJ.

◆Concept Application 12 — real-engine benchmark

A real engine between 700 K and 300 K has efficiency 35%. What fraction of the Carnot efficiency does it achieve?

Solution

ηCarnot = 1−300/700 ≈ 0.5714. The fraction is 0.35/0.5714 ≈ 0.6125, or about 61.3% of Carnot.

◆Concept Application 13 — theorem contradiction argument

Why must all reversible engines between the same reservoirs have identical efficiency?

Solution

If one reversible engine were more efficient, the more efficient engine could drive the less efficient one in reverse and create a net transfer that violates the Second Law. Therefore their efficiencies must be equal.

◆Concept Application 14 — power warning

Does the Carnot engine deliver maximum power?

Solution

No. Carnot operation is reversible and requires infinitesimal gradients, so the ideal cycle takes infinite time and has zero limiting power. It maximises efficiency, not power.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Carnot efficiency is a universal temperature ceiling

PART 14 COMPLETE

Engine balance

QH = Wout + QC

Efficiency

η = 1 − QC/QH

Carnot limit

η = 1 − TC/TH

Theorem

all reversible engines match between same reservoirs

PART 15 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyReversed Carnot Refrigerator, Heat Pump, COP, and the Entropy Bridge
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYREFRIGERATOR & HEAT-PUMP EDITION

Thermodynamics • Reversed-Cycle Layer

Work does not create cold—it pumps heat uphill

A refrigerator removes heat from a cold region. A heat pump delivers heat to a warm region. Both use the same reversed cycle and must receive work to oppose the natural direction of heat flow.

Reversed-cycle core

QH = QC + Win
COPR = QC/Win
COPHP = QH/Win
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Ideal refrigerator: the Carnot cycle run backward

Heat is absorbed at low temperature and rejected at high temperature by supplying work.

The primary chapter sequence introduces the ideal refrigerator as the reverse of a heat engine: heat \(Q_C\) is removed from a cold reservoir, work is supplied, and a larger heat \(Q_H\) is rejected to a hotter reservoir.

Energy balance

QH = QC + Win

Concept lens

Second-Law meaning

Heat does not pass from colder to hotter surroundings as the sole effect of a cyclic device. External work is required.
02

Refrigerator versus heat pump

The cycle is the same; the desired effect is different.

Energy balance

QH = QC + Win

The heat delivered to the hot side equals extracted heat plus supplied work.

Refrigerator objective

COPR = QC/Win

Desired effect: remove as much heat as possible from the cold space per unit work.

Heat-pump objective

COPHP = QH/Win

Desired effect: deliver as much heat as possible to the warm space per unit work.

Relationship

COPHP = COPR + 1

Because QH = QC + Win.

Concept lens

Refrigerator

The useful output is \(Q_C\): heat removed from the refrigerated space.

Concept lens

Heat pump

The useful output is \(Q_H\): heat delivered to the warm building or process.

Concept lens

COP is not thermal efficiency

A coefficient of performance compares useful heat transfer with work input. It may be greater than one without violating conservation because environmental heat is also transferred.
03

Reversed Carnot cycle

Concept lens

1 → 2

Reversible isothermal expansion at \(T_C\); the working substance absorbs \(Q_C\).

Concept lens

2 → 3

Reversible adiabatic compression; temperature rises from \(T_C\) to \(T_H\).

Concept lens

3 → 4

Reversible isothermal compression at \(T_H\); heat \(Q_H\) is rejected.

Concept lens

4 → 1

Reversible adiabatic expansion; temperature falls from \(T_H\) to \(T_C\).
04

Derivation of the maximum coefficients of performance

The reversible device requires the minimum work for a specified heat transfer.

Step 1

Reversible heat ratio

QH/QC = TH/TC

The same entropy magnitude crosses the two isothermal legs.

Step 2

Work input

Win = QH − QC

The reversed device requires net supplied work.

Step 3

Refrigerator COP

COPR = QC/(QH−QC)

Substitute the reversible temperature ratio.

Step 4

Carnot refrigerator

COPR,Carnot = TC/(TH−TC)

Maximum possible refrigerator COP between the two reservoirs.

Step 5

Heat-pump COP

COPHP = QH/(QH−QC)

The useful effect is heat delivered at the hot side.

Step 6

Carnot heat pump

COPHP,Carnot = TH/(TH−TC)

Equivalent to COPR,Carnot + 1.

Carnot refrigerator

COPR,max = TC/(TH−TC)

Carnot heat pump

COPHP,max = TH/(TH−TC)

Universal relationship

COPHP = COPR + 1

Concept lens

Absolute temperature requirement

All Carnot temperature formulas require kelvin.
05

Engine, refrigerator, and heat-pump relationships

DeviceDesired effectPerformance definitionReversible value
Carnot heat enginework outputη = Wout/QH1 − TC/TH
Carnot refrigeratorheat removed from cold sideCOPR = QC/WinTC/(TH−TC)
Carnot heat pumpheat delivered to hot sideCOPHP = QH/WinTH/(TH−TC)

In terms of engine efficiency

COPHP = 1/η

Refrigerator relationship

COPR = (1−η)/η

Heat-pump relationship

COPHP = COPR + 1

Concept lens

Same reservoir temperatures

These compact relations use the Carnot engine, refrigerator, and heat pump operating between the same \(T_H\) and \(T_C\).
06

Temperature lift controls work demand

Concept lens

Small temperature gap

When \(T_H-T_C\) is small, the reversible COP can be very large because little work is required per unit heat transferred.

Concept lens

Large temperature gap

Deep freezing on a hot day demands a large temperature lift. Work input rises and COP falls.
07

Original complete worked example

Original Synergic Bond worked example

Carnot refrigerator and heat-pump performance

FULL ENERGY AUDIT

A reversible refrigerator operates between a cold compartment at 260 K and a room at 300 K. It removes 5.20 kJ of heat from the compartment per cycle. Find the work input, heat rejected, refrigerator COP, and heat-pump COP.

Carnot refrigerator COP

COPR = TC/(TH−TC) = 260/40 = 6.50

Work input

Win = QC/COPR = 5.20/6.50 = 0.800 kJ

Heat rejected

QH = QC + Win = 6.00 kJ

Heat-pump COP

COPHP = QH/Win = 6.00/0.800 = 7.50

Relationship check

COPHP = COPR + 1 = 7.50

Concept lens

Interpretation

A COP greater than one does not violate energy conservation. The device does not create heat; it transfers\(Q_C\) from the cold space and adds the supplied work before rejecting \(Q_H\).
08

Practical refrigerator

Real devices approximate the objective but not the reversible Carnot path.

Concept lens

Evaporator

The circulating refrigerant absorbs heat from the cold interior.

Concept lens

Compressor

Electrical work raises refrigerant pressure and temperature.

Concept lens

Condenser

Heat is rejected to the surrounding room at the rear coil.

Concept lens

Expansion device

Pressure drops irreversibly before the refrigerant returns to the cold side.

Concept lens

Chapter boundary

The operating-cycle direction is treated here. Detailed latent heat, phase-change enthalpy and refrigerant calorimetry belong to the separate Thermochemistry notes.
09

Why real COP is below Carnot COP

Loss 1

Finite temperature gaps

Heat exchangers require non-zero driving differences.

Loss 2

Compressor friction

Mechanical and electrical dissipation raise work demand.

Loss 3

Pressure losses

Flow through pipes and valves destroys useful pressure potential.

Loss 4

Throttling

The expansion device is strongly irreversible and produces entropy.

10

Entropy bridge

The refrigerator reveals the formal state function needed to quantify direction and irreversibility.

Cyclic device

ΔSdevice = 0

The working substance returns to its initial state.

Cold reservoir

ΔSC = −QC/TC

The cold reservoir loses heat.

Hot reservoir

ΔSH = +QH/TH

The hot reservoir gains heat.

Universe

ΔSuniv = QH/TH − QC/TC ≥ 0

Equality holds only for a reversible refrigerator.

Reversible condition

QH/TH = QC/TC

Second-Law inequality

ΔSuniverse = QH/TH − QC/TC ≥ 0

Concept lens

Why entropy becomes unavoidable

The First Law gives only \(Q_H=Q_C+W_{\mathrm{in}}\). It cannot distinguish a possible refrigerator from an impossible work-free cold-to-hot heat transfer. The entropy balance supplies that direction test.
11

Clausius and Kelvin–Planck statements are equivalent

CLAUSIUS STATEMENT

No cyclic device can have the sole effect of transferring heat from a colder body to a hotter body.

KELVIN–PLANCK STATEMENT

No cyclic device can have the sole effect of absorbing heat from one reservoir and converting it completely into work.

Concept lens

Why one violation would create the other

A hypothetical perfect heat engine could power an ordinary refrigerator without external work, violating Clausius. Conversely, a work-free refrigerator could be coupled to an ordinary engine to convert heat from one reservoir completely into work.
12

Thermodynamics around you

Why the back of a refrigerator is warm

The condenser rejects both the heat extracted from the cabinet and the electrical work supplied to the compressor.

Air conditioner on a hot day

As outdoor temperature rises, the temperature lift grows and the ideal and actual COP both fall.

Heat pump in winter

A heat pump can deliver several joules of indoor heating per joule of electrical work by extracting environmental heat.

Freezer frost and dirty coils

Poor heat transfer increases required temperature differences, raising compressor work and lowering practical COP.

13

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
A refrigerator creates cold.IncorrectIt extracts heat from a cold region and rejects a larger heat quantity to a warmer region.
COP must be less than one.IncorrectCOP is not an efficiency. It may exceed one because the useful heat includes transferred environmental energy.
A refrigerator and a heat pump are different thermodynamic cycles.IncorrectThe same reversed cycle can serve both purposes; the desired heat transfer differs.
COPHP equals COPR.IncorrectCOPHP = COPR + 1 because QH = QC + Win.
The larger the temperature gap, the larger the COP.IncorrectA larger temperature lift requires more work and lowers COP.
A reversible refrigerator transfers heat from cold to hot without work.IncorrectEven the reversible device requires work input; reversibility only minimises it.
Opening a refrigerator cools the room.IncorrectThe room gains the electrical work input as net energy and warms.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements — equivalence

Kelvin–PlanckIt is impossible to construct a heat engine operating in a cycle that absorbs heat from a reservoir and converts it entirely to work.
ClausiusIt is impossible to construct a device operating in a cycle whose sole effect is to transfer heat from a cold reservoir to a hot reservoir.
Equivalence proof (sketch)Assume Kelvin–Planck is violated → build a device with η = 1 → drive a reverse Carnot (refrigerator) → net result violates Clausius. And vice versa.
Carnot theoremNo engine operating between two fixed temperatures can be more efficient than the Carnot engine.
14

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — direct refrigerator COP

A Carnot refrigerator operates between 250 K and 300 K. Find COPR.

Solution

COPR = TC/(TH−TC) = 250/50 = 5.

◆Concept Application 2 — heat-pump COP

For the same temperatures, find COPHP.

Solution

COPHP = TH/(TH−TC) = 300/50 = 6, also equal to COPR + 1.

◆Concept Application 3 — energy balance

A refrigerator removes 900 J from its cold compartment while consuming 300 J work. Find heat rejected and COPR.

Solution

QH = QC + Win = 1200 J. COPR = QC/Win = 900/300 = 3.

◆Concept Application 4 — work requirement

A reversible refrigerator removes 12 kJ from a 270 K space and rejects heat to a 300 K room. Find minimum work.

Solution

COPR = 270/(300−270) = 9. Therefore Win,min = 12/9 = 1.333 kJ.

◆Concept Application 5 — unknown cold temperature

A Carnot refrigerator has COPR = 4 and rejects heat to 300 K. Find TC.

Solution

4 = TC/(300−TC). Hence 1200−4TC = TC, so TC = 240 K.

◆Concept Application 6 — unknown hot temperature

A reversible heat pump has COPHP = 5 and extracts heat from 280 K surroundings. Find TH.

Solution

5 = TH/(TH−280). Thus 5TH−1400 = TH, so TH = 350 K.

◆Concept Application 7 — temperature-lift penalty

For a refrigerator with TC = 260 K, compare ideal COP when TH is 280 K and 320 K.

Solution

At 280 K, COPR = 260/20 = 13. At 320 K, COPR = 260/60 ≈ 4.33. A larger temperature lift sharply reduces performance.

◆Concept Application 8 — impossible COP

A refrigerator between 250 K and 300 K claims COPR = 7. Assess it.

Solution

Carnot maximum is 250/50 = 5. A COP of 7 exceeds the reversible limit and is impossible.

◆Concept Application 9 — entropy test

A refrigerator removes 500 J from 250 K and rejects 650 J to 300 K. Is the cycle thermodynamically possible?

Solution

ΔSuniv = 650/300 − 500/250 = 2.1667−2.0000 = +0.1667 J K⁻¹. It is possible and irreversible. Work input is 150 J.

◆Concept Application 10 — forbidden refrigerator

A device transfers 400 J from 250 K to 300 K with no work and no other effect. Test it.

Solution

ΔSuniv = 400/300−400/250 = −0.2667 J K⁻¹, which is impossible. It violates the Clausius statement.

◆Concept Application 11 — COP greater than one

Explain why COPHP = 4 does not imply 400% energy efficiency.

Solution

COP compares useful heat delivered with work input, not output energy with total energy input. The delivered heat includes both extracted environmental heat and supplied work.

◆Concept Application 12 — engine relationship

For the same TH and TC, express the Carnot refrigerator COP in terms of Carnot-engine efficiency η.

Solution

η = (TH−TC)/TH. Therefore COPR = TC/(TH−TC) = (1−η)/η.

◆Concept Application 13 — heat-pump relationship

Express Carnot heat-pump COP in terms of engine efficiency η.

Solution

COPHP = TH/(TH−TC) = 1/η.

◆Concept Application 14 — real device losses

Why does throttling lower the COP of a practical refrigerator relative to a reversed Carnot device?

Solution

Throttling is irreversible and produces entropy. Additional compressor work is required for the same cooling effect, so actual COP falls below the reversible maximum.

◆Concept Application 15 — open door paradox

Can an open refrigerator cool a closed room?

Solution

No. The refrigerator rejects QH = QC + Win into the room while removing only QC from it. The net room energy gain equals the electrical work input, so the room warms.

◆Concept Application 16 — reversible condition

For a reversible refrigerator, prove QH/TH = QC/TC.

Solution

The cyclic working substance has zero entropy change. Reversibility also requires zero total entropy change, so QH/TH−QC/TC = 0.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

A reversed cycle moves heat uphill; entropy sets the minimum work

PART 15 COMPLETE

Energy balance

QH = QC + Win

Refrigerator

COPR = QC/Win

Heat pump

COPHP = QH/Win = COPR + 1

Carnot limit

COPR,max = TC/(TH−TC)

PART 16 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyEntropy as a State Function, Second-Law Meaning, and Molecular Interpretation
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYENTROPY FOUNDATIONS

Thermodynamics • Second-Law State Function

Entropy converts the arrow of natural change into a calculable state function

Carnot’s reversible cycle reveals a quantity whose cyclic integral vanishes. That quantity is entropy—a state function connecting heat, temperature, energy dispersal, and lost work potential.

Entropy core

∮ δqrev/T = 0
dS = δqrev/T
S is extensive and additive
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

From the Carnot cycle to entropy

The reversible cyclic integral identifies an exact differential.

For a reversible Carnot cycle, the heat exchanges satisfy the temperature-weighted cancellation:

Carnot heat relation

QH/TH − QC/TC = 0

Generalising a reversible cycle into many small reversible heat exchanges gives:

Clausius theorem for a reversible cycle

∮ δqrev/T = 0

Definition of entropy

dS = δqrev/T

Cyclic state-function test

∮dS = 0

Concept lens

Why this proves state-function behaviour

A differential whose integral around every reversible closed path is zero is exact. Therefore its finite change depends only on the initial and final equilibrium states.
02

Entropy change for any process

Use a reversible path for evaluation, even when the real process is irreversible.

Finite entropy change

ΔS = S₂−S₁ = ∫₁² δqrev/T

Concept lens

The reversible path is a calculation path

The system need not actually travel reversibly. A hypothetical reversible path connecting the same equilibrium states is sufficient to calculate \(\Delta S\).

Concept lens

Do not replace δqrev by the actual irreversible heat

In general, \(dS\ne\delta q_{\mathrm{irr}}/T\). The missing contribution is entropy generation, developed in Part 17.
03

Second-Law statements

Clausius statement

Heat cannot, as the sole effect of a cyclic process, pass from a colder body to a hotter body without external work or an equivalent compensating change.

Kelvin–Planck statement

No cyclic engine can absorb heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work.

Entropy statement

For an isolated system, spontaneous change proceeds with increasing total entropy; reversible change has no entropy generation.

Entropy form for an isolated system

spontaneous process ⇒ ΔSisolated > 0

Reversible limit

reversible process in the isolated universe ⇒ ΔSuniverse = 0

Concept lens

“Entropy of the universe always increases” needs one refinement

It increases for irreversible spontaneous change and remains constant in the reversible limit. It never decreases for an isolated universe.
04

Entropy properties and units

PropertyExpressionMeaning
SymbolSstate variable
Differential definitiondS = δqrev/Treversible evaluation
SI unitJ K⁻¹total entropy
Molar entropyJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹intensive after division by amount
Specific entropyJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹intensive after division by mass
TypeextensiveS doubles when an identical subsystem is duplicated
AdditivityStotal = ΣSifor independent subsystems
Cyclic integral∮dS = 0state-function test

Concept lens

Extensive versus molar entropy

Total entropy scales with system size. Dividing by amount or mass creates molar or specific entropy, which is intensive.
05

What entropy means physically

Randomness is useful intuition, but energy dispersal and accessible states are more precise.

Concept lens

Energy dispersal

Entropy grows when energy can be distributed among more particles, modes, and locations.

Concept lens

Spatial dispersal

Gas expansion and mixing increase the volume and arrangements accessible to particles.

Concept lens

Microscopic multiplicity

A macrostate compatible with more microscopic arrangements has greater entropy.

Concept lens

Ordered and disordered are not moral labels

“Disorder” describes multiplicity and uncertainty in microscopic arrangement. It does not mean visual messiness alone.
06

Unavailable energy and lost work potential

The chapter intuition is retained with dimensional and exergy corrections.

A common description treats entropy as a measure of unavailable energy. The rigorous statement requires a reference environment at temperature \(T_0\).

Destroyed work potential

Wlost = T0Sgen

Entropy transfer with rejected heat at T0

Qrejected = T0ΔS for reversible rejection

Concept lens

Why T0 is essential

Entropy is measured in joules per kelvin, not joules. Multiplication by a specified environmental temperature converts entropy generation into lost work potential.

Concept lens

Greater entropy does not mean all energy is unusable

Available work depends on the complete state relative to an environment. The precise lost-work statement concerns entropy generation, not entropy in isolation.
07

Primary entropy trends

01

Temperature

T ↑ ⇒ S generally ↑

Higher temperature opens access to more translational, rotational and vibrational energy distributions.

Compare the same substance and phase unless a phase transition is handled explicitly.

02

Pressure of a gas

P ↑ at fixed T ⇒ S ↓

Compression reduces available volume and the number of accessible positional arrangements.

This is a gas trend under specified T and composition, not a universal rule for every condensed phase.

03

Molecular complexity

more atoms / modes ⇒ usually larger molar S

More complex molecules possess more rotational and vibrational modes and therefore more ways to distribute energy.

Comparisons require similar temperature, phase and standard-state conditions.

04

Intermixing gases

mixing distinct gases ⇒ ΔS > 0

Each gas gains access to the combined volume and more positional arrangements become available.

05

Number of gas particles

more gas moles ⇒ greater total S

Entropy is extensive. Additional particles add accessible microscopic states.

06

Physical state

Ssolid < Sliquid < Sgas

Molecular positional and orientational freedom generally increases from solid to liquid to gas.

This is a broad trend for the same substance at compatible conditions.

07

Structural flexibility

more flexible / softer modes ⇒ larger S

Low-frequency motions and multiple conformations increase accessible arrangements.

The example graphite > diamond is valid, but “2D always exceeds 3D” is not a universal law.

08

Noble-gas molar mass

He < Ne < Ar < Kr < Xe in standard molar S

At comparable T and P, heavier monatomic gases have denser translational energy levels.

08

Retained molecular-complexity comparisons

ComparisonRetained trendPhysical basis
C₂H₄ versus CH₄S(C₂H₄) > S(CH₄)more atoms and internal modes
SO₃, SO₂, O₂S(SO₃) > S(SO₂) > S(O₂)qualitative complexity/mass trend
CO₂ versus COS(CO₂) > S(CO)extra atom and vibrational modes
Nitrogen oxidesN₂O₅ > N₂O₄ > N₂O₃ > N₂O > NOqualitative same-condition trend from chapter sequence

Concept lens

Comparison conditions matter

The listed orderings are qualitative trends from the chapter sequence. Reliable numerical comparison requires the same temperature, pressure, phase, and standard-state definition.
09

Retained structural and chemical examples

Heating an egg

overall ΔSuniverse > 0

Heat transfer and irreversible protein denaturation increase the total entropy of system plus surroundings. Molecular unfolding may increase configurational possibilities, but the exact system-only entropy depends on conditions.

Stretching rubber

ΔSrubber < 0 at constant T

Polymer chains become more aligned and lose configurational freedom. The effect is chain ordering—not every bond being stretched to a maximum length.

Chelate formation

ΔS often > 0

[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ + 3 en → [Co(en)₃]³⁺ + 6 NH₃. More independently moving solute species are released, favouring a positive entropy contribution.

Polymerisation

ΔS < 0

n CH₂=CH₂ → (CH₂CH₂)n combines many freely translating molecules into a constrained macromolecule.

White phosphorus to red phosphorus

ΔS < 0

Discrete P₄ units transform into a more extended polymeric/network structure with reduced molecular freedom.

Cyclopropane to propene

ΔS > 0

Ring opening increases conformational and rotational freedom; the example identifies the gas-phase isomerisation as entropy-favoured.

Ice to liquid water

ΔS > 0

Melting increases molecular mobility and orientational freedom. Detailed latent-heat calculation belongs to Thermochemistry.

Water to water vapour

ΔS > 0

Vaporisation greatly increases translational freedom and accessible volume. Detailed enthalpy treatment remains in Thermochemistry.

Micelle formation

overall ΔS may be > 0

Aggregation orders surfactant molecules, but releases structured water from hydrophobic surfaces. The solvent entropy gain can dominate above the critical micelle concentration.

10

Original solved foundation examples

◆Same heat at two temperatures

A system reversibly absorbs 600 J at 300 K and another system absorbs the same heat at 600 K. Compare their entropy increases.

Solution

ΔS300 = 600/300 = 2.00 J K⁻¹. ΔS600 = 600/600 = 1.00 J K⁻¹. The same heat causes the larger entropy change at the lower temperature.

◆Extensivity check

One mole of a substance has entropy 180 J K⁻¹ at a stated condition. What is the entropy of 2.5 mol at the same condition?

Solution

Entropy is extensive, so S = 2.5×180 = 450 J K⁻¹. The molar entropy remains 180 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Reversible path evaluation

An irreversible process carries a system from A to B. A convenient reversible route between A and B gives ∫δqrev/T = 24 J K⁻¹. Find ΔSsystem.

Solution

Because entropy is a state function, ΔSsystem = 24 J K⁻¹ regardless of the actual irreversible path.

◆Destroyed work potential

A real process generates 15 J K⁻¹ of entropy in an environment at 300 K. Find the lost work potential.

Solution

Wlost = T0Sgen = 300×15 = 4500 J = 4.50 kJ.

11

Thermodynamics around you

A hot bath becomes uniform

Energy spreads from hotter regions to colder regions until thermal equilibrium. The combined isolated water system moves toward greater total entropy.

Perfume fills a room

Molecules gain access to a much larger spatial region, producing many more positional arrangements.

Rubber band warms on rapid stretching

Chain alignment reduces configurational entropy; an approximately adiabatic stretch raises temperature.

Detergent micelles form in water

Hydrophobic tails aggregate, but structured water is released, often giving a favourable total entropy contribution.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Entropy is simply disorder.RefineDisorder is a heuristic. Entropy is a state function linked to energy dispersal and the number of accessible microscopic states.
Entropy and unavailable energy have the same units.IncorrectEntropy has units J K⁻¹. Work potential destroyed is T0Sgen, which has units J.
dS = δq/T for every actual process.IncorrectThe equality uses reversible heat: dS = δqrev/T.
An adiabatic process must have ΔS = 0.IncorrectOnly a reversible adiabatic process has zero entropy change. Irreversible adiabatic processes generate entropy.
Higher pressure always means lower entropy for every substance.IncorrectThe simple trend is reliable for gas compression at specified T and composition, not universally for all phases.
A three-dimensional structure always has less entropy than a two-dimensional structure.IncorrectThe graphite–diamond example depends on actual lattice dynamics; dimensionality alone is not a universal criterion.
Stretching rubber lowers entropy because all bonds reach maximum length.IncorrectOrdinary elastic stretching primarily aligns chains and reduces conformational freedom; covalent bonds are not all extended to a maximum.
Micelle formation must decrease total entropy because aggregation creates order.IncorrectSolvent entropy can increase enough to make the total entropy change positive.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Clausius inequality — derivation

For any cycleΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr ≥ 0
ΔS_surr for surroundings at TΔS_surr = −δq_sys/T (heat absorbed by system)
Integrate over cycleΔS_cycle,sys + ΔS_surr,cycle ≥ 0
S is a state functionΔS_cycle,sys = 0
Therefore∮ δq/T ≤ 0 (Clausius inequality)
Equality∮ δq/T = 0 for all reversible cycles
Strict inequality∮ δq/T < 0 for irreversible cycles
Define entropydS ≡ δq_rev/T → S is a well-defined state function
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — state-function test

For a reversible cycle, ∮δqrev/T = 0. What mathematical conclusion follows?

Solution

The integrand defines an exact differential. A state function S exists such that dS = δqrev/T and ∮dS = 0.

◆Concept Application 2 — actual irreversible heat

During an irreversible process, may one generally write dS = δqirr/Tsystem?

Solution

No. The equality uses reversible heat. For an irreversible process, the entropy change is evaluated through a reversible path, or by the entropy-balance inequality developed next.

◆Concept Application 3 — entropy and size

A sample is divided into two equal equilibrium halves. How do total entropy and molar entropy change?

Solution

Each half has half the total entropy, because S is extensive. The molar entropy remains unchanged because it is intensive.

◆Concept Application 4 — pressure trend

At constant temperature, one mole of ideal gas is reversibly compressed. What is the sign of ΔS?

Solution

Negative. Compression reduces accessible volume. Quantitatively, ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = −nR ln(P₂/P₁).

◆Concept Application 5 — gas mixing

Two different ideal gases initially occupy separate equal volumes at the same T and P. The partition is removed. What happens to entropy?

Solution

Entropy increases because each gas expands into the full volume and the number of accessible positional arrangements rises.

◆Concept Application 6 — identical-gas caution

Does removing a partition between two samples of the same ideal gas at identical T and P create a macroscopic mixing entropy?

Solution

No. The initial and final macroscopic state are indistinguishable, so the thermodynamic mixing entropy is zero.

◆Concept Application 7 — phase trend

Rank the molar entropy of a pure substance in solid, liquid and gas states near compatible conditions.

Solution

Generally Ssolid < Sliquid < Sgas because translational and orientational freedom increases.

◆Concept Application 8 — graphite versus diamond

Why can graphite possess a larger molar entropy than diamond although both are pure carbon solids?

Solution

Graphite has softer lattice modes and layered structural freedom. Diamond’s rigid three-dimensional network restricts low-energy vibrations more strongly.

◆Concept Application 9 — stretched rubber

An ideal rubber band is stretched reversibly at constant temperature. What is the sign of the rubber’s configurational entropy change?

Solution

Negative. Stretching aligns polymer chains and reduces the number of accessible coil conformations.

◆Concept Application 10 — rubber heating effect

Why can an elastomer warm when stretched rapidly?

Solution

Rapid stretching is approximately adiabatic. Chain ordering lowers configurational entropy, so temperature rises to satisfy the entropy/energy balance.

◆Concept Application 11 — chelate entropy

Why can replacing six monodentate ligands by three bidentate ligands produce a favourable entropy change?

Solution

The reaction can release more independent small molecules into solution than it consumes, increasing translational entropy. This is one component of the chelate effect.

◆Concept Application 12 — polymerisation sign

Predict the entropy sign for addition polymerisation of gaseous ethene under comparable conditions.

Solution

Usually negative because many independently translating monomer molecules become one constrained macromolecular chain.

◆Concept Application 13 — entropy and complexity

Can molecular complexity alone guarantee the entropy ordering of two substances?

Solution

No. Temperature, phase, pressure, symmetry and intermolecular interactions also matter. Complexity is a trend, not an absolute law.

◆Concept Application 14 — low-temperature heat

The same reversible heat q is absorbed at T₁ and T₂ with T₂ > T₁. Which entropy increase is larger?

Solution

q/T₁ is larger. Heat transfer at lower temperature produces a larger entropy change for the same q.

◆Concept Application 15 — micelle formation

Surfactant molecules become more ordered in a micelle. How can the overall entropy still increase?

Solution

Hydrophobic hydration shells around separate tails are released. The resulting increase in solvent freedom can exceed the loss in surfactant configurational entropy.

◆Concept Application 16 — unavailable energy

Why is it safer to write Wlost = T0Sgen than to say simply “entropy equals unavailable energy”?

Solution

Entropy has units J K⁻¹, whereas energy has units J. Multiplication by the specified environment temperature converts entropy generation into destroyed work potential.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Entropy is an endpoint property evaluated through reversible heat transfer

extensive, additive state function

PART 17 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyClausius Inequality, Entropy Generation, and Universe Entropy Balance
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYCLAUSIUS INEQUALITY

Thermodynamics • Irreversibility Accounting

Entropy is transferred with heat—and generated by irreversibility

Reversible heat defines entropy change. Real processes require an additional non-negative term: entropy generation. That single term separates ideal limits from natural irreversible change.

Entropy balance

dS ≥ δQ/Tb
dS = δQ/Tb + dSgen
ΔSuniverse ≥ 0
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Clausius inequality

The reversible path supplies the equality; irreversibility creates the excess entropy.

Reversible differential

dS = δqrev/T

General differential inequality

dS ≥ δq/Tb

Unified entropy balance

dS = δq/Tb + dSgen, dSgen ≥ 0

Concept lens

Boundary temperature Tb

Entropy transfer with heat is evaluated using the local boundary temperature at which that heat crosses, not an arbitrary average temperature of the system.
02

Chapter pressure–volume derivation

Retained in sequence and made explicit for expansion and compression.

1. Entropy definition

dS = δqrev/T

Use a reversible path connecting the same neighbouring equilibrium states.

2. Compare heat transfers

δqrev − δqirr = δwirr − δwrev

Because dU is the same state-function change for both paths.

3. Pressure–volume work

δqrev − δqirr = (P − Pext)dV

Using δwrev = −P dV and δwirr = −Pext dV.

4. Expansion sign

P > Pext and dV > 0

The product (P−Pext)dV is positive.

5. Compression sign

P < Pext and dV < 0

The product is again positive.

6. Inequality

dS ≥ δq/Tb

Equality holds for a reversible step; strict inequality for an irreversible step.

Concept lens

Equality exceptions

The chapter note mentions isobaric and isochoric cases as special. The deeper criterion is not the process label: equality requires zero entropy generation. An isobaric or isochoric process can still be irreversible.
03

System, surroundings, and universe entropy

System

ΔSsys = entropy transfer + entropy generated inside

Surroundings

ΔSsurr = ΣQsurr,k/Tsurr,k

Universe

ΔSuniv = ΔSsys + ΔSsurr

Complete Second-Law test

ΔSuniv = Sgen,total ≥ 0

Concept lens

Normally ΔS without a subscript means system entropy

A thermodynamic problem must still calculate the surroundings and universe separately when testing spontaneity or reversibility.
04

Reversible and irreversible expansion/compression

Concept lens

Reversible path

The system and surroundings entropy changes cancel exactly:\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}+\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}=0\).

Concept lens

Irreversible path

The system endpoint entropy change remains fixed, but the actual heat/work exchange produces\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{univ}}>0\).
05

Retained scientific statements—scientific audit

Chapter shorthandAuditScientifically precise form
“State functions are defined only for the system.”Incorrect.The surroundings can also be modelled as a thermodynamic system with U, H, S, T, P and other properties.
“The change of the surroundings is always reversible.”Incorrect as a universal statement.Textbook surroundings are often idealised as a large internally equilibrated reservoir, so ΔSsurr = qsurr/Tsurr can be evaluated simply. The combined real process may still be irreversible.
“Entropy may be created but never destroyed.”Correct only for entropy generation.Sgen ≥ 0. A system’s entropy itself may decrease when entropy exported with heat exceeds entropy generated internally.
“At equilibrium dS = 0.”Needs constraints.For a stable isolated system at fixed U, V and composition constraints, the first variation of S vanishes and S is a maximum.
06

Spontaneity, impossibility, and equilibrium

SituationEntropy criterionGeneration statementMeaning
Reversible processΔSuniverse = 0No entropy generationideal limiting path
Irreversible spontaneous processΔSuniverse > 0Positive entropy generationnatural real process
Proposed non-spontaneous isolated changeΔSuniverse < 0Forbidden unless coupled/drivencannot occur as the sole isolated change
Stable isolated equilibriumS is maximumNo remaining macroscopic driving forcefirst variation zero; stable maximum

Isolated system

δQ = 0 ⇒ dS = dSgen ≥ 0

Stable isolated equilibrium at fixed constraints

(∂S/∂ξ) = 0, (∂²S/∂ξ²) < 0

Concept lens

Energy and entropy play different roles

The energy of an isolated system remains constant. Its entropy may increase until the constrained maximum is reached.
07

Complete expansion comparison

Original Synergic Bond worked example

Reversible, one-step, and free isothermal expansions between the same states

UNIVERSE ENTROPY COMPARISON

One mole of ideal gas expands isothermally at 300 K from 10.0 L to 20.0 L. Compare the entropy changes for: (i) reversible expansion, (ii) one-step expansion against the final equilibrium pressure, and (iii) insulated free expansion.

System entropy change for all three paths

ΔSsys = R ln(V₂/V₁) = R ln2 = 5.763 J K⁻¹

Reversible

Heat absorbed

qrev = RT ln2 = 1.729 kJ

Surroundings

ΔSsurr = −q/T = −5.763 J K⁻¹

Universe

ΔSuniv = 0

One-step at Pext = P₂

Final pressure

P₂ = RT/V₂

Actual heat

q = P₂(V₂−V₁) = RT/2 = 1.247 kJ

Surroundings

ΔSsurr = −q/T = −R/2 = −4.157 J K⁻¹

Universe

ΔSuniv = R(ln2−1/2) = 1.606 J K⁻¹

Insulated free expansion

Boundary transfers

q = 0 and w = 0

Surroundings

ΔSsurr = 0

Universe

ΔSuniv = R ln2 = 5.763 J K⁻¹

Concept lens

Irreversibility ranking

The endpoints give the same \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}\), but entropy generation increases as the path becomes less controlled: reversible \(0\), one-step finite-pressure expansion \(1.606\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\), and free expansion \(5.763\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
08

Complete compression comparison

Original Synergic Bond compression audit

Sudden isothermal compression against the final pressure

SIGN-CORRECT SOLUTION

One mole of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed isothermally from 20.0 L to 10.0 L against a constant external pressure equal to the final gas pressure.

System entropy change

ΔSsys = R ln(10/20) = −R ln2 = −5.763 J K⁻¹

Work on gas

w = −P₂(V₂−V₁) = +RT = +2.494 kJ

Heat rejected

q = −w = −2.494 kJ

Surroundings entropy

ΔSsurr = −q/T = +R = +8.314 J K⁻¹

Universe entropy

ΔSuniv = R(1−ln2) = 2.551 J K⁻¹ > 0

Concept lens

A system may lose entropy during a spontaneous process

The gas entropy decreases, but the surroundings gain still more entropy. The Second Law constrains the total, not the sign of \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}\) alone.
09

Finite-temperature heat flow

Original finite-temperature-gradient example

Heat transfer from 400 K to 300 K

ENTROPY GENERATION

A quantity of 600 J passes directly from a 400 K reservoir to a 300 K reservoir.

Hot reservoir

ΔShot = −600/400 = −1.50 J K⁻¹

Cold reservoir

ΔScold = +600/300 = +2.00 J K⁻¹

Universe

ΔSuniv = +0.50 J K⁻¹

Concept lens

Finite temperature difference creates entropy

The transfer conserves energy, yet it is irreversible because the reservoirs are separated by a finite temperature difference.
10

Cyclic Clausius inequality

Continuous form

∮ δQ/Tb ≤ 0

Discrete reservoir form

Σk Qk/Tk ≤ 0

Concept lens

Sign convention

\(Q_k\) is positive when heat enters the cyclic device. Equality holds for a reversible cycle; a strict negative sum indicates irreversibility.
11

Thermodynamics around you

Coffee cools on a desk

The coffee loses entropy, but the room gains more because it receives the heat at a lower temperature. Total entropy increases.

Gas rushes into a vacuum

No heat or work crosses the outer boundary, yet the gas entropy rises through internal entropy generation.

Brakes become hot

Organised mechanical energy is dissipated by friction. Entropy generation quantifies the destroyed work potential.

Two gases mix

Removal of a separating constraint increases accessible arrangements. Spontaneous mixing generates entropy.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Entropy of every system must increase.IncorrectThe entropy of the isolated universe cannot decrease. A subsystem may lose entropy by exporting it.
Adiabatic means isentropic.IncorrectAdiabatic only means q = 0. Entropy remains constant only when the adiabatic process is reversible.
The surroundings have no state functions.IncorrectThe surroundings can be treated as another thermodynamic system with its own state properties.
The surroundings are always reversible.IncorrectOnly an ideal reservoir model is maintained in internal equilibrium; the total real process may be irreversible.
Entropy is destroyed when a system cools.IncorrectA system may export entropy. Entropy generation itself is never negative.
At equilibrium ΔS is always zero for every imagined change.IncorrectAt stable isolated equilibrium the first variation vanishes for allowed infinitesimal changes, and entropy is locally maximal.
If ΔSsystem = 0, the process is reversible.IncorrectAn irreversible steady or cyclic system may have zero state change while generating entropy and exporting it.
Clausius inequality uses the system’s average temperature.IncorrectEntropy transfer with heat uses the boundary temperature where that heat crosses.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Entropy change for reversible processes

Phase transition at T_trΔS_tr = ΔH_tr/T_tr (reversible, isothermal, isobaric)
Heating at constant pressureΔS = ∫[T₁→T₂] Cp/T dT
If Cp ≈ constantΔS = Cp ln(T₂/T₁)
Reversible isothermal ideal gasΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = −nR ln(P₂/P₁)
Reversible adiabaticΔS = 0 (isentropic process)
Irreversible adiabaticΔS > 0 (internal irreversibility)

Derivation 2

Entropy is a state function — path independence proof

Two paths A and B from state 1 to state 2∫_A δq/T and ∫_B δq/T
Reverse path B and combine with A∮ δq/T = ∫_A δq/T − ∫_B δq/T
If both reversible∮ δq_rev/T = 0 → ∫_A δq_rev/T = ∫_B δq_rev/T
Conclusion∫ δq_rev/T is path-independent → it defines a state function S
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — inequality sign

For a closed system undergoing an irreversible process, write the differential entropy balance.

Solution

dS = δQ/Tb + dSgen, where Tb is the boundary temperature at the location of heat transfer and dSgen > 0 for an irreversible process.

◆Concept Application 2 — reversible limit

What conditions make the Clausius inequality an equality?

Solution

The process must be internally reversible and heat must cross the boundary through an infinitesimal temperature difference, so dSgen = 0.

◆Concept Application 3 — isolated adiabatic free expansion

An ideal gas freely expands in an insulated container. Determine ΔSsurr and the sign of ΔSsys.

Solution

ΔSsurr = 0 because no heat crosses the outer boundary. ΔSsys = nR ln(V₂/V₁) > 0, so all of the increase is entropy generation.

◆Concept Application 4 — reversible adiabat

A gas expands reversibly and adiabatically. Find ΔSsys, ΔSsurr and ΔSuniv.

Solution

All three are zero: q = 0 and dSgen = 0, so the process is isentropic.

◆Concept Application 5 — entropy export

Can ΔSsystem be negative in a real spontaneous process?

Solution

Yes. A system may export entropy with heat faster than it generates entropy internally. The required condition is ΔSuniverse ≥ 0.

◆Concept Application 6 — reservoir formula

A large reservoir at constant temperature T receives heat Q. Find its entropy change.

Solution

ΔSreservoir = Q/T, with Q positive when heat is absorbed by the reservoir.

◆Concept Application 7 — two-reservoir transfer

Heat Q passes from TH to TC, where TH > TC. Derive the universe entropy change.

Solution

ΔSuniv = −Q/TH + Q/TC = Q(1/TC−1/TH) > 0.

◆Concept Application 8 — impossible proposal

An isolated system is proposed to undergo a change with ΔS = −3 J K⁻¹. Can it occur spontaneously?

Solution

No. For an isolated system, ΔS = Sgen ≥ 0. The proposed change requires external coupling or is impossible as stated.

◆Concept Application 9 — equilibrium maximum

State the local stability conditions for an isolated system at equilibrium along an allowed coordinate ξ.

Solution

At fixed constraints, (∂S/∂ξ) = 0 and stability requires (∂²S/∂ξ²) < 0.

◆Concept Application 10 — one-step expansion inequality

For an isothermal ideal-gas expansion ending at P₂ = Pext, show ΔSuniv > 0.

Solution

Let x = V₂/V₁ > 1. Then ΔSuniv/Rn = ln x − (1−1/x). Since ln x > 1−1/x for x > 1, the total is positive.

◆Concept Application 11 — one-step compression inequality

For sudden isothermal compression from V₁ to V₂ against Pext = P₂, prove positive entropy generation.

Solution

Let x = V₁/V₂ > 1. Then ΔSuniv/Rn = x−1−ln x > 0 for x > 1.

◆Concept Application 12 — surroundings correction

Why is it wrong to say that the surroundings are always reversible?

Solution

Real surroundings may contain finite gradients, friction and mixing. A reservoir is only an ideal internally equilibrated model used to calculate its entropy change simply.

◆Concept Application 13 — cyclic Clausius inequality

Write the Clausius inequality for any cyclic device exchanging heats δQk with reservoirs at Tk.

Solution

The cyclic sum satisfies ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, or for discrete reservoirs ΣQk/Tk ≤ 0, with equality only for a reversible cycle.

◆Concept Application 14 — entropy generation from work loss

A process destroys 6.0 kJ of work potential in an environment at 300 K. Find Sgen.

Solution

Sgen = Wlost/T0 = 6000/300 = 20 J K⁻¹.

◆Concept Application 15 — stable versus unstable extremum

Why is dS = 0 alone insufficient to prove stable equilibrium?

Solution

A stationary point may be a maximum, minimum or saddle point. Stable isolated equilibrium requires a local maximum of entropy under the allowed constraints.

◆Concept Application 16 — system plus surroundings

A system entropy decreases by 8 J K⁻¹ while its surroundings increase by 11 J K⁻¹. Classify the process.

Solution

ΔSuniv = +3 J K⁻¹, so the process is thermodynamically possible and irreversible.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Reversibility means zero entropy generation; natural irreversibility means positive generation

PART 17 COMPLETE

Clausius inequality

dS ≥ δQ/Tb

Entropy balance

dS = δQ/Tb + dSgen

Universe

ΔSuniv = Sgen,total ≥ 0

Isolated equilibrium

S reaches a constrained maximum
