PART 18 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyEntropy Changes in Phase Transitions, Reactions, and Real Fluids
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYPHASE & REACTION ENTROPY

Thermodynamics • Entropy Calculation Layer

Phase changes create entropy jumps; reactions create stoichiometric entropy balances

At an equilibrium transition, heat and entropy are linked by temperature. For reactions, the entropy change is obtained by subtracting the stoichiometric reactant total from the product total.

Master relations

ΔStr = ΔHtr/Ttr
ΔrS = ΣνSproducts − ΣνSreactants
dS = (dU + P dV)/T
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Entropy change during a reversible phase transition

The two phases coexist in equilibrium at the transition temperature.

Reversible transition

ΔSsys = qrev/Ttr = ΔHtr/Ttr

Surroundings and universe

ΔSsurr = −ΔHtr/Ttr, ΔSuniv = 0

Fusion

ΔSfus = ΔHfus/Tm

ΔSfreezing = −ΔHfus/Tm

Vaporisation

ΔSvap = ΔHvap/Tb

ΔScond = −ΔHvap/Tb

Sublimation

ΔSsub = ΔHsub/Tsub

ΔSdeposition = −ΔHsub/Tsub

Crystalline transition

ΔStr = ΔHtr/Ttr

reverse transition changes sign

Concept lens

Why equilibrium matters

The ratio \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{tr}}/T_{\mathrm{tr}}\) is the system entropy change only when the transition is carried out reversibly at the equilibrium transition temperature.
02

Fusion and freezing

Concept lens

Fusion

Solid becomes liquid. Molecular mobility increases, so \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{fus}}>0\).

Concept lens

Freezing

Liquid becomes solid. The same state-function difference reverses sign:\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{freeze}}=-\Delta S_{\mathrm{fus}}\).

At melting point Tm

ΔSfus = ΔHfus/Tm

Concept lens

Thermochemistry boundary

This section uses transition enthalpy only as an input to entropy. Measurement, calorimetry, Hess cycles, and detailed fusion enthalpy theory remain in Thermochemistry.
03

Vaporisation, condensation, and Trouton’s rule

At normal boiling point Tb

ΔSvap = ΔHvap/Tb

Condensation

ΔScond = −ΔHvap/Tb

Empirical estimate

ΔSvap ≈ 10.5R ≈ 87 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Concept lens

Why associated liquids deviate

Strong hydrogen bonding or other liquid-state association creates extra order before vaporisation. Destroying that organisation can produce an entropy change larger than the basic Trouton estimate.
04

Sublimation and deposition

Sublimation at equilibrium

ΔSsub = ΔHsub/Tsub

Reverse deposition

ΔSdep = −ΔHsub/Tsub

Concept lens

State-function additivity

A reversible alternative path may pass through liquid: solid → liquid → gas. Entropy changes add, with heat-capacity corrections when the steps occur at different temperatures.
05

Crystalline modification transitions

Solid I → Solid II

ΔStr = ΔHtr/Ttr

Concept lens

A solid can have multiple entropy levels

Different crystal structures possess different vibrational spectra, orientational order, and defects. A solid–solid transition can therefore produce a finite entropy jump.
06

Entropy change of a chemical reaction

Balanced stoichiometry and physical states are mandatory.

General reaction

aA + bB → cC + dD

Reaction entropy

ΔrS = cSC + dSD − aSA − bSB

Standard-state form

ΔrS° = ΣνiS°m,i(products) − ΣνjS°m,j(reactants)

Concept lens

Physical state is part of the chemical equation

\(S_m^\circ\) for a gas, liquid, solid, or dissolved species can differ greatly. State symbols cannot be omitted from a rigorous reaction-entropy calculation.

Concept lens

Gas-mole count is only a first estimate

More gaseous product moles often suggest positive \(\Delta_rS\), but actual tabulated molar entropies decide the sign.
07

General entropy differential

The chapter derivation is retained with chemistry-sign correction.

Fundamental entropy route

dS = δqrev/T = (dU + P dV)/T

Chemistry sign convention: reversible PV work on the system is δwrev = −P dV.

Expand dU(T,V)

dU = nCv,m dT + (∂U/∂V)T dV

This separates temperature and volume effects.

General T–V entropy differential

dS = nCv,m dT/T + [(∂U/∂V)T + P]dV/T

Valid for a simple compressible closed system of fixed composition.

Thermodynamic identity

(∂U/∂V)T = T(∂P/∂T)V − P

Substitution gives dS = nCv,m dT/T + (∂P/∂T)V dV.

Concept lens

Sign correction

With \(\delta w_{\mathrm{rev}}=-P\,dV\), the First Law gives\(\delta q_{\mathrm{rev}}=dU-\delta w_{\mathrm{rev}}=dU+P\,dV\). The pressure term is therefore positive in the entropy differential.
08

Van der Waals gas entropy

Equation of state

(P + an²/V²)(V−nb) = nRT

Internal-energy volume derivative

(∂U/∂V)T = an²/V²

Differential

dS = nCV,mdT/T + nR dV/(V−nb)

Integrated result for constant Cv,m

ΔS = nCV,mln(T₂/T₁) + nRln[(V₂−nb)/(V₁−nb)]

Concept lens

Physical reading

The attraction parameter affects internal energy and pressure in cancelling ways. The entropy volume term reflects the translational space actually available after excluded volume is removed.
09

Heating solids and liquids

Constant-volume heating

General

ΔS = n∫T₁T₂ CV,m(T)dT/T

Constant Cv,m

ΔS = nCV,mln(T₂/T₁)

Constant-pressure heating

General

ΔS = n∫T₁T₂ CP,m(T)dT/T

Constant Cp,m

ΔS = nCP,mln(T₂/T₁)

Concept lens

Why the chapter Cv expression is useful

At constant volume the exact relation uses \(C_V\). For ordinary constant-pressure heating of condensed phases, use \(C_P\). Because thermal expansion is small, \(C_P\) and \(C_V\) are often close, but not identical.
10

Original complete worked examples

◆Fusion at equilibrium

A substance melts reversibly at 320 K with molar enthalpy of fusion 8.00 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the entropy changes of system, surroundings, and universe.

Solution

ΔSsys = 8000/320 = +25.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The surroundings supply the same heat at 320 K, so ΔSsurr = −25.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. ΔSuniv = 0.

◆Trouton-rule estimate

A non-associated liquid has normal boiling point 360 K. Estimate its molar enthalpy of vaporisation using Trouton’s rule.

Solution

ΔSvap ≈ 10.5R ≈ 87.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Thus ΔHvap ≈ TbΔSvap = 360×87.3 ≈ 31.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

◆Crystalline transition

A reversible solid-I → solid-II transition occurs at 410 K with ΔHtr = 1.64 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔStr.

Solution

ΔStr = 1640/410 = +4.00 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The reverse transition has −4.00 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Reaction entropy

For A(g) + 2B(g) → C(g), the molar entropies are SA = 210, SB = 190, and SC = 300 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find ΔrS.

Solution

ΔrS = SC − SA − 2SB = 300−210−380 = −290 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Van der Waals gas

For one mole with constant Cv,m = 3R/2, temperature rises from 300 K to 400 K while available volume V−b doubles. Find ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = (3R/2)ln(400/300) + Rln2 ≈ 3.59 + 5.76 = 9.35 J K⁻¹.

◆Heating a solid

Two moles of a solid with constant Cp,m = 25.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ are heated reversibly at constant pressure from 300 K to 500 K. Find ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = nCp,m ln(T₂/T₁) = 2×25.0×ln(500/300) ≈ 25.5 J K⁻¹.

11

Thermodynamics around you

Steam burns severely

Condensing steam releases energy and loses a large vaporisation entropy while transferring heat to skin. Detailed energy calculations belong to Thermochemistry.

Dry ice disappears

Solid carbon dioxide sublimes directly to gas, producing a large increase in molecular translational freedom.

Chocolate crystal forms

Different crystalline modifications have different entropies and stabilities; controlled temperature histories select the desired form.

Chemical reaction tables

Tabulated standard molar entropies let reaction entropy be calculated without reproducing the actual reaction path.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Every phase transition is irreversible.IncorrectAt phase equilibrium with infinitesimal driving force, the transition can be treated reversibly.
ΔStransition = ΔHtransition/T at any arbitrary temperature.IncorrectThe simple ratio applies to a reversible equilibrium transition at its transition temperature.
Trouton’s rule is exact for all liquids.IncorrectIt is an empirical estimate for many non-associated liquids at their normal boiling points.
Water must obey ΔSvap = 10.5R exactly.IncorrectStrong hydrogen bonding makes water a well-known deviation.
Reaction entropy equals product entropy minus reactant entropy without coefficients.IncorrectEvery molar entropy must be multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Only gaseous mole count determines ΔrS.IncorrectIt is a heuristic; actual molar entropies and physical states determine the result.
The chapter general differential should contain −P dV with chemistry work convention.IncorrectBecause δwrev = −P dV and δqrev = dU−δwrev, the heat term is dU + P dV.
For all solids and liquids, Cp = Cv exactly.IncorrectThey are often close, not identical; the appropriate path heat capacity must be used.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Entropy of mixing for ideal gases

Before mixingeach gas i occupies volume Vᵢ at T and Pᵢ
After mixingeach gas i occupies total volume V at partial pressure pᵢ = yᵢP
Entropy change for gas iΔS_i = −nᵢR ln(pᵢ/P) = −nᵢR ln yᵢ
Total entropy of mixingΔS_mix = −R Σᵢ nᵢ ln yᵢ = −nR Σᵢ xᵢ ln xᵢ
Signyᵢ < 1 → ln yᵢ < 0 → ΔS_mix > 0 always for genuine mixing
MaximumΔS_mix is maximum for equimolar mixture (x₁ = x₂ = 0.5): ΔS_mix = nR ln 2
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — freezing sign

One mole of a liquid freezes reversibly at its normal freezing point. What are the signs of ΔSsys and ΔSsurr?

Solution

ΔSsys < 0 because molecular freedom decreases. The surroundings receive heat, so ΔSsurr > 0 with equal magnitude; ΔSuniv = 0.

◆Concept Application 2 — supercooling

Can ΔSsys = −ΔHfus/T be used directly for irreversible freezing of a supercooled liquid at a temperature below Tm?

Solution

Not as a complete universe balance. The system entropy is a state-function difference and must include any temperature path; the surroundings entropy uses the actual heat-transfer temperature. Irreversible freezing gives ΔSuniv > 0.

◆Concept Application 3 — vaporisation entropy

Why is ΔSvap positive at the normal boiling point?

Solution

Vaporisation increases accessible translational volume and microscopic arrangements. Since ΔHvap > 0 and Tb > 0, ΔSvap = ΔHvap/Tb > 0.

◆Concept Application 4 — condensation

At the same equilibrium temperature, compare the magnitudes of vaporisation and condensation entropy changes.

Solution

They are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign because entropy is a state function and the processes are reverses.

◆Concept Application 5 — Trouton exception

Why may a strongly hydrogen-bonded liquid have ΔSvap significantly different from 10.5R?

Solution

Its liquid state is unusually ordered by association. Vaporisation destroys this organisation, producing a larger entropy increase than the simple non-associated-liquid estimate.

◆Concept Application 6 — sublimation relation

Express ΔSsub in terms of fusion and vaporisation entropies along a reversible path.

Solution

For compatible reference temperatures with necessary heat-capacity corrections included, entropy is additive: ΔSsub = ΔSfus + ΔSvap along a solid→liquid→gas path.

◆Concept Application 7 — crystalline transition sign

Must every higher-temperature crystal form have larger entropy?

Solution

For an equilibrium transition with ΔHtr > 0, the higher-temperature form has larger entropy because ΔStr = ΔHtr/Ttr. The sign follows the measured transition enthalpy.

◆Concept Application 8 — reaction coefficients

Why must stoichiometric coefficients multiply molar entropies in ΔrS?

Solution

Reaction entropy refers to the balanced reaction event. Each coefficient specifies the number of moles created or consumed.

◆Concept Application 9 — physical states

Why is N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) not thermodynamically equivalent to a hypothetical equation with liquid ammonia?

Solution

Molar entropy depends strongly on physical state. Reaction entropy must use the specified equilibrium state of every species.

◆Concept Application 10 — gas-mole heuristic

If gaseous moles decrease in a reaction, is ΔrS always negative?

Solution

No. It is a useful first estimate, but molecular complexity, condensed species, temperature, and actual tabulated molar entropies can overturn the heuristic.

◆Concept Application 11 — standard reaction entropy

Write the standard entropy change for aA + bB → cC + dD.

Solution

ΔrS° = cS°m(C) + dS°m(D) − aS°m(A) − bS°m(B).

◆Concept Application 12 — general differential

Starting from dS = (dU + P dV)/T, derive the T–V entropy differential.

Solution

Use dU = nCv,m dT + (∂U/∂V)T dV. Then dS = nCv,m dT/T + [(∂U/∂V)T + P]dV/T.

◆Concept Application 13 — ideal-gas limit

Recover the ideal-gas T–V entropy differential from the general expression.

Solution

For an ideal gas, (∂U/∂V)T = 0 and P/T = nR/V. Hence dS = nCv,m dT/T + nR dV/V.

◆Concept Application 14 — van der Waals attraction

Why does parameter a disappear from the final entropy expression of a van der Waals gas?

Solution

The attraction contribution +(an²/V²) in (∂U/∂V)T cancels the −an²/V² term in pressure. The remaining volume factor is nR/(V−nb).

◆Concept Application 15 — condensed phases

Why are Cp and Cv often numerically close for solids and liquids?

Solution

Their thermal expansion and compressibility are small, so heating at constant pressure performs little expansion work compared with gases.

◆Concept Application 16 — complete heating path

Describe the entropy calculation for heating a solid through melting and then heating the liquid.

Solution

Add three state-function contributions: ∫solid Cp/T dT + ΔHfus/Tm + ∫liquid Cp/T dT. Use each heat capacity in the appropriate phase.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Transition entropy is heat divided by equilibrium temperature; reaction entropy is a stoichiometric difference

PART 18 COMPLETE

Phase transition

ΔStr = ΔHtr/Ttr

Trouton estimate

ΔSvap ≈ 10.5R

Reaction entropy

ΣνSproducts − ΣνSreactants

van der Waals

V is replaced by available volume V−nb

Integrated Enrichment

Entropy of Mixing and Phase Transitions

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Why entropy of mixing drives miscibility

For ideal gases or ideal solutions, ΔG_mix = ΔH_mix − TΔS_mix = 0 − TΔS_mix < 0 always (since ΔH_mix = 0 for ideal mixing). The purely entropic driving force makes all ideal mixtures spontaneously miscible at any composition.

Connects → Connects to: Gibbs energy of mixing, Part 28.

Entropy of a first-order phase transition

At a first-order transition (melting, boiling), the entropy jumps discontinuously by ΔS_tr = ΔH_tr/T_tr. For water freezing at 273 K: ΔS_fus = 6010/273 = 22.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The slope of the G vs T plot changes discontinuously by this amount.

Connects → Connects to: Gibbs energy, Clapeyron equation.

PART 19 / 30Second Law, Carnot & EntropyEntropy Changes of Ideal Gases
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYIDEAL-GAS ENTROPY MAP

Thermodynamics • Process Entropy Layer

Ideal-gas entropy separates temperature effects from expansion and compression effects

Heating changes the distribution of molecular energy. Expansion changes accessible positional space. The ideal-gas entropy equations combine both contributions without depending on the actual path.

Master endpoint forms

ΔS = n∫CV,mdT/T + nRln(V₂/V₁)
ΔS = n∫CP,mdT/T − nRln(P₂/P₁)
reversible adiabat: ΔS = 0
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

General entropy change of an ideal gas

Two independent variables describe the endpoint change.

Fundamental differential

T dS = dU + P dV

Ideal-gas internal energy

dU = nCV,m(T)dT

T–V differential

dS = nCV,m(T)dT/T + nR dV/V

T–V integrated form

ΔS = n∫T₁T₂CV,m(T)dT/T + nRln(V₂/V₁)

Concept lens

Temperature and volume terms may oppose one another

Cooling contributes negatively, while expansion contributes positively. The sign of the total depends on which effect dominates.
02

Equivalent T–P form

Ideal-gas logarithmic differential

dV/V = dT/T − dP/P

Use Cp,m = Cv,m + R

dS = nCP,m(T)dT/T − nR dP/P

Integrated form

ΔS = n∫T₁T₂CP,m(T)dT/T − nRln(P₂/P₁)

Concept lens

Pressure decrease

At fixed temperature, reducing pressure increases entropy because the gas occupies more volume.

Concept lens

Pressure increase

At fixed temperature, compression decreases entropy.
03

Temperature-independent and temperature-dependent heat capacities

The chapter polynomial integration is retained explicitly.

Constant Cv,m

ΔS = nCV,mln(T₂/T₁) + nRln(V₂/V₁)

Constant Cp,m

ΔS = nCP,mln(T₂/T₁) − nRln(P₂/P₁)

Constant volume

Heat-capacity model

CV,m(T) = a + bT + cT²

Entropy change

ΔS = n[a ln(T₂/T₁) + b(T₂−T₁) + c(T₂²−T₁²)/2]

Constant pressure

Heat-capacity model

CP,m(T) = a + bT + cT²

Entropy change

ΔS = n[a ln(T₂/T₁) + b(T₂−T₁) + c(T₂²−T₁²)/2]

Concept lens

Use the fitted range only

A polynomial heat-capacity expression is valid only over the temperature range for which it was fitted.

Concept lens

Architecture boundary

This part uses heat-capacity functions only as entropy inputs. Detailed molecular heat-capacity theory remains in Thermochemistry.
04

Isochoric entropy change

Constant volume

ΔS = n∫T₁T₂CV,m(T)dT/T

Constant Cv,m

ΔS = nCV,mln(T₂/T₁)

Concept lens

Heating

\(T_2>T_1\) gives \(\Delta S>0\).

Concept lens

Cooling

\(T_2<T_1\) gives \(\Delta S<0\). The surroundings may gain more entropy, so the total can still be positive.
05

Isobaric entropy change

Constant pressure

ΔS = n∫T₁T₂CP,m(T)dT/T

Constant Cp,m

ΔS = nCP,mln(T₂/T₁)

Concept lens

Why Cp appears

At constant pressure, heat changes internal energy and also supports expansion work. The reversible heat is \(nC_{P,m}dT\).
06

Reversible and irreversible heating balances

Heating pathΔSsystemΔSsurroundingsΔSuniverse
Isochoric reversiblenCv,m ln(T₂/T₁)−nCv,m ln(T₂/T₁)0
Isochoric irreversible, reservoir at T₂nCv,m ln(T₂/T₁)−nCv,m(T₂−T₁)/T₂nCv,m[ln(T₂/T₁)−(T₂−T₁)/T₂]
Isobaric reversiblenCp,m ln(T₂/T₁)−nCp,m ln(T₂/T₁)0
Isobaric irreversible, reservoir at T₂nCp,m ln(T₂/T₁)−nCp,m(T₂−T₁)/T₂nCp,m[ln(T₂/T₁)−(T₂−T₁)/T₂]

Concept lens

Finite temperature difference creates entropy

A single hot reservoir heats the gas irreversibly. A reversible heating path requires a sequence of reservoirs differing infinitesimally from the gas temperature.
07

Isothermal expansion and compression

The system entropy depends only on the volume or pressure ratio.

System entropy

ΔSsys = nRln(V₂/V₁) = −nRln(P₂/P₁)

Concept lens

Reversible

\(q_{\mathrm{rev}}=nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)\), and\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}=-\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}\).

Concept lens

One-step

\(q=P_{\mathrm{ext}}(V_2-V_1)\) for ideal-gas isothermal expansion, and\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{univ}}>0\).

Concept lens

Free expansion

\(q=w=\Delta U=\Delta T=0\), yet\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}=nR\ln(V_2/V_1)>0\).

One-step expansion ending at Pext = P₂

ΔSuniv = nR[ln x − (1−1/x)], x = V₂/V₁ > 1

Sudden compression ending at Pext = P₂

ΔSuniv = nR[x−1−ln x], x = V₁/V₂ > 1
08

Adiabatic entropy change

No heat transfer does not imply zero entropy generation.

Actual heat condition

q = 0 ⇒ ΔSsurr = 0 for an insulated outer boundary

Endpoint T–V form

ΔSsys = nCV,mln(T₂/T₁) + nRln(V₂/V₁)

Endpoint T–P form

ΔSsys = nCP,mln(T₂/T₁) − nRln(P₂/P₁)

Concept lens

Reversible adiabatic

Temperature and volume contributions cancel exactly:\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}=0\).

Concept lens

Irreversible adiabatic

Entropy is generated internally:\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{univ}}=S_{\mathrm{gen}}>0\).

Concept lens

Scientific correction to “heat produced”

During adiabatic compression, no heat crosses the boundary. Work input raises internal energy and temperature while irreversibility generates entropy.

General T–Pn∫Cp,m(T)dT/T − nR ln(P₂/P₁)ideal gas, fixed composition
Constant Cp,mnCp,m ln(T₂/T₁) − nR ln(P₂/P₁)ideal gas
Isochoricn∫Cv,m(T)dT/TV₂ = V₁
Isobaricn∫Cp,m(T)dT/TP₂ = P₁
IsothermalnR ln(V₂/V₁) = −nR ln(P₂/P₁)T₂ = T₁
Reversible adiabatic0q = 0 and Sgen = 0
Irreversible adiabatic> 0 for isolated closed systemq = 0 and Sgen > 0
10

Original complete worked examples

◆General T–V change

Two moles of an ideal diatomic gas with constant Cv,m = 5R/2 change from 300 K, 5.00 L to 450 K, 12.0 L. Find ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = nCv,m ln(T₂/T₁) + nR ln(V₂/V₁) = 2(5R/2)ln(1.5) + 2Rln(2.4) ≈ 31.41 J K⁻¹.

◆Temperature-dependent Cv

One mole is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 600 K with Cv,m = 20.0 + 0.0100T J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = 20.0ln(600/300) + 0.0100(600−300) = 13.863 + 3.000 = 16.86 J K⁻¹.

◆General T–P change

A 1.50 mol ideal diatomic gas with Cp,m = 7R/2 changes from 500 K, 10.0 bar to 350 K, 2.00 bar. Find ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = nCp,m ln(350/500) − nR ln(2/10) ≈ 4.50 J K⁻¹. Cooling lowers entropy, while the large pressure drop raises it slightly more.

◆Three isothermal routes

One mole of ideal gas at 320 K expands from 4.00 L to 12.0 L by reversible expansion, one-step expansion against the final pressure, and free expansion. Compare entropy balances.

Solution

For every path, ΔSsys = Rln3 = 9.134 J K⁻¹. Reversible: q = 2.923 kJ, ΔSsurr = −9.134 J K⁻¹, ΔSuniv = 0. One-step: q = RT(1−1/3) = 1.774 kJ, ΔSsurr = −5.543 J K⁻¹, ΔSuniv = 3.591 J K⁻¹. Free: q = w = 0, ΔSsurr = 0, ΔSuniv = 9.134 J K⁻¹.

◆Irreversible adiabatic expansion

One mole of monatomic ideal gas at 300 K expands adiabatically from 10.0 L to 20.0 L against a constant external pressure equal to the final gas pressure. Find T₂ and ΔSsys.

Solution

Energy balance gives (3R/2)(T₂−300) = −(RT2/20)(20−10), so T₂ = 225 K. Then ΔS = (3R/2)ln(225/300) + Rln2 ≈ +2.18 J K⁻¹. Since q = 0, this equals entropy generated.

◆Irreversible isochoric heating

One mole with constant Cv,m = 3R/2 is heated in a rigid vessel from 300 K to 600 K by a 600 K reservoir. Find ΔSsystem, ΔSsurroundings, and ΔSuniverse.

Solution

ΔSsys = (3R/2)ln2 = 8.644 J K⁻¹. qsys = (3R/2)(300) = 3.742 kJ. ΔSsurr = −3742/600 = −6.236 J K⁻¹. Hence ΔSuniv = +2.408 J K⁻¹.

11

Thermodynamics around you

Compressed-air cylinder

Rapid filling is approximately adiabatic and irreversible, so the gas heats and generates entropy.

Aerosol cooling

Rapid expansion lowers temperature; the actual path is irreversible even when heat transfer is initially small.

Rigid gas thermometer

Heating at fixed volume changes temperature and pressure while entropy rises through the Cv/T integral.

Gas escaping into an evacuated chamber

Ideal-gas free expansion has q = w = ΔU = ΔT = 0 but positive entropy change.

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
The T–V and T–P formulas give different entropy changes.IncorrectThey are equivalent descriptions connected by PV = nRT.
Heat capacity can always be treated as constant.IncorrectThe logarithmic formulas assume constant Cv,m or Cp,m; otherwise integrate C(T)/T.
An isothermal ideal-gas process always has q = 0.IncorrectΔU = 0, so q = −w. Only free expansion has q = w = 0 under the stated idealised conditions.
Free expansion is reversible because initial and final states can be connected reversibly.IncorrectA reversible reference path is only a calculation device. The actual free expansion is irreversible.
Adiabatic and isentropic mean the same thing.IncorrectOnly reversible adiabatic change is isentropic.
During irreversible adiabatic compression, heat is produced and transferred.IncorrectNo heat crosses the boundary. Work input raises internal energy and temperature while entropy is generated.

Surroundings entropy is always −ΔSsystem.IncorrectThat cancellation occurs only for a reversible total process.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Third Law of Thermodynamics — Nernst heat theorem

Nernst (1906)As T → 0, ΔS → 0 for any pure crystalline solid at thermal equilibrium
Planck's formulationS → 0 as T → 0 for a perfect crystalline substance (Ω = 1 at absolute zero)
Consequenceabsolute (Third-Law) entropies can be assigned to all pure substances
Residual entropysome substances retain Ω > 1 at T = 0 due to orientational disorder (CO, NO, ice) → S₀ > 0
CO residual entropyS₀(CO) ≈ R ln 2 = 5.76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (each CO can point either way in crystal)
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — derive T–V form

Derive the entropy differential of an ideal gas in terms of T and V.

Solution

For an ideal gas, dU = nCv,m(T)dT and P = nRT/V. Since T dS = dU + P dV, dS = nCv,m(T)dT/T + nR dV/V.

◆Concept Application 2 — derive T–P form

Convert the T–V entropy differential into the T–P form.

Solution

From PV = nRT, dV/V = dT/T − dP/P. Substitute into dS = nCv,m dT/T + nR dV/V to obtain dS = nCp,m dT/T − nR dP/P.

◆Concept Application 3 — isochoric cooling

An ideal gas cools at constant volume. What determines the sign of ΔS?

Solution

ΔS = n∫Cv,m(T)dT/T. Since Cv,m > 0 and T₂ < T₁, the integral is negative.

◆Concept Application 4 — isobaric heating

For constant Cp,m and constant pressure heating from T₁ to T₂, write ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = nCp,m ln(T₂/T₁), positive when T₂ > T₁.

◆Concept Application 5 — pressure drop at constant temperature

One mole of ideal gas undergoes an isothermal pressure drop from P₁ to P₂. Write ΔS.

Solution

ΔS = −R ln(P₂/P₁) = R ln(P₁/P₂). It is positive when P₂ < P₁.

◆Concept Application 6 — isothermal compression

What is the sign of the system entropy change during isothermal compression?

Solution

Negative: ΔSsys = nR ln(V₂/V₁), and V₂ < V₁.

◆Concept Application 7 — route independence

Why is ΔSsys identical for reversible and free expansion between the same ideal-gas endpoints?

Solution

Entropy is a state function. The actual heat and work differ, but the initial and final equilibrium states are the same.

◆Concept Application 8 — q = 0 trap

During free expansion qactual = 0. Why is ΔSsystem not zero?

Solution

The defining integral uses reversible heat along a reversible reference path, not the actual irreversible heat. For ideal-gas isothermal free expansion, ΔSsystem = nR ln(V₂/V₁) > 0.

◆Concept Application 9 — one-step expansion proof

For isothermal one-step expansion ending at Pext = P₂, prove ΔSuniverse > 0.

Solution

Let x = V₂/V₁ > 1. Then ΔSuniv/(nR) = ln x − (1−1/x). This is positive for x > 1.

◆Concept Application 10 — reversible adiabat

Use TV^(γ−1) = constant to prove ΔS = 0.

Solution

ΔS = nCv,m ln(T₂/T₁) + nR ln(V₂/V₁). Since ln(T₂/T₁) = −(γ−1)ln(V₂/V₁) and R = (γ−1)Cv,m, the two terms cancel.

◆Concept Application 11 — irreversible adiabat

Can an irreversible adiabatic process have ΔSsystem < 0 in an isolated closed system?

Solution

No. With q = 0, ΔSsystem = Sgen ≥ 0. A strict irreversible change gives ΔSsystem > 0.

◆Concept Application 12 — temperature ranking

An ideal gas expands adiabatically to the same final volume by reversible and irreversible paths. Which final temperature is higher?

Solution

The irreversible path generally performs less work, so it loses less internal energy and ends at the higher temperature.

◆Concept Application 13 — compression ranking

For the same initial state and final smaller volume, compare reversible and irreversible adiabatic final temperatures.

Solution

Irreversible compression requires greater work input, so the irreversible final temperature is higher.

◆Concept Application 14 — variable heat capacity

If C(T) = a + bT + cT², evaluate ∫T₁^T₂ C(T)dT/T.

Solution

The result is a ln(T₂/T₁) + b(T₂−T₁) + (c/2)(T2²−T1²).

◆Concept Application 15 — identical endpoints

Two ideal-gas processes connect identical T₁,V₁ and T₂,V₂ endpoints. One is reversible and one irreversible. Compare ΔSsystem.

Solution

They are equal because system entropy depends only on endpoints. The universe entropy distinguishes the paths.

◆Concept Application 16 — spontaneous heating

A colder ideal gas is suddenly placed in contact with a hotter reservoir. Why is ΔSuniverse positive?

Solution

The gas gains entropy nC ln(T₂/T₁), while the reservoir loses q/Treservoir. Because heat crosses a finite temperature difference, the gas gain exceeds the reservoir loss.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

Entropy is fixed by endpoints; route irreversibility appears in the universe balance

Multistage entropy: liquid water to compressed vapour

A convenient reversible route converts a difficult endpoint change into additive pieces.

Retained chapter multistage problem

One mole of liquid water at 27 °C and 1 atm to vapour at 127 °C and 5 atm

WORDING CHECKED

The chapter heading says “molar enthalpy change,” but the complete written solution uses\(\Delta S\) expressions. The calculation is therefore retained as a molar entropy-change problem. Data: liquid-water specific heat \(=1.0\ \mathrm{cal\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\), molar mass \(=18\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\), and latent heat of vaporisation at\(100^\circ\mathrm C\) and 1 atm \(=540\ \mathrm{cal\,g^{-1}}\).

Stage A: heat liquid from 300 K to 373 K

ΔS₁ = 18(1.0)ln(373/300) = 3.920 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Stage B: vaporise reversibly at 373 K

ΔS₂ = (540×18)/373 = 26.059 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Stage C: heat vapour to 400 K and compress 1 atm → 5 atm

ΔS₃ = 4Rln(400/373) − Rln5 = −2.642 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Total system entropy

ΔSsys = 27.337 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 114.4 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Concept lens

Why the final-pressure term is negative

At fixed final temperature, increasing pressure reduces the accessible gas volume and lowers the vapour entropy.

Concept lens

Why surroundings entropy is not fixed by endpoints

\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}\) is path independent. The surroundings entropy depends on the actual heat exchanges and the temperatures of the external reservoirs. It cannot be reconstructed from an arbitrary convenient system path unless those same reservoirs physically carry out the process.

Concept lens

Literal enthalpy reading

Under the stated assumptions and ideal-vapour approximation, the literal molar enthalpy change would be approximately \(11.25\ \mathrm{kcal\,mol^{-1}}\), independent of the final ideal-gas pressure. That is a different question from the written entropy solution.

Entropy of mixing two distinct ideal gases

Each species undergoes an isothermal expansion into the total mixture volume.

Binary ideal-gas mixing

ΔSmix = −R[nAlnxA + nBlnxB]

Molar form

ΔSmix,m = −R[xAlnxA + xBlnxB]

Component AnA R ln(Vfinal/VA)−nA R ln xA
Component BnB R ln(Vfinal/VB)−nB R ln xB
TotalΣniR ln(Vfinal/Vi)−RΣni ln xi
Per mole of mixtureΔSmix/ntotal−RΣxi ln xi
Binary equimolar maximumxA = xB = 1/2ΔSmix,m = R ln2
Identical gasesno distinguishable composition changeΔSmix = 0

Retained chapter ideal-gas mixing problem

Mix 5 mol of ideal gas A with 10 mol of ideal gas B at the same temperature and pressure

Mole fractions

xA = 5/15 = 1/3, xB = 10/15 = 2/3

Each-gas expansion form

ΔSmix = 5Rln(15/5) + 10Rln(15/10)

Numerical result

ΔSmix = 79.38 J K⁻¹

Molar entropy of mixing

ΔSmix,m = 5.292 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Concept lens

Ideal-gas energy properties

For ideal gases mixed at the same temperature, \(\Delta U_{\mathrm{mix}}=0\) and\(\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}=0\), while \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}>0\) for distinct gases.

Concept lens

Gibbs-paradox safeguard

The formula applies to distinguishable components. Mixing two portions of the same ideal gas at the same temperature and pressure creates no thermodynamic mixing entropy.
03

Maximum entropy of binary mixing

Fixed total moles

ΔSmix,m = −R[xlnx + (1−x)ln(1−x)]

Stationary condition

d(ΔSmix,m)/dx = −Rln[x/(1−x)] = 0

Maximum

xA = xB = 1/2, nA:nB = 1:1

Maximum molar value

ΔSmix,m,max = Rln2 = 5.763 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Concept lens

Constraint must be stated

Equal amounts maximise the molar mixing entropy, or the total entropy when the total amount is fixed. Without a fixed total amount, adding more matter increases the extensive total entropy without a finite maximum.
04

Mixing bodies initially at different temperatures

The word “mixing” here means thermal contact; material mixing may add further terms.

Adiabatic energy balance

ΣCi(Tf−Ti) = 0

Constant heat capacities

Tf = (ΣCiTi)/(ΣCi)

Total entropy change

ΔStotal = ΣCiln(Tf/Ti) > 0

Retained chapter thermal-equilibration problem

400 g of liquid A at 27 °C mixed thermally with 100 g of liquid B at 87 °C

\(c_A=2\ \mathrm{cal\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\), \(c_B=4\ \mathrm{cal\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\), and the combined enclosure is taken as adiabatic.

Energy balance

100(4)(360−Tf) = 400(2)(Tf−300)

Final equilibrium temperature

Tf = 320 K

Cold liquid A

ΔSA = 800ln(320/300) = +51.631 cal K⁻¹

Hot liquid B

ΔSB = 400ln(320/360) = −47.113 cal K⁻¹

Total

ΔStotal = +4.518 cal K⁻¹ ≈ 18.90 J K⁻¹

Concept lens

Condition correction

Complete immiscibility is one sufficient way to eliminate entropy and enthalpy of material mixing. More generally, this calculation assumes no phase change, constant heat capacities, negligible volume work, no heat of mixing, and no additional composition entropy. If miscible non-ideal liquids are actually mixed, extra mixing terms must be included.

Retained chapter constant-temperature block problem

A 400 K block transfers 1000 cal to a 300 K block

Cold block

ΔScold = +1000/300 = +3.333 cal K⁻¹

Hot block

ΔShot = −1000/400 = −2.500 cal K⁻¹

Combined

ΔStotal = +0.833 cal K⁻¹ ≈ 3.49 J K⁻¹

Concept lens

Reservoir interpretation

“Maintained at constant temperature” means each block behaves as a thermal reservoir. Heat flow through the finite 100 K difference is irreversible, so the total entropy increases.

A. Reversible adiabatic

Retained van der Waals numerical

Retained chapter van der Waals numerical

One mole changes from 298 K, 1 dm³ to 373 K, 10 dm³

Why the attraction parameter a is absent

Thermodynamics around you

Opening a perfume bottle

Distinct molecules spread into the surrounding air. Each component gains accessible volume and the mixing entropy rises.

Hot milk and cold coffee

Energy conservation sets the final temperature; the logarithmic entropy balance proves the equilibration is irreversible.

10

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — binary mixing derivation

Derive the ideal-gas entropy of mixing for nA moles of A and nB moles of B initially at the same T and P.

Solution

Each gas expands isothermally from its own initial volume to the total volume. Since Vtotal/VA = 1/xA and Vtotal/VB = 1/xB, ΔSmix = −R(nA ln xA + nB ln xB).

◆Concept Application 2 — maximum composition

For fixed total moles of two distinct ideal gases, find the composition that maximises molar entropy of mixing.

Solution

Differentiate −R[x ln x +(1−x)ln(1−x)]. The derivative is −R ln[x/(1−x)], which vanishes at x = 1/2. The second derivative is negative, so the maximum is equimolar.

◆Concept Application 3 — maximum value

Find the maximum molar entropy of mixing for two ideal gases.

Solution

At xA = xB = 1/2, ΔSmix,m = −R[2(1/2)ln(1/2)] = Rln2.

◆Concept Application 4 — identical gases

Why is the entropy of mixing zero when the partition separates identical ideal gases at the same T and P?

Solution

Removing the partition creates no new distinguishable thermodynamic composition. The initial and final macrostates are identical.

◆Concept Application 5 — dilution limit

What happens to the partial molar mixing entropy −R ln xi as xi approaches zero?

Solution

It grows without bound because a trace component gains access to a very large volume per molecule. The total contribution ni(−R ln xi) still tends to zero as ni tends to zero.

◆Concept Application 6 — multicomponent mixture

Write the entropy of mixing for k distinct ideal gases.

Solution

ΔSmix = −RΣi ni ln xi, and the molar value is −RΣi xi ln xi.

◆Concept Application 7 — thermal equilibrium temperature

Two insulated bodies with constant heat capacities C₁ and C₂ start at T₁ and T₂. Derive Tf.

Solution

Energy conservation gives C₁(Tf−T₁)+C₂(Tf−T₂)=0, hence Tf=(C1T1+C2T2)/(C₁+C₂).

◆Concept Application 8 — positivity of thermal mixing entropy

Why is C1ln(Tf/T₁)+C2ln(Tf/T₂) positive when T₁ ≠ T₂?

Solution

The final temperature is the heat-capacity-weighted arithmetic mean, while the entropy expression compares it with a corresponding weighted geometric mean. The arithmetic mean exceeds the geometric mean for unequal temperatures.

◆Concept Application 9 — reservoir heat transfer

Heat Q flows from TH to TC, with TH > TC. Write the entropy generated.

Solution

Sgen = Q(1/TC−1/TH) > 0.

◆Concept Application 10 — finite and infinitesimal gradients

How can the same total heat be transferred reversibly between two temperature ranges?

Solution

Use an infinite sequence of intermediate reservoirs whose temperatures differ infinitesimally from the receiving body at every step. Then total entropy generation tends to zero.

◆Concept Application 11 — water multistage pressure effect

In the retained water problem, why does compression from 1 atm to 5 atm lower the vapour entropy?

Solution

For an ideal gas at fixed temperature, ΔS = −Rln(P₂/P₁). Raising pressure reduces accessible volume.

◆Concept Application 12 — system versus surroundings

Why can the water-system entropy be calculated from any reversible route while the surroundings entropy cannot?

Solution

System entropy is a state function. Surroundings entropy depends on the actual heat amounts and reservoir temperatures used in the real path.

◆Concept Application 13 — adiabatic path ranking

Rank the final temperatures in the retained neon expansion.

Solution

Reversible adiabatic gives the lowest temperature, about 328 K; constant-external-pressure expansion gives 359.48 K; free expansion gives 473 K. Less work output means less cooling.

◆Concept Application 14 — entropy ranking of neon routes

Rank entropy generation for the three neon routes.

Solution

Reversible: 0; constant external pressure: about 0.954 J K⁻¹; free expansion: about 3.81 J K⁻¹.

◆Concept Application 15 — van der Waals excluded volume

Why does the mixing-space logarithm of a van der Waals gas involve V−nb rather than V?

Solution

The molecular cores exclude volume nb from translational access. The available configurational volume is V−nb.

◆Concept Application 16 — heat of mixing caveat

Why is the simple two-liquid thermal-equilibration formula incomplete for non-ideal miscible liquids?

Solution

Actual mixing can have non-zero enthalpy, volume, and composition entropy. These contributions alter both the final temperature and total entropy.

Integrated Enrichment

Absolute Entropy — Measurement and Application

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Calorimetric vs spectroscopic entropy

Calorimetric entropy integrates Cp/T from 0 K to 298 K. Spectroscopic entropy calculates S from molecular partition functions (statistical mechanics). Agreement within ≈0.1 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹ validates both approaches. Discrepancies signal residual entropy.

Connects → Connects to: Third Law, statistical mechanics.

Standard molar entropies in biochemistry

Hydrolysis of ATP at pH 7 has a large negative ΔG° (≈−30 kJ mol⁻¹) partly because the entropy of the products (ADP + Pᵢ + H⁺ + H₂O rearrangement) exceeds that of ATP. Thermodynamics of biological reactions uses the same formalism with biochemical standard states.

Connects → Connects to: Gibbs energy, equilibrium.

ΔSsurr = −ΔrH/T
ΔrG = ΔrH − TΔrS

01

Standard absolute molar entropy

One mole in a specified standard state, referenced through the Third Law.

Symbol and unit

S°m in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Standard absolute molar entropy is the entropy of one mole of a substance in its specified standard state, normally at a standard pressure of 1 bar and a stated temperature. Its numerical construction begins from the Third-Law reference for a perfect crystal at \(0\ \mathrm K\), then integrates reversible heating and includes all equilibrium phase-transition entropy changes.

Concept lens

Why “absolute” still uses a reference

Unlike enthalpy differences, Third-Law entropy provides a common physically motivated zero. A substance with residual orientational disorder at \(0\ \mathrm K\) requires a residual-entropy correction.

Concept lens

Label correction

The given \(41.8\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\) entry in the softness sequence corresponds to\(\mathrm{SiO_2(s)}\), not \(\mathrm{O_2(s)}\). The chemically consistent species is shown here.

Concept lens

Trends are conditional, not universal laws

Entropy comparisons require comparable temperature, pressure, physical state, standard-state convention, molecular symmetry, and intermolecular interactions.
03

Dissolution and solvation entropy

Concept lens

Solid or liquid dissolving

Particle dispersion often increases entropy, as in the listed methanol and sodium chloride examples. Strong solvent ordering can nevertheless make the total trend smaller or even reverse it.

Concept lens

Gas dissolving

Gas molecules lose most of their translational volume and become solvated, so their standard molar entropy is often much lower in solution.
04

Entropy change of a chemical reaction

Balanced coefficients and physical states are part of the thermodynamic equation.

General reaction

aA(m) + bB(n) → cC(o) + dD(p)

Reaction entropy

ΔrS = cSC + dSD − aSA − bSB

Standard-state form

ΔrS° = ΣνS°m(products) − ΣνS°m(reactants)

Concept lens

Why absolute entropies are usable here

All species share the same Third-Law reference convention, so their stoichiometric difference gives a meaningful reaction entropy.
05

Entropy change of the surroundings

At constant pressure, the reaction enthalpy controls reservoir entropy.

System heat at constant pressure

qp,sys = ΔrH

Heat received by surroundings

qsurr = −ΔrH

Large reservoir at temperature T

ΔSsurr = qsurr/T = −ΔrH/T

Concept lens

Exothermic reaction

\(\Delta_rH<0\), so \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}>0\).

Concept lens

Endothermic reaction

\(\Delta_rH>0\), so \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}<0\).

Concept lens

Assumptions behind −ΔH/T

The surroundings are modelled as a large uniform-temperature reservoir, the reaction occurs at constant pressure, and the only relevant exchange is the reaction heat.

Concept lens

System entropy cannot be obtained from ΔH alone

\(\Delta_rS\) is calculated from state entropies or another valid entropy route. Enthalpy determines the reservoir contribution, not the complete system entropy.
06

Driving force of a spontaneous chemical process

The given two-condition shortcut is replaced by the complete thermodynamic criterion.

Universe criterion

ΔSuniv = ΔrS − ΔrH/T

Gibbs connection

ΔrG = ΔrH − TΔrS = −TΔSuniv

At constant T and P

spontaneous: ΔrG < 0 • equilibrium: ΔrG = 0

Concept lens

Critical correction

A spontaneous reaction does not require both \(\Delta H<0\) and \(\Delta S>0\). Those signs guarantee favourability at every temperature, but the other sign combinations may be spontaneous over restricted temperature ranges.
07

Temperature and all four sign combinations

08

Predicting the sign of reaction entropy

More gaseous product moles

usually ΔrS > 0

Gas particles have much larger translational entropy than condensed species. Count gaseous stoichiometric moles as a first estimate.

Solid → liquid → gas

usually ΔrS > 0

Phase change toward greater molecular mobility and accessible volume generally raises entropy.

Cyclisation

usually ΔrS < 0

Ring formation commonly reduces conformational freedom. This—not a universal replacement of rotation by vibration—is the safer explanation.

Molecular complexity

often raises molar S°

Additional atoms, vibrational modes, and conformations generally increase the absolute molar entropy.

HCOOH(g) → H₂(g) + CO₂(g)

Δn₍g₎ = +1 ⇒ ΔrS predicted positive

The gaseous-mole count rises from one to two, so a positive entropy change is a strong qualitative prediction.

H₂O(l) → H₂O(g)

ΔrS positive

Vaporisation creates a large increase in translational freedom.

C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(g)

Δn₍g₎ = +6 ⇒ ΔrS predicted positive

Under the given gas-phase water specification, gaseous moles increase from six to twelve.

Concept lens

Heuristics require final verification

Gas-mole count, phase change, cyclisation, and molecular complexity are useful rapid predictors. Quantitative work must use tabulated molar entropies.

Concept lens

Standard-state direction is not permanent conversion

“Spontaneous” in the sign table means the forward reaction has negative standard Gibbs energy under the stated conditions. Equilibrium composition and reaction quotient still determine the actual direction away from standard state.
10

Original complete worked examples

◆Reaction entropy from tabulated values

At 298 K, use S°(H₂)=130.7, S°(Cl₂)=223.1, and S°(HCl)=186.7 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ to calculate ΔrS° for H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(g).

Solution

ΔrS° = 2(186.7)−130.7−223.1 = +19.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Surroundings entropy

A reaction at 298 K has ΔrH° = −92.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔSsurr for an ideal constant-temperature reservoir.

Solution

ΔSsurr = −ΔrH°/T = 92000/298 = +308.7 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Universe and Gibbs criteria

For the same reaction, ΔrS° = −150 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Determine ΔSuniv and ΔrG° at 298 K.

Solution

ΔSuniv = −150 + 308.7 = +158.7 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. ΔrG° = −TΔSuniv = −47.3 kJ mol⁻¹, so the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

◆Threshold temperature

A process has ΔH = +60.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +120 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Above what temperature is it spontaneous?

Solution

Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 60000/120 = 500 K. The forward process is spontaneous for T > 500 K.

◆Low-temperature spontaneity

A reaction has ΔH = −80.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −200 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the temperature range for forward spontaneity.

Solution

ΔG = −80000 + 200T. It is negative for T < 400 K.

◆Dissolution comparison

Using the given data, find the standard entropy change for NaCl(s)→NaCl(aq).

Solution

ΔS° = 115.4−72.4 = +43.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. This is the standard-state entropy difference for the listed conventions.

11

Thermodynamics around you

An ice cube melts in a warm room

The system entropy rises during melting, and the room entropy falls as it supplies heat. The total remains positive for spontaneous melting above the equilibrium temperature.

Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating

The reaction is endothermic but produces gaseous molecules, so a positive entropy term can dominate at high temperature.

Hydrogen chloride dissolves in water

The gas loses translational freedom and becomes strongly solvated, explaining the large fall in the listed standard molar entropy.

Ozone formation needs energy

Forming fewer gas molecules is entropically unfavourable, and the reaction is endothermic; the forward standard process is not spontaneous.

12

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Every spontaneous reaction must have ΔH<0 and ΔS>0.IncorrectThe complete criterion at constant T and P is ΔG=ΔH−TΔS<0.
An exothermic reaction is always spontaneous.IncorrectA sufficiently negative entropy change can make ΔG positive at high temperature.
An endothermic reaction is never spontaneous.IncorrectPositive entropy can drive an endothermic process at sufficiently high temperature.
Dissolving a solid always raises entropy.IncorrectSolute dispersion competes with solvent ordering and specific interactions.
Absolute entropy means entropy without any reference convention.RefineThird-Law entropy uses the reference S=0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K; residual entropy is added when disorder remains.
Tabulated values should be copied without checking.IncorrectOne water-formation enthalpy entry is internally inconsistent and has been corrected using standard thermochemical data.
More product gas moles guarantee positive ΔrS.IncorrectIt is a strong heuristic, not a proof; actual standard molar entropies decide.
Thermodynamic favourability predicts speed.IncorrectKinetics and activation energy control rate.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Maxwell relations derived from exact differentials

From dU = T dS − P dV(∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V
From dH = T dS + V dP(∂T/∂P)_S = (∂V/∂S)_P
From dA = −S dT − P dV(∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V
From dG = V dP − S dT(∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P = −Vα (α = thermal expansion coeff.)
Why usefulMaxwell relations express unmeasurable quantities (∂S/∂P)_T in terms of measurable (∂V/∂T)_P

Derivation 2

Gibbs–Helmholtz equation derivation

Start from G = H − TSG/T = H/T − S
Differentiate w.r.t. T at constant P∂(G/T)/∂T = (T∂G/∂T − G)/T² = (T(−S) − G)/T² = −(G + TS)/T² = −H/T²
Result[∂(G/T)/∂T]_P = −H/T²
Reaction form[∂(ΔG°/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔH°/T²
IntegrateΔG°(T₂)/T₂ − ΔG°(T₁)/T₁ = ΔH°(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) (if ΔH° ≈ const)
13

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — standard molar entropy

What is meant by the standard absolute molar entropy S°m of a substance?

Solution

It is the entropy of one mole in its specified standard state, usually at 1 bar and a stated temperature, referenced through the Third-Law zero for a perfect crystal at 0 K.

◆Concept Application 2 — phase ranking

Why is the gas entropy usually much larger than the liquid entropy of the same substance?

Solution

The gas has access to a vastly larger translational volume and many more positional microstates.

◆Concept Application 3 — dissolution warning

Must dissolving every solid increase the total entropy?

Solution

No. Solute dispersion tends to raise entropy, but solvent ordering and strong ion hydration can offset or exceed that contribution.

◆Concept Application 4 — dissolved gas

Why is the standard molar entropy of dissolved HCl much lower than gaseous HCl in the comparison?

Solution

Dissolution removes most gas-phase translational freedom and introduces strong solvation constraints.

◆Concept Application 5 — mass trend

Why does F₂(g)<Cl₂(g)<Br₂(g) in standard molar entropy under comparable conditions?

Solution

Increasing molecular mass compresses the spacing of translational and rotational energy levels, increasing the number of thermally accessible states.

◆Concept Application 6 — graphite versus diamond

Explain why graphite has a higher standard molar entropy than diamond.

Solution

Graphite has softer lattice modes and layered structural freedom, whereas diamond is a rigid three-dimensional covalent network.

◆Concept Application 7 — reaction entropy

Write ΔrS° for aA+bB→cC+dD.

Solution

ΔrS° = cS°m(C)+dS°m(D)−aS°m(A)−bS°m(B), using the stated physical form of every species.

◆Concept Application 8 — surroundings formula

Under what conditions may one use ΔSsurr = −ΔrH/T?

Solution

For a constant-pressure reaction exchanging heat with a large surroundings reservoir maintained at uniform temperature T, with only the stated heat exchange contributing.

◆Concept Application 9 — exothermic reaction

What is the sign of ΔSsurr for an exothermic reaction at constant T and P?

Solution

Positive, because ΔrH<0 and ΔSsurr=−ΔrH/T.

◆Concept Application 10 — endothermic reaction

Can an endothermic reaction be spontaneous?

Solution

Yes. If ΔS is positive and TΔS exceeds ΔH, then ΔG=ΔH−TΔS<0.

◆Concept Application 11 — exothermic and negative entropy

A reaction has ΔH<0 and ΔS<0. Explain its temperature dependence.

Solution

It is favoured at low temperature, where the favourable negative enthalpy dominates the positive contribution −TΔS.

◆Concept Application 12 — entropy-only prediction

Can the sign of ΔrS alone determine spontaneity at constant T and P?

Solution

No. Both ΔrH and ΔrS enter ΔrG=ΔrH−TΔrS.

◆Concept Application 13 — gas-mole heuristic

Why is gaseous mole count only a heuristic for ΔrS?

Solution

Molecular complexity, symmetry, phase, solvation, and actual tabulated molar entropies may alter or reverse the simple mole-count prediction.

◆Concept Application 14 — cyclisation

Why does intramolecular ring formation often give a negative entropy change?

Solution

The cyclic product usually has fewer accessible conformations than the flexible acyclic reactant.

◆Concept Application 15 — equilibrium condition

Relate ΔG and ΔSuniverse at constant T and P.

Solution

ΔG = −TΔSuniverse. At equilibrium both are zero for an infinitesimal permitted change.

◆Concept Application 16 — rate versus spontaneity

Does a large negative ΔG guarantee a rapid reaction?

Solution

No. ΔG determines thermodynamic direction, while the rate depends on the activation barrier and reaction mechanism.

Integrated Enrichment

Free Energy — Experimental Connections

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Electrochemical cells and ΔG

For an electrochemical cell: ΔG = −nFE_cell where F = 96485 C mol⁻¹ (Faraday constant) and E_cell is the cell potential. Maximum electrical work delivered reversibly equals −ΔG. This connects thermodynamics directly to measurable voltages.

Connects → Connects to: Nernst equation, electrochemistry.

Rubber elasticity as a Helmholtz energy example

A stretched rubber band at constant T and V has ΔA > 0 (work done on rubber). When released isothermally, it returns work. The restoring force is entropy-driven: stretching reduces conformational microstates. Helmholtz energy A = U − TS is the appropriate free energy for constant-V elastic work.

Connects → Connects to: Helmholtz energy, Parts 24–25.

Thermodynamics • Absolute-Entropy Foundation

The Third Law gives entropy a physical zero—and Boltzmann explains when that zero fails

Perfect order with one ground-state arrangement gives \(S(0)=0\). Degenerate frozen arrangements create residual entropy. Calorimetry then builds the entropy upward through \(C_p/T\) integrals and equilibrium transition jumps.

Third-Law core

S = kBlnΩ
Ω0 = 1 ⇒ S(0) = 0
S°m(T) = Sres,m + ∫C°p,m/T dT + ΣΔH°tr/Ttr
📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Third Law of Thermodynamics

The zero-entropy statement needs purity, crystalline perfection, equilibrium, and a unique ground state.

Planck form

limT→0S = 0 for a pure perfect crystal with Ω₀ = 1
FormulationStatementRole
Planck statementS → 0 as T → 0 for a pure perfect crystal with a unique ground statedefines the Third-Law zero
Nernst heat theoremΔS → 0 as T → 0 for equilibrium isothermal transformationsentropy differences vanish near 0 K
Unattainability principle0 K cannot be reached by a finite sequence of operationsseparate operational form
Statistical formS(0) = kB lnΩ0zero only when Ω0 = 1
Residual-entropy caseΩ0 > 1 ⇒ Sres > 0frozen orientational/configurational degeneracy

Concept lens

Scientific correction to “the zero is merely assumed”

The zero is not an arbitrary bookkeeping choice like choosing an enthalpy origin. Statistical mechanics supplies a physical basis: \(S=k_B\ln\Omega\), so a unique ground state has \(S=0\). Residual degeneracy must be added when \(\Omega_0>1\).

Concept lens

Absolute zero and unattainability

The Third-Law entropy statement and the unattainability of exactly \(0\ \mathrm K\) are related but distinct formulations. Zero kelvin cannot be reached by a finite sequence of thermodynamic operations.
02

Nernst heat theorem

Low-temperature entropy-difference limit

limT→0ΔStransformation(T) = 0

Concept lens

Scope

The theorem concerns equilibrium isothermal transformations between well-defined states as the temperature approaches zero. It is not a statement that every arbitrary irreversible process has zero entropy change.

Concept lens

Connection to a common zero

If entropy differences among perfect crystalline equilibrium forms vanish at \(0\ \mathrm K\), they may consistently share the perfect-crystal zero.
03

Boltzmann entropy and thermodynamic probability

A macrostate may be realised by many microscopic arrangements.

Microscopic entropy

S = kBlnΩ

Independent subsystems

ΩAB = ΩAΩB ⇒ SAB = SA + SB

w orientations per molecule

Ω = wᴺ ⇒ S = NkBlnw = nRlnw

Concept lens

Ω versus w

\(\Omega\) is the multiplicity of the whole system. \(w\) may denote the number of independent orientations available to each molecule. Confusing them can introduce an incorrect factor of \(N\).
04

Residual entropy

Residual entropy

Sres = kBlnΩ₀

Molar form for independent w-fold disorder

Sres,m = Rlnw

Concept lens

Ice

Each oxygen has two short covalent O-H bonds and two longer hydrogen-bond contacts, but many global arrangements satisfy these local rules. The given value is about\(3.4\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).

Concept lens

AB orientational disorder

If AB and BA orientations are nearly degenerate and frozen randomly, multiple ground-state arrangements remain accessible and \(S(0)>0\).

Concept lens

Hydrogen example—required correction

The stated model uses an idealised \(w=2\) ortho/para example. Equilibrium hydrogen at very low temperature tends toward para-H₂ in its lowest rotational state. Residual entropy belongs to a frozen non-equilibrium ortho/para mixture and depends on its composition; \(R\ln2\) is only a simplified binary-degeneracy model.

Concept lens

Perfect crystal, imperfect crystal, and glass

A perfect crystal may have \(\Omega_0=1\). Defects, orientational disorder, or an amorphous frozen structure can retain configurational entropy at \(0\ \mathrm K\).
05

Debye low-temperature extrapolation

Near zero kelvin, a non-metallic crystal’s lattice heat capacity follows a cubic law.

Debye T³ law

Cp,m ≈ CV,m = aT³

Low-temperature entropy

Sm(T)−Sm(0) = ∫₀ᵀaT′³dT′/T′ = aT³/3

Endpoint shortcut

Sm(T)−Sm(0) = Cp,m(T)/3

Concept lens

Validity gate

The cubic law is a low-temperature lattice approximation for non-metallic crystals. Metals require an additional electronic term, commonly \(C_p\approx\gamma T+\beta T^3\).

Retained chapter numerical

Low-temperature entropy from one heat-capacity measurement

DEBYE T³ LAW

The molar constant-pressure heat capacity of a non-metallic solid at \(4.2\ \mathrm K\) is\(0.43\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\). Find its molar entropy at that temperature, assuming a perfect crystal and validity of \(C_{p,m}=aT^3\) from \(0\) to \(4.2\ \mathrm K\).

Third-Law integral

Sm(T) = Sm(0) + ∫₀ᵀ aT′³ dT′/T′

Integration

Sm(T) = Sm(0) + aT³/3

Use Cp,m(T) = aT³

Sm(T) = Sm(0) + Cp,m(T)/3

Perfect-crystal result

Sm(4.2 K) = 0 + 0.43/3 = 0.143 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 0.14 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Concept lens

Why the formula is unusually simple

The cubic law makes \(C_p/T\propto T^2\), whose integral is exactly one third of the endpoint heat capacity.
06

Calorimetric construction of absolute entropy

Integrate within phases and add every reversible transition jump.

Heating within one phase

S(T₂) = S(T₁) + ∫T₁T₂Cp(T′)dT′/T′

Transition contribution

ΔStr = ΔHtr/Ttr

Complete standard molar construction

S°m(T) = Sres,m + Σ∫C°p,m(T′)dT′/T′ + ΣΔH°tr/Ttr

Concept lens

Full route above the boiling point

Heat the solid from \(0\) to \(T_f\), add \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{fus}}/T_f\), heat the liquid to \(T_b\), add \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}}/T_b\), then heat the gas to the final temperature. Any solid-solid transition adds its own \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{tr}}/T_{\mathrm{tr}}\).

Concept lens

Thermochemistry boundary

This part uses measured \(C_p\) and transition enthalpies as inputs to entropy. Their experimental determination and detailed enthalpy theory remain in Thermochemistry.
07

Graphical evaluation of the entropy integral

Equivalent areas

∫Cp,m(T)dT/T = ∫Cp,md(lnT)

Concept lens

Standard entropy

When the pure substance follows its standard state at \(1\ \mathrm{bar}\), the calorimetric total is\(S^\circ(T)\); dividing by the amount gives \(S_m^\circ(T)\).
08

Calorimetric and statistical routes

Two independent routes should agree for an equilibrium substance.

Calorimetric route

Measure \(C_p(T)\), extrapolate to \(0\ \mathrm K\), and add every phase-transition entropy.

Statistical/spectroscopic route

Determine molecular energy levels and degeneracies, evaluate state populations, and calculate entropy statistically.

Concept lens

Residual entropy appears as a route mismatch

If calorimetry assumes \(S(0)=0\) but spectroscopy reveals frozen degeneracy, the difference identifies a residual-entropy contribution.
09

Aqueous-ion entropy convention

Conventional single-ion reference

S°m(H⁺, aq) = 0 at each stated temperature

Concept lens

Not a directly measurable absolute single-ion entropy

Thermodynamic measurements give entropy changes for electrically neutral combinations. Individual aqueous-ion entropies require a convention; relative tabulated values can therefore be negative.

Concept lens

Reaction entropies remain measurable

In a charge-balanced reaction, the arbitrary single-ion convention cancels from the stoichiometric entropy difference.
10

Retained complete summary

01

Calorimetric determination

Measure Cp from low temperature to the target temperature and add every transition entropy.

02

Debye extrapolation

Use Cp,m = aT³ for a non-metallic crystal sufficiently close to 0 K.

03

Nernst theorem

For equilibrium transformations, ΔS approaches zero as T approaches zero.

04

Third Law

A pure perfect crystal with one ground-state arrangement has S(0)=0.

05

Residual entropy

Disorder frozen into the ground-state manifold gives Sres>0.

06

Third-Law entropy

Absolute entropy is constructed from the 0 K reference plus measured contributions.

07

Aqueous-ion convention

Single-ion standard entropies use S°m(H⁺,aq)=0 by convention at each temperature.

08

Reaction entropy

ΔrS° is the stoichiometric product total minus the reactant total.

11

Residual entropy exceptions

Exception to the Third Law

Residual entropy of imperfect crystals

S(0) > 0

The Third Law statement Sm(0) = 0 applies strictly to a perfect crystal, meaning every lattice site has one unique, ordered orientation. Some molecular solids freeze into a rigid lattice before every molecule can settle into its lowest-energy orientation. The disorder becomes trapped, so the crystal reaches 0 K without ever reaching a single unique microstate.

Statistical origin of residual entropy

S(0) = k ln Ω(0), with Ω(0) > 1 for a frozen orientational disorder

Carbon monoxide, CO(s)

Two nearly identical orientations (C≡O and O≡C) per site ⇒ Ω(0) ≈ 2ᴺ ⇒ Sm(0) = R ln 2 ≈ 5.76 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Ice, H₂O(s)

Pauling residual entropy from proton disorder in the hydrogen-bonded lattice: Sm(0) = R ln(3/2) ≈ 3.37 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Concept lens

How residual entropy is detected experimentally

The calorimetric (Third-Law) entropy, built by integrating Cp/T from 0 K, is compared with the spectroscopic entropy calculated independently from molecular and rotational data. A calorimetric value that falls short of the spectroscopic value by a fixed amount reveals the residual entropy frozen into the solid at 0 K.

Concept lens

Why perfectly ordered solids do not show this gap

For a substance with only one possible ground-state orientation (Ω(0) = 1), S(0) = k ln 1 = 0 exactly, and calorimetric and spectroscopic entropies agree. Residual entropy appears only when near-degenerate orientations remain kinetically frozen rather than annealing into a single arrangement before 0 K is reached.
12

Original and retained worked examples

◆Binary orientational disorder

Each molecule in a frozen crystal may occupy either of two exactly degenerate orientations independently. Find the residual molar entropy.

Solution

For N molecules, Ω=2^N. Therefore S=kBlnΩ=NkBln2. Per mole, Sres,m=Rln2=5.763 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Ice residual entropy

Use the Pauling multiplicity w=3/2 per water molecule to estimate the residual molar entropy of ordinary ice.

Solution

Sres,m=Rln(3/2)=8.314ln1.5=3.37 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, consistent with the given value near 3.4 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Infer effective multiplicity

A disordered crystal has residual molar entropy 4.00 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the effective degeneracy per molecule w.

Solution

Rlnw=4.00, so w=exp(4.00/8.314)=1.618.

◆One phase transition

A perfect crystal has Cp,m=aT³ up to a transition at 20 K, where ΔHtr=80 J mol⁻¹. If Cp,m(20 K)=6.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the entropy just above the transition.

Solution

Below the transition, S= Cp,m(20 K)/3 = 2.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The transition adds ΔHtr/Ttr=80/20=4.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Total = 6.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

◆Aqueous-ion convention

Why may a tabulated standard molar entropy of an aqueous ion be negative even though thermodynamic entropy is non-negative relative to the Third-Law reference?

Solution

A single-ion value is assigned relative to the conventional zero S°m(H⁺,aq)=0. It is not an independently measured absolute single-ion entropy, so relative values may be negative.

◆Cp versus lnT graph

Explain why the area under Cp,m versus lnT equals the entropy increase.

Solution

Because d(lnT)=dT/T. Therefore ∫Cp,m d(lnT)=∫Cp,m dT/T=ΔS for reversible heating at constant pressure.

13

Thermodynamics around you

Why crystals are cooled before heat-capacity measurement

Low-temperature data anchor the Third-Law integral and reveal whether a Debye extrapolation is appropriate.

Why ordinary ice retains disorder

Hydrogen-bond orientations satisfy local ice rules in many equivalent ways, leaving residual configurational entropy.

Why glass is not a perfect Third-Law crystal

A glass freezes a disordered structure rather than reaching a unique long-range ordered equilibrium crystal.

Why spectroscopy can predict entropy

Rotational, vibrational, electronic, and translational energy-level information determines molecular state counts.

14

Trap detector

Tempting statementVerdictCorrection
Every solid has S=0 at 0 K.IncorrectOnly a pure perfect crystal with a unique ground state has zero entropy. Frozen disorder gives residual entropy.
The Third-Law zero is arbitrary in exactly the same way as an enthalpy zero.RefineIt is tied to the statistical state Ω0=1 for a perfect crystal, although practical conventions remain necessary for quantities such as single-ion entropies.
Nernst theorem says every arbitrary process has ΔS=0 near 0 K.IncorrectIt concerns equilibrium isothermal transformations in the low-temperature limit.
Cp=aT³ is valid for every material at every temperature.IncorrectIt is a low-temperature lattice approximation for non-metallic crystals.
Residual entropy comes from thermal vibration at 0 K.IncorrectIt comes from configurational or orientational ground-state degeneracy, not ordinary thermal excitation.
The given H2 w=2 statement applies to equilibrium hydrogen automatically.IncorrectEquilibrium hydrogen tends toward para-H2; a frozen ortho/para mixture requires a composition-dependent treatment.
A negative tabulated aqueous-ion entropy violates the Third Law.IncorrectSingle-ion entropies are relative to a convention and are not individually measurable absolute entropies.
Only the Cp/T graph can yield calorimetric entropy.IncorrectAn equivalent area is obtained from Cp versus lnT because dlnT=dT/T.

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Fundamental relation for open systems — chemical potential

Closed system dUdU = T dS − P dV
Open systemmatter can enter/leave → U also depends on nᵢ
Extended fundamental relationdU = T dS − P dV + Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ
Chemical potential definitionμᵢ ≡ (∂U/∂nᵢ)_{S,V,nⱼ≠ᵢ} = (∂G/∂nᵢ)_{T,P,nⱼ≠ᵢ}
Euler's theoremG = Σᵢ nᵢ μᵢ (consequence of G being extensive in nᵢ)
Gibbs–Duhem equationΣᵢ nᵢ dμᵢ = 0 at constant T, P
15

Complete worked examples and applications

◆Concept Application 1 — Third-Law condition

State the microscopic condition required for S(0)=0.

Solution

The equilibrium crystal must have a unique ground-state arrangement, so Ω0=1.

◆Concept Application 2 — Nernst theorem

What tends to zero according to the Nernst heat theorem?

Solution

The entropy change of an equilibrium isothermal physical or chemical transformation tends to zero as T→0.

◆Concept Application 3 — unattainability

Does the statement S→0 prove that 0 K can be reached?

Solution

No. The unattainability principle is a separate formulation: no finite sequence of thermodynamic operations reaches exactly 0 K.

◆Concept Application 4 — logarithm and additivity

Why does Boltzmann entropy use lnΩ rather than Ω itself?

Solution

For independent systems, multiplicities multiply: ΩAB=ΩAΩB. The logarithm converts multiplication into addition, so SAB=SA+SB.

◆Concept Application 5 — per-particle degeneracy

N independent molecules each have w accessible orientations. Derive the entropy.

Solution

Ω=w^N, so S=kBln(w^N)=NkBlnw. For one mole, S=Rlnw.

◆Concept Application 6 — residual entropy

Can a crystal have non-zero entropy at 0 K without violating the statistical definition?

Solution

Yes. If multiple degenerate configurations remain frozen, Ω0>1 and Sres=kBlnΩ0>0.

◆Concept Application 7 — equilibrium hydrogen correction

Does ordinary equilibrium H2 necessarily have Rln2 residual entropy at 0 K?

Solution

No. Equilibrium hydrogen tends toward para-H2 in its unique lowest rotational state. Residual entropy can occur in a frozen non-equilibrium ortho/para mixture, and depends on its composition.

◆Concept Application 8 — amorphous solid

Why is an amorphous solid excluded from the simple perfect-crystal Third-Law statement?

Solution

It lacks a unique long-range ordered crystalline arrangement and can retain configurational disorder as T→0.

◆Concept Application 9 — Debye entropy

If Cp,m=aT³, derive Sm(T)−Sm(0).

Solution

Integrate aT³/T=aT² from 0 to T: the result is aT³/3=Cp,m(T)/3.

◆Concept Application 10 — metallic caveat

Why is the simple Cp∝T³ law not the complete low-temperature heat capacity of a metal?

Solution

Metals also have an electronic contribution approximately proportional to T, so Cp≈γT+βT³ at sufficiently low temperature.

◆Concept Application 11 — transition jump

A reversible phase transition has enthalpy ΔHtr at Ttr. What entropy contribution must be added?

Solution

ΔStr=ΔHtr/Ttr.

◆Concept Application 12 — several transitions

How is absolute entropy constructed when a substance has multiple solid-solid transitions before melting?

Solution

Integrate Cp/T within every stable phase and add ΔHtr/Ttr for every reversible transition in sequence.

◆Concept Application 13 — standard molar entropy

What conditions make a calorimetrically obtained entropy a standard molar entropy?

Solution

Measurements must follow the pure substance in its standard state, conventionally at 1 bar, and the total entropy is divided by the amount of substance.

◆Concept Application 14 — spectroscopy route

Why can spectroscopic data be used to calculate entropy?

Solution

Spectroscopy reveals energy levels and degeneracies, allowing the molecular partition function and statistical entropy to be evaluated.

◆Concept Application 15 — single-ion entropy

Are standard molar entropies of isolated aqueous ions directly measurable as absolute quantities?

Solution

No. Only electrically neutral combinations are directly measurable; single-ion values require an extrathermodynamic convention such as S°m(H⁺,aq)=0.

◆Concept Application 16 — reaction entropy

How do Third-Law entropies give a standard reaction entropy?

Solution

Use ΔrS°=ΣνS°m(products)−ΣνS°m(reactants), including stoichiometric coefficients and physical states.

Synergic Bond rapid recall

A unique ground state gives zero entropy; measured heat capacities build the absolute entropy upward

Maxwell Relations — Practical Consequences

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

(∂P/∂T)_V = (∂S/∂V)_T — the pressure coefficient

This Maxwell relation from dA connects the pressure coefficient (measurable) to the entropy change with volume. For ideal gas: (∂P/∂T)_V = nR/V > 0. For a real gas, this allows calculation of entropy from P–V–T data without calorimetry.

Connects → Connects to: equations of state, internal pressure.

Joule–Thomson as a Maxwell relation application

Using the Maxwell relation (∂H/∂P)_T = V − T(∂V/∂T)_P and μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H, the Joule–Thomson coefficient can be computed from volumetric data alone. For van der Waals gas: μ_JT = (2a/RT − b)/Cp,m at moderate pressures.

Connects → Connects to: Joule–Thomson, Part 25.

Retained Third-Law entropy numerical

Five additive contributions from 0 K to 350 K

Solid heating, 0→200 K

ΔS₁=∫[0.035(T/K)+0.0012(T/K)²]dT/T=31.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Fusion at 200 K

ΔS₂=7.5×10³/200=37.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Liquid heating, 200→300 K

ΔS₃=60ln(300/200)+0.016(300−200)=25.93 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Vaporisation at 300 K

ΔS₄=30×10³/300=100 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Gas heating, 300→350 K

ΔS₅=50ln(350/300)=7.71 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Total

S°m(350 K)=202.14 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
02

Relative standard entropies of aqueous ions

Convention

S°m(H⁺,aq)=0 at every stated temperature

Concept lens

Why negative values are possible

A single aqueous ion cannot be isolated thermodynamically without a counter-ion. Tables therefore use a relative convention. Negative listed values do not mean a negative physical total entropy.
03

Explicit microstate counting

Concept lens

Counting convention

The stated example gives 20 microstates for three distinguishable particles with total energy \(5\varepsilon\), then five occupation patterns for the corresponding indistinguishable-particle treatment. Because counting depends on allowed levels and distinguishability, the exact convention is stated rather than hidden.

Boltzmann bridge

S=kBlnΩ

η=1−Tc/Th

If Tc=0.9Th

η=1−0.9=0.10=10%

Concept lens

Interpretation

A sink only ten percent colder than the source permits at most ten percent Carnot efficiency.
05

Effect of temperature on reaction entropy

General relation

ΔrS°(T₂)=ΔrS°(T₁)+∫T₁T₂ΔrC°p/T dT

Constant ΔrCp°

ΔrS°(T₂)=ΔrS°(T₁)+ΔrC°pln(T₂/T₁)

Reaction

½N₂(g)+O₂(g)→NO₂(g)

At 298 K

Effect of pressure on reaction entropy

Temperature effect on reaction entropy

Kirchhoff-type entropy relation

ΔrS°(T₂)=ΔrS°(T₁)+∫T₁T₂ΔrC°p/T dT

Constant ΔCp

ΔrS°(T₂)=ΔrS°(T₁)+ΔrC°pln(T₂/T₁)

Pressure effect on ideal-gas reaction entropy

At fixed T

Direction

Ideal-gas reaction

Concept lens

Physical meaning

Compression lowers the entropy of each gas. A reaction producing more gas moles is therefore penalised more strongly by pressure.
07

Bridge to Helmholtz free energy

Definition

A=U−TS

Differential

dA=−S dT−P dV for a simple closed system of fixed composition

Constant T,V criterion

spontaneous: ΔA<0 • equilibrium: ΔA=0

Concept lens

Why Helmholtz appears now

Entropy alone gives the isolated-system criterion. At fixed temperature and volume, the same direction test is packaged into Helmholtz free energy.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Temperature correction of reaction entropy using Kirchhoff-type integral

Differentiate ΔrS° w.r.t. T[∂(ΔrS°)/∂T]_P = ΔrCp°/T
Integrate from T₁ to T₂ΔrS°(T₂) = ΔrS°(T₁) + ∫[T₁→T₂] ΔrCp°/T dT
If ΔrCp° ≈ constantΔrS°(T₂) = ΔrS°(T₁) + ΔrCp° ln(T₂/T₁)
Example½N₂ + O₂ → NO₂: ΔrS°₂₉₈ = −16.805 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹, ΔrCp° = −6.725 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹
At 348 KΔrS°₃₄₈ = −16.805 + (−6.725) ln(348/298) = −16.805 − 1.048 = −17.85 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹
08

Complete worked examples and applications

Third-Law sum

Why are transition terms added rather than integrated?

A first-order transition occurs at one equilibrium temperature and contributes the finite jump ΔHtr/Ttr.

Ion convention

Why may absolute entropies of aqueous ions appear negative?

Single-ion values are relative to S°m(H+,aq)=0; only neutral combinations are directly measurable.

Three distinguishable particles

How many microstates have total energy 5ε in non-degenerate levels 0,ε,2ε,...?

Count non-negative ordered triples a+b+c=5: C(7,2)=21 if each particle's level index can include 0. If the level scheme instead requires every particle to occupy at least the first level (no particle at the zero-energy level), the shifted count gives 20 arrangements — the two totals reflect different level-numbering conventions, not a contradiction.

Three bosons

How many occupation-number patterns satisfy Σni=3 and Σεini=5ε?

The source reports five allowed patterns for its shown level set.

Temperature correction

If ΔrCp°<0, what happens to ΔrS° as T rises?

It decreases because the integral of ΔrCp°/T is negative.

Pressure correction

For N2O4(g)→2NO2(g), how does pressure affect ΔrS?

Δng=+1, so increasing pressure lowers the reaction entropy by Rln(P₂/P₁).

Heat-engine percentage

For a Carnot engine, η=1−Tc/Th. If Tc=0.9Th, what is η?

η=1−0.9=0.10, or 10%.

Helmholtz bridge

Which free energy is natural at constant T and V?

Helmholtz energy A=U−TS; spontaneous change at constant T,V has ΔA<0.

Rapid recall

Absolute entropy adds by thermal route; reaction entropy shifts with temperature and pressure

Consistency check for Third-Law entropy from spectroscopy

For the five-step calculation yielding S°_m(350 K) = 202.14 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹, the equivalent spectroscopic value would come from molecular partition functions. Agreement between calorimetric and spectroscopic entropies within ±0.5 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹ confirms the Third Law.

Visible Third-Law, microstate and reaction-entropy applications

Worked application 1

Third-Law entropy staircase

Given

Add the solid-heating, fusion, liquid-heating, vaporisation and gas-heating contributions.

Solution

31.0 + 37.5 + 25.93 + 100 + 7.71 = 202.14 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 350 K.

Worked application 2

Aqueous-ion entropy convention

Given

Explain why S°m(H⁺,aq) is assigned zero and why some listed single-ion values may be negative.

Solution

Individual single-ion entropies are relative conventional values. Charge-balanced reaction entropies remain convention independent.

Worked application 3

Microstate counting

Given

Compare distinguishable-particle arrangements with occupation-pattern counting.

Solution

Distinguishable labels multiply the number of arrangements, whereas indistinguishable particles are counted through unique occupation patterns. Entropy follows S = k ln Ω.

Worked application 4

Reaction-entropy temperature dependence

Given

Determine how ΔrS° changes when reactant and product heat capacities differ.

Solution

Use d(ΔrS°)/dT = ΔrCp°/T and integrate over temperature. The sign and magnitude depend on ΔrCp°.
