PART 24 / 30Free Energies & EquilibriumHelmholtz and Gibbs Free Energies
SYNERGIC BOND MASTER NOTESCOMPLETE THEORYHELMHOLTZ & GIBBS ENERGY

Free energy converts the universe’s entropy test into a system-only criterion

Helmholtz energy governs constant-temperature, constant-volume change. Gibbs energy governs constant-temperature, constant-pressure change and measures the maximum reversible non-expansion work.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
01

Why free-energy functions are introduced

Entropy of the universe is the universal spontaneity criterion, but calculating the surroundings explicitly may be inconvenient. Free-energy functions absorb the surroundings contribution under specified constraints, allowing direction to be decided from system properties alone.

Concept lens

Constraint gate

A free-energy criterion is valid only when its stated constraints are satisfied. Using \(\Delta G\) for a rigid constant-volume process or \(\Delta A\) for an unrestricted constant-pressure process is conceptually wrong.
02

Helmholtz free energy

Definition

A = U − TS

Differential

dA = dU − T dS − S dT

Fundamental substitution

dU = T dS − P dV

Result

dA = −S dT − P dV

Concept lens

Name and symbol

The chapter notes that \(A\) comes from the German word Arbeit, meaning work. Many books also use \(F\) for Helmholtz energy.

Concept lens

Properties

\(A\) is a state function, extensive, and has the dimensions of energy.
03

Helmholtz spontaneity and equilibrium at constant T,V

Clausius inequality at constant T,V

dA ≤ 0

Spontaneous

ΔA < 0

Equilibrium

ΔA = 0

Stable equilibrium

A is minimum under the allowed constraints

Concept lens

Reversible versus irreversible

A reversible infinitesimal change at equilibrium gives \(dA=0\). An irreversible spontaneous change gives \(dA<0\).
04

Helmholtz energy and maximum work

Constant T,V reversible process

wmax,by = −ΔA

Concept lens

Sign convention

With chemistry convention, work done on the system is positive. Therefore the maximum work done by the system is the positive quantity \(-\Delta A\) when \(\Delta A<0\).
05

Gibbs free energy

Definition

G = H − TS = U + PV − TS

Differential

dG = dH − T dS − S dT

For a simple closed system

dH = T dS + V dP

Result

dG = V dP − S dT

Concept lens

Properties

\(G\) is a state function, extensive, and has the dimensions of energy.
06

Gibbs spontaneity and equilibrium at constant T,P

Constant T,P criterion

dG ≤ 0

Spontaneous

ΔG < 0

Equilibrium

ΔG = 0

Stable equilibrium

G is minimum under the allowed constraints
ConditionCriterionInterpretation
Spontaneous at fixed T,VΔA < 0A decreases
Equilibrium at fixed T,VΔA = 0A is locally minimum
Non-spontaneous forward at fixed T,VΔA > 0reverse direction is favoured
Spontaneous at fixed T,PΔG < 0G decreases
Equilibrium at fixed T,PΔG = 0G is locally minimum
Non-spontaneous forward at fixed T,PΔG > 0reverse direction is favoured
07

Gibbs energy and entropy of the universe

At constant T,P

ΔGsys = −TΔSuniverse

Spontaneous

ΔSuniv>0 ⇔ ΔGsys<0

Equilibrium

ΔSuniv=0 ⇔ ΔGsys=0

Concept lens

Why this is powerful

The Gibbs criterion uses only system quantities, while remaining exactly equivalent to the universe entropy criterion under constant temperature and pressure.
08

Gibbs energy and non-PV work

Reversible constant T,P process

wnon-PV,max,by = −ΔG

Concept lens

Examples of non-PV work

Electrical work, surface work, magnetic work, and elastic work can all contribute.

Concept lens

Available energy

The decrease in Gibbs energy is the maximum reversible non-expansion work available from the process. Irreversibility makes the actual useful work smaller.
09

Fundamental free-energy matrix

ItemExpressionMeaning
Helmholtz definitionA = U − TSnatural variables T,V
Helmholtz differentialdA = −S dT − P dVsimple closed fixed-composition system
At constant T,VdA ≤ 0spontaneous decrease; equality at equilibrium

10

Original worked examples

Helmholtz criterion

A closed system at constant temperature and volume changes from A1 = 18.0 kJ to A2 = 12.5 kJ. Classify the change and find the maximum work obtainable from the system.

ΔA = 12.5−18.0 = −5.5 kJ. The change is spontaneous. For a reversible process, the maximum work done by the system is −ΔA = 5.5 kJ.

Gibbs criterion

At constant temperature and pressure, a reaction has ΔH = −40.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −80.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 298 K. Find ΔG.

ΔG = −40.0 − 298(−0.0800) = −16.16 kJ mol⁻¹. The forward reaction is spontaneous at 298 K.

Universe connection

A process at constant T = 300 K and P has ΔG = −9.00 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔSuniverse.

ΔG = −TΔSuniverse, so ΔSuniverse = 9000/300 = 30.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Maximum non-PV work

A reversible electrochemical process at constant T,P has ΔG = −125 kJ mol⁻¹. What maximum non-expansion work can be delivered?

w_non-PV,max,by = −ΔG = 125 kJ mol⁻¹.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Helmholtz energy A = U − TS: complete derivation of spontaneity criterion

DefinitionA ≡ U − TS
DifferentialdA = dU − T dS − S dT
First LawdU = δq + δw = δq − P_ext dV
Second Lawδq ≤ T dS (equality for reversible)
Combine at constant TdA = dU − T dS ≤ δw_total
At constant T,V (no PV work)dA ≤ 0 (equality for reversible)
Maximum workw_max,by = −ΔA (reversible, constant T)

Derivation 2

Gibbs energy G = H − TS: complete derivation of spontaneity criterion

DefinitionG ≡ H − TS = U + PV − TS
DifferentialdG = dH − T dS − S dT
From dH = dU + P dV + V dPdG = dU + P dV + V dP − T dS − S dT
At constant T, PdG = dU + P dV − T dS
Second LawT dS ≥ δq = dU − δw_non-PV + P dV
ThereforedG ≤ δw_non-PV,by (at constant T,P)
If no non-PV workdG ≤ 0 (equality for reversible)
Maximum non-PV workw_non-PV,max,by = −ΔG (reversible, constant T,P)
11

Complete worked examples and applications

Natural variables

What are the natural variables of A and G?

A=A(T,V); G=G(T,P) for a simple closed fixed-composition system.

Differential of A

Derive dA from A=U−TS.

dA=dU−TdS−SdT. With dU=TdS−PdV, dA=−SdT−PdV.

Differential of G

Derive dG from G=H−TS.

dG=dH−TdS−SdT. With dH=TdS+VdP, dG=VdP−SdT.

Equilibrium minimum

Why is ΔG=0 not enough to prove stable equilibrium?

A stationary point must also be a local minimum under the allowed constraints.

Irreversibility

Why is actual useful work less than −ΔG?

Entropy generation destroys work potential; equality is reached only reversibly.

Constant-volume chemistry

Which free energy is relevant in a rigid isothermal vessel?

Helmholtz energy A.

Constant-pressure chemistry

Which free energy is relevant for most laboratory reactions open to atmospheric pressure?

Gibbs energy G.

State-function status

Are A and G path functions?

No. Both are state functions because they are combinations of state functions.

Extensivity

Are A and G extensive?

Yes, for ordinary homogeneous systems they scale with system size.

Spontaneity versus rate

Does ΔG<0 imply a fast reaction?

No. It predicts direction, not kinetic speed.

PV-work caveat

Why does −ΔG represent non-PV work rather than total work at constant pressure?

The PV expansion contribution is already included in enthalpy H=U+PV.

Ideal-gas isothermal

For one mole of ideal gas expanding isothermally from P₁ to P₂, what is ΔG?

ΔG=RTln(P₂/P₁).

Rapid recall

Fixed T,V: minimise A. Fixed T,P: minimise G.

Helmholtz and Gibbs Energy — Applications Beyond Chemistry

Extended connections, applications and deeper insights for advanced understanding.

Gibbs energy and biological membranes

Ion transport across a membrane against a concentration gradient (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ pump) requires ΔG > 0 input. The pump couples this non-spontaneous step to ATP hydrolysis (ΔG_ATP < 0) so that the combined ΔG < 0. Gibbs energy is the universal criterion for all constant-T, P processes.

Connects → Connects to: chemical potential, equilibrium.

Part 25

Fundamental Equations, Maxwell Relations & Response Coefficients

Complete derivations of the four fundamental differential forms, all four principal Maxwell relations, the general heat-capacity relation, and the Joule–Thomson coefficient with inversion analysis.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
1

The Four Fundamental Differential Relations

Exact derived results — each follows from the combined First and Second Laws and the definition of each potential

Every thermodynamic potential satisfies an exact differential. Each potential is defined to have particular natural variables: when those variables are held constant, the potential is minimised (or stationary) at equilibrium and no further information about entropy or energy is lost.

Derivation of dU = T dS − P dV

Classification: Exact derived result from the combined First and Second Laws.

First LawdU = δq + δw
Reversible heatδq_rev = T dS (Second Law, Clausius)
Reversible PV workδw_rev = −P dV (mechanical equilibrium)
CombinedU = T dS − P dV
Natural variablesU is a function of S and V; both are extensive
Partial derivatives(∂U/∂S)_V = T and (∂U/∂V)_S = −P

Concept

Why the minus sign on P?

The work term is −P dV because positive volume change (expansion) means the system does work on the surroundings, reducing U. When S and V both increase, U may increase (T> 0) or decrease (−P < 0 for P > 0) depending on the relative magnitudes.

Derivation of dH = T dS + V dP

Classification: Exact derived result via Legendre transform of U.

DefinitionH = U + PV
DifferentiatedH = dU + P dV + V dP
Substitute dUdH = (T dS − P dV) + P dV + V dP
SimplifydH = T dS + V dP
Natural variablesH is a function of S and P
Partials(∂H/∂S)_P = T and (∂H/∂P)_S = V

Derivation of dA = −S dT − P dV

Classification: Exact derived result; A = U − TS (Legendre transform removing S).

DefinitionA = U − TS
DifferentiatedA = dU − T dS − S dT
Substitute dUdA = (T dS − P dV) − T dS − S dT
SimplifydA = −S dT − P dV
Natural variablesA is a function of T and V
Partials(∂A/∂T)_V = −S and (∂A/∂V)_T = −P

Derivation of dG = −S dT + V dP

Classification: Exact derived result; G = H − TS (Legendre transform removing S from H).

DefinitionG = H − TS = U + PV − TS
DifferentiatedG = dH − T dS − S dT
Substitute dHdG = (T dS + V dP) − T dS − S dT
SimplifydG = −S dT + V dP
Natural variablesG is a function of T and P — the laboratory variables
Partials(∂G/∂T)_P = −S and (∂G/∂P)_T = V
2

The Four Principal Maxwell Relations

Derived from equality of mixed second partial derivatives — each converts an unobservable entropy derivative into a measurable PVT quantity

For any continuously differentiable function f(x,y), the mixed partial derivatives are equal: ∂²f/∂y∂x = ∂²f/∂x∂y. Applying this to each thermodynamic potential yields a Maxwell relation.

Derivation from U(S,V)

From dU = T dS − P dVM = T, N = −P for variables x = S, y = V
Maxwell condition(∂M/∂y)_x = (∂N/∂x)_y
Left side(∂T/∂V)_S
Right side(∂(−P)/∂S)_V = −(∂P/∂S)_V
Result(∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V

Derivation from H(S,P)

From dH = T dS + V dPM = T, N = V for variables x = S, y = P
Left side(∂T/∂P)_S
Right side(∂V/∂S)_P
Result(∂T/∂P)_S = (∂V/∂S)_P

Derivation from A(T,V) — Most useful for PVT work

From dA = −S dT − P dVM = −S, N = −P for variables x = T, y = V
Left side(∂(−S)/∂V)_T = −(∂S/∂V)_T
Right side(∂(−P)/∂T)_V = −(∂P/∂T)_V
Result(∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V
Physical useEntropy change with volume = isochoric pressure–temperature coefficient (measurable)

Derivation from G(T,P) — Most useful for chemistry

From dG = −S dT + V dPM = −S, N = V for variables x = T, y = P
Left side(∂(−S)/∂P)_T = −(∂S/∂P)_T
Right side(∂V/∂T)_P
Result−(∂S/∂P)_T = (∂V/∂T)_P or (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P
Physical useCompression decreases entropy when volume increases with temperature (the common case)
3

General Heat-Capacity Relation C_P − C_V

Exact derived result relating the two heat capacities to measurable PVT response functions

This derivation proceeds without assumptions about the equation of state. It applies to any homogeneous closed system in a stable equilibrium state.

Write U(T,V)dU = (∂U/∂T)_V dT + (∂U/∂V)_T dV = C_V dT + π_T dV
Internal pressureπ_T = (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P [from Maxwell + 1st law]
H = U + PV → C_PC_P = (∂H/∂T)_P = (∂U/∂T)_P + P(∂V/∂T)_P
(∂U/∂T)_P along isobar= C_V + π_T(∂V/∂T)_P
CombineC_P = C_V + (π_T + P)(∂V/∂T)_P = C_V + T(∂P/∂T)_V(∂V/∂T)_P
Cyclic rule(∂P/∂T)_V = −(∂V/∂T)_P / (∂V/∂P)_T = (∂V/∂T)_P · [−(∂P/∂V)_T]
Final general formC_P − C_V = −T(∂P/∂V)_T [(∂V/∂T)_P]²
Always ≥ 0Mechanical stability requires (∂P/∂V)_T ≤ 0, so −(∂P/∂V)_T ≥ 0 ✓

Convenient compact form using α and κ_T

Isobaric expansion coefficient

α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)_P

Isothermal compressibility

κ_T = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)_T
Rewrite (∂V/∂T)_P= αV
Rewrite −(∂P/∂V)_T= 1/(κ_T V)
SubstituteC_P − C_V = T · (1/κ_T V) · (αV)² = TVα²/κ_T

General result

C_P − C_V = TVα²/κ_T

Ideal-gas special case: C_P − C_V = nR

Ideal gas V = nRT/P(∂V/∂T)_P = nR/P
α= (1/V)(nR/P) = nR/(PV) = 1/T
(∂V/∂P)_T = −nRT/P²κ_T = (1/V)(nRT/P²) = 1/P
Substitute into TVα²/κ_T= T·V·(1/T²)/(1/P) = T·V·P/(T²) = PV/T = nR
ResultC_P − C_V = nR → C_{P,m} − C_{V,m} = R

Concept

Physical meaning

At constant pressure, some heat goes into PV expansion work (nR per mole per kelvin) rather than raising temperature, so C_P is always larger than C_V. For liquids and solids α is small and κ_T is small, so C_P ≈ C_V; for gases the difference is significant.
4

Joule Coefficient

Measures temperature change during free expansion at constant internal energy

In the Joule experiment, a gas expands into a vacuum. No work is done (P_ext = 0) and if the container is insulated, no heat crosses the boundary. Therefore dU = 0: the process is at constant internal energy.

Definition — exact derived result

μ_J = (∂T/∂V)_U
Cyclic relation in U(∂T/∂V)_U · (∂V/∂U)_T · (∂U/∂T)_V = −1
(∂U/∂T)_V = C_Vμ_J = −(∂U/∂V)_T / C_V = −π_T / C_V
Internal pressureπ_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P
Ideal gas: (∂P/∂T)_V = nR/V = P/Tπ_T = T(P/T) − P = P − P = 0
Ideal gas resultμ_J = 0: temperature unchanged by free expansion ✓

Concept

Real gas behaviour

For a real gas at moderate temperatures, intermolecular attractions are dominant. As the gas expands against these attractive forces, it gains potential energy, which must come from kinetic energy — so the gas cools (π_T > 0, μ_J < 0). At very high temperatures or low densities, repulsive interactions dominate and the gas may warm.
5

Joule–Thomson Coefficient

Temperature change during throttling (isenthalpic process) — the basis of gas liquefaction

In a throttling process (Joule–Thomson expansion), gas flows steadily from high pressure to low pressure through a porous plug or valve. The process is isenthalpic: H is constant.

Definition — exact derived result

μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H

Complete Derivation

Cyclic relation at constant H(∂T/∂P)_H · (∂P/∂H)_T · (∂H/∂T)_P = −1
(∂H/∂T)_P = C_Pμ_JT = −(1/C_P)(∂H/∂P)_T
Need (∂H/∂P)_TFrom dH = T dS + V dP: (∂H/∂P)_T = T(∂S/∂P)_T + V
Maxwell from G(∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P
Substitute(∂H/∂P)_T = −T(∂V/∂T)_P + V
Final resultμ_JT = (1/C_P)[T(∂V/∂T)_P − V]

Joule–Thomson coefficient

μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H = (1/C_P)[T(∂V/∂T)_P − V]

Inversion Condition and Ideal-Gas Result

Inversion conditionμ_JT = 0 when T(∂V/∂T)_P = V
Cooling regionμ_JT > 0: gas cools when P drops (inside inversion curve)
Heating regionμ_JT < 0: gas warms when P drops (outside inversion curve)
Ideal gas: V = nRT/PT(∂V/∂T)_P = T(nR/P) = nRT/P = V → μ_JT = 0

Concept

Why ideal gas has zero JT coefficient

T(∂V/∂T)_P = V is identically true for an ideal gas, making the numerator zero. An ideal gas has no intermolecular potential energy, so work done against such forces during expansion is zero. There is no mechanism to convert kinetic energy into potential energy, so temperature cannot change.

Molecular Interpretation

A real gas below its inversion temperature has net attractive intermolecular forces. Throttling decreases pressure and increases average intermolecular separation. Overcoming these attractive forces requires energy; this comes from kinetic energy, so the gas cools.

Above the inversion temperature, repulsive short-range forces dominate. Throttling releases stored repulsive potential energy as kinetic energy — the gas heats.

Van der Waals Inversion Temperature (Low-Pressure Limit)

vdW at low PV ≈ RT/P + b − a/(RT) per mole
(∂V/∂T)_P low P≈ R/P + a/(RT²)
T(∂V/∂T)_P≈ RT/P + a/(RT)
V≈ RT/P + b − a/(RT)
T(∂V/∂T)_P − V= a/(RT) − b + a/(RT) = 2a/(RT) − b
μ_JT = 0 → T_inv2a/(RT_inv) − b = 0 → T_inv = 2a/(Rb)
Cooling when T < T_invand inside the inversion curve at finite P

Maximum Joule–Thomson inversion temperature (van der Waals, P→0)

T_inv = 2a/(Rb)
6

Worked Examples

Foundation through Olympiad level

Foundation

Identifying natural variables

Which thermodynamic potential has T and P as its natural variables?

Method: Natural variables are the variables held constant when the potential reaches a minimum (or is stationary) at equilibrium.

Gibbs energy G(T, P). From dG = −S dT + V dP, G is stationary with respect to internal changes at constant T and P. It is the correct potential for laboratory chemistry conducted at constant temperature and pressure.

Concept trap: Helmholtz energy A has T and V as natural variables, not T and P.

JEE Main

Maxwell relation application

Show that (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V using the Maxwell relation from Helmholtz energy, and evaluate it for an ideal gas.

Method: Derive from dA = −S dT − P dV by equality of mixed partials.

From A(T,V): (∂²A/∂V∂T) = (∂²A/∂T∂V). Left side: ∂/∂V[−S] = −(∂S/∂V)_T. Right side: ∂/∂T[−P] = −(∂P/∂T)_V. Therefore (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V. For ideal gas PV = nRT: (∂P/∂T)_V = nR/V. So (∂S/∂V)_T = nR/V > 0: isothermal expansion always increases entropy.

Concept trap: The sign matters — failing to track the minus signs in dA gives the wrong Maxwell relation.

JEE Advanced

Deriving the Joule–Thomson coefficient

Derive μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H = (1/C_P)[T(∂V/∂T)_P − V] and evaluate for an ideal gas.

Method: Write T as a function of P and H, then use a cyclic relation plus the Maxwell relation from G.

Step 1 — Cyclic relation: (∂T/∂P)_H · (∂P/∂H)_T · (∂H/∂T)_P = −1. Step 2 — (∂H/∂T)_P = C_P by definition. Step 3 — (∂H/∂P)_T: use dH = T dS + V dP. At constant T: (∂H/∂P)_T = T(∂S/∂P)_T + V. Step 4 — Maxwell from G: (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P. Step 5 — Substitute: (∂H/∂P)_T = −T(∂V/∂T)_P + V. Step 6 — From cyclic relation: μ_JT = −(∂H/∂P)_T / C_P = [T(∂V/∂T)_P − V] / C_P. Ideal gas: V = nRT/P → (∂V/∂T)_P = nR/P = V/T → T(∂V/∂T)_P = V → μ_JT = (V − V)/C_P = 0. An ideal gas has zero Joule–Thomson coefficient; it neither cools nor heats on throttling.

Concept trap: μ_JT = 0 for ideal gas because there are no intermolecular forces. The sign of μ_JT for real gases depends on whether attractive or repulsive interactions dominate at the given state.

Physical Chemistry

C_P − C_V general derivation

Prove C_P − C_V = −T(∂P/∂V)_T[(∂V/∂T)_P]² and hence C_P − C_V = nR for an ideal gas.

Method: Start from the identity for H, write U as a function of T and V, use internal pressure.

Start: H = U + PV → (∂H/∂T)_P = (∂U/∂T)_P + P(∂V/∂T)_P. Write U = U(T, V): (∂U/∂T)_P = (∂U/∂T)_V + (∂U/∂V)_T(∂V/∂T)_P = C_V + π_T(∂V/∂T)_P. Internal pressure: π_T = (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P (from Maxwell and first law). Substituting: C_P = C_V + π_T(∂V/∂T)_P + P(∂V/∂T)_P = C_V + [T(∂P/∂T)_V − P + P](∂V/∂T)_P = C_V + T(∂P/∂T)_V(∂V/∂T)_P. Cyclic rule: (∂P/∂T)_V = −(∂V/∂T)_P/(∂V/∂P)_T = (∂V/∂T)_P · [−1/(∂V/∂P)_T]. So C_P − C_V = T(∂V/∂T)_P² · [−1/(∂V/∂P)_T] = −T(∂P/∂V)_T[(∂V/∂T)_P]² ≥ 0 (stable matter). Ideal gas: (∂V/∂T)_P = nR/P and (∂P/∂V)_T = −P/V = −P²/(nRT). C_P − C_V = −T · (−P²/nRT) · (nR/P)² = −T · (−P²/nRT) · n²R²/P² = nR. Molar form: C_{P,m} − C_{V,m} = R.

Concept trap: The general result C_P − C_V = −T(∂P/∂V)_T[(∂V/∂T)_P]² is always ≥ 0 for stable matter because (∂P/∂V)_T ≤ 0 (mechanical stability). At the spinodal limit (∂P/∂V)_T → 0, C_P → ∞.

Olympiad

Inversion temperature of van der Waals gas

For a van der Waals gas (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT per mole, find the maximum inversion temperature T_inv at P → 0.

Method: Set μ_JT = 0, i.e., T(∂V/∂T)_P = V, and solve in the low-pressure limit.

From the van der Waals equation at low P: V ≈ RT/P + b − a/(RT). (∂V/∂T)_P ≈ R/P + a/(RT²). T(∂V/∂T)_P ≈ RT/P + a/(RT). Set equal to V ≈ RT/P + b − a/(RT): RT/P + a/(RT) = RT/P + b − a/(RT). 2a/(RT) = b → T_inv = 2a/(Rb). For N₂: a = 1.370 L² atm mol⁻², b = 0.0387 L mol⁻¹ → T_inv = 2(1.370)/[(0.08206)(0.0387)] = 862 K. The experimental maximum inversion temperature of N₂ is ~621 K; the van der Waals model overestimates it but gives the correct functional form.

Concept trap: At room temperature (298 K) N₂ is well below its inversion temperature, so it cools on throttling. H₂ has T_inv ≈ 202 K — at room temperature H₂ heats on throttling, which is why liquid-air precooling is needed before liquefying hydrogen by Joule–Thomson expansion.

7

Concept Traps

G has T,P as natural variables

G is minimised at equilibrium under constant-T, constant-P constraints — the normal laboratory situation. Helmholtz A is the potential for constant-T, constant-V constraints.

Maxwell relations equate partials of different functions

Each Maxwell relation equates two second derivatives of the SAME potential. You cannot mix (∂T/∂V)_S from U with (∂S/∂P)_T from G.

μ_JT = 0 for ideal gas does NOT mean μ_JT is zero at all states

For real gases at moderate T and P, μ_JT > 0 (cooling on throttle). Only above T_inv or outside the inversion curve does μ_JT < 0.

C_P − C_V = nR is exact only for ideal gases

For liquids and solids, C_P ≈ C_V because α² is very small. For water near 4 °C, α ≈ 0 so C_P − C_V ≈ 0 at that temperature.

(∂T/∂V)_U is the Joule coefficient; (∂T/∂P)_H is the Joule–Thomson coefficient

These measure different experimental conditions: free expansion vs. steady throttling.

The inversion curve is NOT the boiling curve

The inversion curve exists in the gas phase above the critical point and has no direct connection to the liquid–vapour boundary.

Practice Problems

1.Write the natural variables for each of U, H, A, G.

Answer

U(S,V); H(S,P); A(T,V); G(T,P).

2.State the Maxwell relation derived from G(T,P).

Answer

−(∂S/∂P)_T = (∂V/∂T)_P. Because entropy decreases with pressure and volume increases with temperature (for most systems), these responses are equal.

3.Explain why C_P > C_V for any stable system.

Answer

From C_P − C_V = −T(∂P/∂V)_T[(∂V/∂T)_P]². Mechanical stability requires (∂P/∂V)_T < 0, so the product is non-negative. Equality holds only for incompressible systems or at absolute zero.

4.For an ideal gas, what is the Joule coefficient (∂T/∂V)_U? Derive it.

Answer

μ_J = (∂T/∂V)_U = −(∂U/∂V)_T / C_V = −π_T/C_V. For ideal gas π_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P = T(nR/V) − P = P − P = 0. Therefore μ_J = 0: ideal gas temperature is unchanged by free expansion.

5.A gas has (∂V/∂T)_P = αV and (∂V/∂P)_T = −κ_T V. Express C_P − C_V in terms of α and κ_T.

Answer

C_P − C_V = TVα²/κ_T. This is the standard form using the isobaric expansion coefficient α and isothermal compressibility κ_T.

6.At T = 400 K and P = 10 MPa, a gas has V_m = 2.80 × 10⁻³ m³ mol⁻¹ and (∂V/∂T)_P = 1.12 × 10⁻⁵ m³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. C_P,m = 35.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate μ_JT.

Answer

T(∂V/∂T)_P = 400 × 1.12 × 10⁻⁵ = 4.48 × 10⁻³ m³ mol⁻¹. T(∂V/∂T)_P − V_m = 4.48 × 10⁻³ − 2.80 × 10⁻³ = 1.68 × 10⁻³ m³ mol⁻¹. μ_JT = 1.68 × 10⁻³ / 35.0 = 4.80 × 10⁻⁵ K Pa⁻¹ = 0.048 K bar⁻¹. Gas cools (μ_JT > 0).

7.Why does liquefaction of hydrogen by Joule–Thomson expansion require pre-cooling but liquefaction of nitrogen does not (at room temperature)?

Answer

The maximum Joule–Thomson inversion temperature of N₂ is about 621 K, well above room temperature, so N₂ at room temperature lies inside the inversion curve (μ_JT > 0) and cools on throttling. The maximum inversion temperature of H₂ is about 202 K, below room temperature. At 300 K, H₂ lies outside the inversion curve (μ_JT < 0) and heats on throttling. It must be pre-cooled below 202 K before Joule–Thomson expansion can produce further cooling.

Part 25 Complete

Key results

  • • dU = T dS − P dV (natural variables S, V)
  • • dH = T dS + V dP (natural variables S, P)
  • • dA = −S dT − P dV (natural variables T, V)
  • • dG = −S dT + V dP (natural variables T, P)
  • • Four Maxwell relations from second mixed partials of U, H, A, G
  • • C_P − C_V = TVα²/κ_T = nR for ideal gas
  • • μ_J = −π_T/C_V = 0 for ideal gas
  • • μ_JT = [T(∂V/∂T)_P − V]/C_P = 0 for ideal gas
  • • T_inv = 2a/(Rb) for van der Waals gas at P → 0

PART 26 / 30Free Energies & EquilibriumPressure and Temperature Dependence of Gibbs Energy

Part 26

Pressure and Temperature Dependence of Gibbs Energy

Complete derivations of how G depends on T and P, the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation, phase stability from G–T slopes, and the ideal-gas logarithmic form.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
1

Theory: The Fundamental Gibbs Differential

dG = −S dT + V dP — exact derived result from the Legendre transform of H

From Part 25: the natural variables of Gibbs energy are T and P. The exact differential encodes how G responds to small changes in temperature and pressure:

Fundamental Gibbs differential

dG = −S dT + V dP

The two partial derivatives follow immediately:

Temperature derivative at constant pressure

(∂G/∂T)_P = −S

Pressure derivative at constant temperature

(∂G/∂P)_T = V

Concept

Physical meaning of each derivative

(∂G/∂T)_P = −S: because entropy is always positive, G always decreases as temperature rises at constant pressure. The rate depends on the phase — highest for gas, lowest for solid. (∂G/∂P)_T = V: because volume is always positive, G always increases as pressure rises at constant temperature.
2

Temperature Dependence: G vs T Plots and Phase Stability

At fixed pressure, G_m decreases linearly with T (to first approximation) with slope −S_m. The stable phase at each temperature is whichever has the lowest G_m.

The melting point T_m is where G_m(solid) = G_m(liquid). The boiling point T_b is where G_m(liquid) = G_m(gas). These intersections correspond to first-order phase transitions with a discontinuous jump in entropy:

Entropy of transition

ΔS_tr = (ΔG_m,α − ΔG_m,β) / (T slope change) = ΔH_tr / T_tr

Concept

Curvature of the G–T line

The second derivative (∂²G/∂T²)_P = −(∂S/∂T)_P = −C_P/T is always negative (C_P > 0), so G curves downward with T. The G–T line is slightly concave, not strictly straight.
3

Pressure Dependence: Integrating dG = V dP at Constant T

Integrating at constant temperature from a reference pressure P₁ to P₂:

General isothermal Gibbs change

G(T, P₂) − G(T, P₁) = ∫_{P₁}^{P₂} V(T, P) dP

Ideal Gas (V = nRT/P):

G(T,P₂) − G(T,P₁) = ∫_{P₁}^{P₂} (nRT/P) dP

= nRT [ln P]_{P₁}^{P₂}

= nRT ln(P₂/P₁)

Standard-state form for ideal gas

G_m(T,P) = G°_m(T) + RT ln(P/P°)

Incompressible Condensed Phase (V ≈ V_m = constant):

Condensed phase approximation

ΔG_m ≈ V_m(P₂ − P₁)

Concept

Why V_m for gases and solids/liquids differ so much

Gas molar volumes at 1 bar are ~20 L mol⁻¹; liquid and solid molar volumes are typically 0.01–0.1 L mol⁻¹. A 100-bar pressure change raises G_m of liquid water by ~1.8 kJ mol⁻¹ but raises ideal-gas G_m by RT ln 100 = 11.4 kJ mol⁻¹.
4

The Gibbs–Helmholtz Equation

Exact derived result connecting G, H and the temperature dependence of G/T

Differentiate G/T with respect to T at constant P:

d(G/T)/dT = (T(∂G/∂T)_P − G) / T²

= (T(−S) − G) / T²

= (−TS − G) / T²

= −(G + TS) / T²

= −H / T²

Gibbs–Helmholtz equation

[∂(G/T)/∂T]_P = −H/T²

Reaction form

[∂(ΔG°/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔH°/T²

Integrating between T₁ and T₂ (assuming ΔH° ≈ constant):

ΔG°(T₂)/T₂ − ΔG°(T₁)/T₁ = −ΔH° ∫_{T₁}^{T₂} dT/T²

= −ΔH° [−1/T]_{T₁}^{T₂}

= ΔH°(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

Integrated Gibbs–Helmholtz

ΔG°(T₂)/T₂ = ΔG°(T₁)/T₁ + ΔH°(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

Concept

Connection to van't Hoff

Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation leads directly to the van't Hoff equation d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²). Part 30 develops this fully.
5

Worked Examples

Pressure effect on liquid water

Estimate ΔG_m for liquid water (V_m = 18.0 cm³ mol⁻¹) when pressure increases from 1 bar to 1001 bar at 298 K.

Method: Integrate dG = V dP at constant T for incompressible condensed phase: ΔG ≈ V_m ΔP.

ΔG ≈ 18.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³ mol⁻¹ × 1000 × 10⁵ Pa = 1.80 × 10³ J mol⁻¹ = 1.80 kJ mol⁻¹. Modest pressure effect on condensed phases.

Trap: For gases, the V ≈ const approximation fails completely — must use V = RT/P leading to ΔG = RT ln(P₂/P₁).

Gibbs–Helmholtz: temperature correction of reaction Gibbs energy

At 298 K, ΔG° = −33.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH° = −92.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate ΔG° at 500 K assuming constant ΔH°.

Method: Integrate the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation [∂(ΔG/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔH/T².

∫d(ΔG°/T) = −ΔH° ∫dT/T² from T₁=298 K to T₂=500 K. ΔG°(T₂)/T₂ − ΔG°(T₁)/T₁ = ΔH°(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). ΔG°(500)/500 − (−33000)/298 = −92000(1/500 − 1/298). ΔG°(500)/500 + 110.74 = −92000(−0.001356) = +124.7 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. ΔG°(500) = 500(124.7 − 110.74) = 500 × 13.96 = 6980 J mol⁻¹ ≈ +7.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The reaction becomes non-spontaneous (ΔG° > 0) at 500 K.

Trap: The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation relates d(G/T)/dT, not dG/dT, to −H/T². Confusing the two leads to a factor of T error.

Phase transition entropy from G slope

The molar Gibbs energy of liquid water at 373 K and 1 bar has slope −S_liquid = −86.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The slope for steam is −S_gas = −195.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is ΔS_vap?

Method: (∂G_m/∂T)_P = −S_m. The slopes are directly −S_m for each phase.

ΔS_vap = S_gas − S_liquid = 195.0 − 86.8 = 108.2 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. ΔH_vap = T_b × ΔS_vap = 373 × 108.2 = 40.4 kJ mol⁻¹. This agrees with the standard enthalpy of vaporisation of water (40.65 kJ mol⁻¹).

Trap: The slopes are negative (G decreases as T increases) because entropy is positive. The steeper slope of gas means G_gas falls faster with T, which is why the gas phase becomes stable at high T.

6

Concept Traps

Pressure raises G, not lowers it

(∂G/∂P)_T = V > 0 always. Compressing any system raises G. Pressure favours reactions that reduce total volume.

G/T is not the same as G

The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation involves d(G/T)/dT, not dG/dT. The RHS is −H/T², not −H.

Phase boundaries are G intersections

Two phases coexist when their G_m values are equal at a given T and P. The phase with lower G_m is stable.

Condensed phase pressure correction is small but not zero

At geologically relevant pressures (GPa), the V_m ΔP term can be thousands of kJ mol⁻¹ — critical for mineral phase equilibria.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Complete derivation of (∂G/∂P)_T and (∂G/∂T)_P

From dG = V dP − S dT(∂G/∂P)_T = V and (∂G/∂T)_P = −S
Pressure integral for ideal gasG_m(T,P) = G°_m(T) + ∫[P°→P] V_m dP = G°_m + RT ln(P/P°)
For condensed phaseG_m(T,P) ≈ G°_m(T) + V_m(P − P°) (V_m ≈ constant)
Second temperature derivative(∂²G/∂T²)_P = −(∂S/∂T)_P = −Cp/T < 0 → G curves downward
Phase stabilitystable phase at T,P has lowest G_m; intersection of G_m lines is a phase transition

Practice Problems

1.State the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation.

Answer

[∂(G/T)/∂T]_P = −H/T². For a reaction: [∂(ΔG°/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔH°/T².

2.Express the pressure dependence of G for an ideal gas.

Answer

G_m(T,P) = G°_m(T) + RT ln(P/P°). This follows from integrating dG = V dP = (RT/P) dP at constant T from P° to P.

3.Why does the gas phase have the steepest negative slope on a G vs T plot?

Answer

The slope is (∂G_m/∂T)_P = −S_m. Gases have the highest molar entropy of the three ordinary states of matter, so their G_m falls most steeply as temperature rises.

4.At what temperature does solid melt, according to G vs T analysis?

Answer

At the melting point T_m, G_m(solid) = G_m(liquid). Below T_m, solid has the lower G_m; above T_m, liquid has the lower G_m.

5.Estimate the Gibbs energy change when 1 mol N₂ (ideal) is compressed from 1 bar to 200 bar at 298 K.

Answer

ΔG = RT ln(P₂/P₁) = 8.314 × 298 × ln 200 = 2478 × 5.298 = 13.13 kJ mol⁻¹.

6.The G–T slope changes discontinuously at a first-order transition. What does this mean physically?

Answer

A discontinuity in (∂G/∂T)_P = −S means a discontinuity in entropy: the two phases have different entropies at T_transition. The latent heat is ΔH_tr = T_tr × ΔS_tr.

Part 26 Complete

PART 27 / 30Free Energies & EquilibriumGibbs Energy of Ideal Gases and Standard States

Part 27

Chemical Potential and Gibbs Energy of Pure Ideal Gases

Definition and physical interpretation of chemical potential, its derivation for ideal gases and mixtures, standard states, and the Euler relation G = Σnᵢμᵢ.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
1

Chemical Potential: Definition

Partial molar Gibbs energy — the Gibbs energy cost of adding one mole of a substance to an infinitely large sample

For a multicomponent system, G depends on composition as well as T and P. Allowing matter to flow adds composition terms to the fundamental differential:

Fundamental relation with composition

dG = −S dT + V dP + Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ

The chemical potential of component i is defined as:

Chemical potential — definition

μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ)_{T,P,nⱼ≠ᵢ}

It measures how the total Gibbs energy changes when a tiny amount of substance i is added at constant T, P while all other amounts are held fixed.

Concept

Euler's theorem and G = Σnᵢμᵢ

Because G is an extensive, homogeneous first-order function of the amounts nᵢ (at fixed T and P), Euler's theorem gives: G = Σᵢ nᵢ μᵢ. This is not an approximation — it is an exact consequence of extensivity.
2

Chemical Potential of a Pure Ideal Gas

Exact derived result from integrating dμ = V_m dP at constant T

For a pure ideal gas at constant T:

dμ = V_m dP = (RT/P) dP

Integrate from P° (standard) to P:

μ(T,P) − μ°(T) = RT ∫_{P°}^{P} dP/P = RT ln(P/P°)

Pure ideal gas chemical potential

μ(T,P) = μ°(T) + RT ln(P/P°)

Concept

Standard chemical potential μ°(T)

μ°(T) is the molar Gibbs energy of the pure ideal gas at temperature T and standard pressure P° = 1 bar. It depends only on T — all the pressure dependence is carried by RT ln(P/P°).
3

Ideal-Gas Component in a Mixture

Each component behaves as an ideal gas at its partial pressure

In an ideal-gas mixture, component i has partial pressure Pᵢ = yᵢP. Each component behaves as a pure ideal gas at its own partial pressure:

Mixture component chemical potential

μᵢ(T,P,{y}) = μ°ᵢ(T) + RT ln(Pᵢ/P°) = μ°ᵢ(T) + RT ln(yᵢP/P°)

This can be split into a pure-gas term and a mixing term:

Split form

μᵢ = [μ°ᵢ(T) + RT ln(P/P°)] + RT ln yᵢ = μᵢ*(T,P) + RT ln yᵢ

Concept

Mixing lowers chemical potential

Since yᵢ < 1 in any mixture, RT ln yᵢ < 0. Every component of an ideal-gas mixture has a lower chemical potential than the pure gas at the same T and P. This is the thermodynamic basis for spontaneous mixing.
4

Pure Solids and Liquids — Standard State Conventions

For a pure condensed phase at fixed T, the pressure correction is V_m ΔP. At ordinary pressures, this is negligible and μ ≈ μ*(T). The activity of a pure standard solid or liquid is defined as 1.

PhaseStandard stateActivityμ form
Pure ideal gasP° = 1 bar (or 1 atm)a = P/P°μ°(T) + RT ln(P/P°)
Gas in ideal mixtureP° = 1 bara_i = P_i/P° = y_i P/P°μ°_i(T) + RT ln(y_i P/P°)
Pure liquid (solvent)Pure liquid at P, Ta = x (Raoult)μ*(l) + RT ln x
Solid (pure)Pure solid at P, Ta = 1μ*(s)
Solute (Henry)Hypothetical ideal solution at c° = 1 mol L⁻¹a = c/c°μ°_solute + RT ln(c/c°)
5

Worked Examples

Pure gas at non-standard pressure

Calculate μ − μ° for N₂(g) at 10 bar and 298 K.

μ − μ° = RT ln(P/P°) = 8.314 × 298 × ln(10) = 2478 × 2.303 = 5.71 kJ mol⁻¹. The chemical potential is raised above the standard value by compression.

Trap: μ° is a function of T only — it includes no pressure term.

Component in ideal-gas mixture

Air is 21% O₂ at total pressure 1 bar. Find (μ_O₂ − μ°_O₂) at 298 K.

P_O₂ = y × P = 0.21 × 1 = 0.21 bar. μ_O₂ − μ°_O₂ = RT ln(0.21/1) = 2478 × ln(0.21) = 2478 × (−1.561) = −3.87 kJ mol⁻¹. The chemical potential of O₂ in air is lower than for pure O₂ at 1 bar.

Trap: Use the partial pressure, not the total pressure, for the activity of a gas mixture component.

Euler's theorem and G = Σn_i μ_i

A binary ideal-gas mixture has n_A = 2 mol, n_B = 1 mol, μ_A = −5 kJ mol⁻¹, μ_B = −3 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the total Gibbs energy.

By Euler's theorem: G = Σn_i μ_i = 2(−5) + 1(−3) = −10 − 3 = −13 kJ. This expresses G as a weighted sum of partial molar Gibbs energies (chemical potentials).

Trap: Euler's theorem G = Σn_i μ_i holds only at constant T and P. The proof requires that G is a homogeneous first-order function of the n_i.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Chemical potential for components in mixtures — complete derivation

Fundamental relationdG = −S dT + V dP + Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ
Chemical potentialμᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ)_{T,P,nⱼ≠ᵢ} = Ḡ_m,i (partial molar Gibbs energy)
Pure ideal gasdμ = V_m dP = (RT/P) dP at constant T
Integrate from P° to Pμ(T,P) = μ°(T) + RT ln(P/P°)
Mixture componentμᵢ = μ°ᵢ(T) + RT ln(yᵢP/P°) = μᵢ*(T,P) + RT ln yᵢ
Dilution lowers μyᵢ < 1 → RT ln yᵢ < 0 → mixing is spontaneous

Practice Problems

1.Write the expression for μ of an ideal gas at T = 298 K and P = 0.50 bar (P° = 1 bar).

μ = μ°(298) + RT ln(0.50) = μ°(298) − 1.72 kJ mol⁻¹. The gas is at lower pressure than the standard state, so μ < μ°.

2.In a binary mixture, μ₁ increases. What does the Gibbs–Duhem relation say about μ₂?

Σnᵢ dμᵢ = 0 → n₁ dμ₁ + n₂ dμ₂ = 0 → dμ₂ = −(n₁/n₂) dμ₁. If μ₁ increases, μ₂ must decrease. Chemical potentials cannot vary independently.

3.For a pure solid, what is its contribution to the equilibrium constant expression?

Activity of pure solid = 1, so its contribution is 1^ν = 1. Pure solids (and pure liquids) do not appear in equilibrium constant expressions.

4.Explain why chemical potential → −∞ as P → 0 for an ideal gas.

μ = μ° + RT ln(P/P°). As P → 0, ln(P/P°) → −∞. This reflects that an infinitely dilute gas has maximum entropy and minimum order — adding it releases maximum free energy.

PART 28 / 30Free Energies & EquilibriumGibbs Energy of Mixing and Ideal-Gas Mixtures

Part 28

Partial Molar Gibbs Energy, Ideal-Gas Mixtures and Entropy of Mixing

Derivation of ΔG_mix and ΔS_mix for ideal-gas mixing, Raoult's law from chemical-potential equality, and the Gibbs–Duhem relation.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
1

Gibbs Energy of Ideal Mixing

Exact derived result: ΔG_mix = RT Σnᵢ ln yᵢ — always negative for genuine mixing

Compare the total G before mixing (each component pure at T,P) with G after mixing at the same T and total P.

Before mixing: Gᵢ(pure) at T, P: μᵢ(pure) = μ°ᵢ + RT ln(P/P°)

After mixing: μᵢ(mix) = μ°ᵢ + RT ln(yᵢP/P°)

Difference per mole of i: Δμᵢ = RT ln yᵢ

Total mixing Gibbs energy: ΔG_mix = Σᵢ nᵢ Δμᵢ = RT Σᵢ nᵢ ln yᵢ

Gibbs energy of ideal mixing

ΔG_mix = RT Σᵢ nᵢ ln yᵢ < 0
2

Entropy and Enthalpy of Ideal Mixing

Since ΔH_mix = 0 for ideal mixing by definition (no interactions between different species):

ΔG_mix = ΔH_mix − T ΔS_mix

ΔH_mix = 0 (ideal mixing)

Therefore: ΔS_mix = −ΔG_mix/T = −R Σᵢ nᵢ ln yᵢ > 0

Entropy of ideal mixing

ΔS_mix = −R Σᵢ nᵢ ln yᵢ = −nR Σᵢ xᵢ ln xᵢ > 0

Concept

Ideal mixing is purely entropy-driven

ΔH_mix = 0 and ΔV_mix = 0 for ideal mixing. The negative ΔG_mix arises entirely from the positive configurational entropy of mixing. In real solutions, ΔH_mix ≠ 0 (positive for unfavourable A–B contacts, negative for favourable ones).
3

Raoult's Law from Chemical-Potential Equality

Phase equilibrium condition μ(liquid) = μ(vapour) at each composition

At liquid–vapour equilibrium for component i:

Ideal liquid: μᵢ(l) = μ*ᵢ(l) + RT ln xᵢ

Ideal vapour: μᵢ(g) = μ°ᵢ(g) + RT ln(Pᵢ/P°)

Pure component at T: μ*ᵢ(l) = μ°ᵢ(g) + RT ln(P*ᵢ/P°)

Subtract the pure equation from the mixture equation:

RT ln xᵢ = RT ln(Pᵢ/P*ᵢ)

Therefore: Pᵢ = xᵢ P*ᵢ

Raoult's law

Pᵢ = xᵢ P*ᵢ

Concept

Physical basis of Raoult's law

The entropy lowering of the liquid chemical potential (RT ln xᵢ term) reduces the tendency to vaporise in proportion to the mole fraction. A solution with x_A = 0.3 has 70% of its surface sites occupied by B molecules, reducing A's escaping tendency to 30% of the pure value.
4

Gibbs–Duhem Relation

Differentiating Euler's relation G = Σnᵢ μᵢ at constant T and P:

dG = Σμᵢ dnᵢ + Σnᵢ dμᵢ

But dG = Σμᵢ dnᵢ (at constant T,P from fundamental relation)

Subtract: Σnᵢ dμᵢ = 0 at constant T, P

Gibbs–Duhem relation

Σᵢ nᵢ dμᵢ = 0 or Σᵢ xᵢ dμᵢ = 0 (at constant T, P)

Concept

Significance

Chemical potentials are not independent. In a binary system, if μ₁ is measured as a function of composition, μ₂ is fully determined. This is the thermodynamic basis for activity coefficient corrections in real solutions.
5

Worked Examples

Gibbs energy of mixing for equimolar binary mixture

Calculate ΔG_mix when 1 mol A and 1 mol B (both ideal gases) are mixed at 298 K and 1 bar.

n_total = 2 mol, x_A = x_B = 0.5. ΔG_mix = RT Σnᵢ ln xᵢ = RT(1 × ln 0.5 + 1 × ln 0.5) = 2RT ln 0.5 = 2 × 8.314 × 298 × (−0.693) = −3.43 kJ. Mixing is spontaneous.

Trap: ΔG_mix uses mole fractions (dimensionless), not pressures. The formula ΔG_mix = RT Σnᵢ ln yᵢ applies here because yᵢ = xᵢ for ideal-gas mixing at the same total pressure.

Entropy and enthalpy of ideal mixing

For the above equimolar mixture, find ΔH_mix and ΔS_mix.

For ideal mixing: ΔH_mix = 0 (no enthalpy of mixing by definition). ΔS_mix = −ΔG_mix/T = 3430/298 = 11.5 J mol_mixture⁻¹ K⁻¹. Alternatively: ΔS_mix = −R Σnᵢ ln xᵢ = −8.314(ln 0.5 + ln 0.5) = 2R ln 2 = 11.5 J K⁻¹.

Trap: ΔH_mix = 0 is the defining feature of an ideal solution or ideal-gas mixture. Real solutions deviate because of different intermolecular interactions.

Raoult's law vapour pressure

A solution contains x_A = 0.30 of component A (P*_A = 200 mmHg) and x_B = 0.70 of B (P*_B = 80 mmHg). Find the total vapour pressure and vapour-phase composition.

P_A = 0.30 × 200 = 60 mmHg. P_B = 0.70 × 80 = 56 mmHg. P_total = 116 mmHg. Vapour: y_A = 60/116 = 0.517; y_B = 56/116 = 0.483. Vapour is richer in A (the more volatile component) than the liquid.

Trap: Raoult uses liquid mole fractions (x) to find partial pressures, then vapour mole fractions (y) are P_i/P_total. Confusing x and y is the most common error in vapour-liquid equilibrium calculations.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Derivation of Raoult's law from chemical-potential equality

Equilibrium conditionμᵢ(l, mixture) = μᵢ(g, vapour)
Ideal liquid phaseμᵢ(l) = μ*ᵢ(l) + RT ln xᵢ
Ideal vapour phaseμᵢ(g) = μ°ᵢ(g) + RT ln(Pᵢ/P°)
Pure component equilibriumμ*ᵢ(l) = μ°ᵢ(g) + RT ln(P*ᵢ/P°)
SubtractRT ln xᵢ = RT ln(Pᵢ/P*ᵢ)
Raoult's LawPᵢ = xᵢ P*ᵢ
Validityholds for ideal solutions (similar intermolecular forces, sizes)

Practice Problems

1.Mix 3 mol A and 1 mol B ideally at 400 K. Find ΔG_mix.

x_A=0.75, x_B=0.25. ΔG_mix = 8.314×400×(3ln0.75+1ln0.25) = 3326×(3×(−0.2877)+1×(−1.386)) = 3326×(−0.8631−1.386) = 3326×(−2.249) = −7479 J = −7.48 kJ.

2.For an ideal mixture with x_A = x_B = 0.5, show ΔS_mix = nR ln 2.

ΔS_mix = −nR Σxᵢ ln xᵢ = −nR(0.5 ln 0.5 + 0.5 ln 0.5) = −nR × 2(0.5)(−ln2) = nR ln 2 ✓

3.State Raoult's law and identify the condition for its validity.

Raoult: Pᵢ = xᵢ P*ᵢ. Valid for: (1) liquid solution is ideal (molecules A and B have similar sizes and intermolecular forces); (2) vapour behaves as an ideal gas.

4.In a binary mixture at constant T,P, if dμ₁ = +2 J mol⁻¹ and n₁/n₂ = 3, find dμ₂.

Gibbs–Duhem: n₁ dμ₁ + n₂ dμ₂ = 0 → dμ₂ = −(n₁/n₂) dμ₁ = −3 × (+2) = −6 J mol⁻¹.

PART 29 / 30Free Energies & EquilibriumReaction Gibbs Energy, Reaction Quotient, and Equilibrium

Part 29

Reaction Gibbs Energy, Reaction Quotient and Equilibrium Constant

Complete derivations of ΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q, the equilibrium condition ΔrG = 0 → K = e^{−ΔrG°/RT}, and direction tests using Q and K.

📚 Full detailed notes — JEE levelderivations · tables · solved examples · click to open
1

Reaction Gibbs Energy ΔrG

Exact derived result: ΔrG = (∂G/∂ξ)_{T,P} — the slope of G vs extent of reaction

For a reaction with stoichiometric coefficients νᵢ and extent of reaction ξ (dξ = dnᵢ/νᵢ):

At constant T, P: dG = Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ = Σᵢ μᵢ νᵢ dξ

ΔrG = (∂G/∂ξ)_{T,P} = Σᵢ νᵢ μᵢ

Reaction Gibbs energy

ΔrG = Σᵢ νᵢ μᵢ = (∂G/∂ξ)_{T,P}

Concept

ΔrG vs ΔG° — critical distinction

ΔrG is the slope of G at the current composition — it depends on Q. ΔrG° is the value of ΔrG when all species are at their standard states (Q = 1). They are equal only when Q = 1, which is rarely the case in a real reaction mixture.
2

Derivation of ΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q

Substitute μᵢ = μ°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ into ΔrG = Σνᵢμᵢ:

ΔrG = Σᵢ νᵢ(μ°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ)

= Σᵢ νᵢ μ°ᵢ + RT Σᵢ νᵢ ln aᵢ

= ΔrG° + RT Σᵢ ln aᵢ^{νᵢ}

= ΔrG° + RT ln Πᵢ aᵢ^{νᵢ}

Define Q = Πᵢ aᵢ^{νᵢ} (reaction quotient)

Therefore ΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q

Key result — exact derived

ΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q
3

Equilibrium: ΔrG = 0 → K = e^{−ΔrG°/RT}

At equilibrium, G is at its minimum with respect to ξ, so ΔrG = 0 and Q = K:

0 = ΔrG° + RT ln K

ΔrG° = −RT ln K

K = exp(−ΔrG°/RT)

Standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

ΔrG° = −RT ln K

Direction formula

ΔrG = RT ln(Q/K)

Concept

Standard Gibbs energy does NOT tell you about rates

K predicts the equilibrium position, not how fast it is reached. A large negative ΔrG° (large K) means the products are thermodynamically strongly favoured at equilibrium, but the reaction may be kinetically inert (e.g., diamond to graphite: ΔrG° ≪ 0 but proceeds immeasurably slowly at room temperature).
4

Kp, Kc and Kn Relations for Gas-Phase Reactions

For ideal-gas reactions, activities aᵢ = Pᵢ/P°. Using Pᵢ = cᵢRT = xᵢP = (nᵢ/n_total)P:

Kp in terms of Kc

Kp = Kc(RT/c°V°)^{Δng} or Kp = Kc(RT)^{Δng}

where Δng = Σνᵢ (gas-phase products) − Σνᵢ (gas-phase reactants).

Concept

Both Kp and Kc are dimensionless

Thermodynamic K is always dimensionless because it uses activities (ratios to standard states). The apparent units in textbook Kp and Kc formulas arise from inconsistent conventions; the correct thermodynamic K is dimensionless throughout.
5

Worked Examples

Finding K from ΔrG°

At 298 K, ΔrG° = −17.1 kJ mol⁻¹ for a reaction. Find K.

ΔrG° = −RT ln K → ln K = −ΔrG°/RT = 17100/(8.314 × 298) = 17100/2478 = 6.908 → K = e^{6.908} = 998 ≈ 1.0 × 10³.

Trap: Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ensure ΔrG° is in joules. ΔrG° in kJ must be multiplied by 1000 before dividing by RT.

Reaction direction test

For a reaction K = 50 at 298 K. At a certain moment Q = 0.020. Determine the direction.

Q/K = 0.020/50 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴. ΔrG = RT ln(Q/K) = 8.314 × 298 × ln(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2478 × (−7.82) = −19.4 kJ mol⁻¹. Since ΔrG < 0, the forward reaction is spontaneous.

Trap: ΔrG tells you direction at the current composition Q; ΔrG° tells you direction only if all species are at standard states (Q = 1).

Heterogeneous equilibrium — writing K

Write K for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g).

Activities of pure solids = 1. Only CO₂(g) appears: K = a_{CO₂} = P_{CO₂}/P°. At 298 K, this K is very small (about 10⁻²³); the reaction requires very high temperature to proceed.

Trap: NEVER include pure solids or pure liquids in K. Their activities are defined as 1 and contribute a factor of 1^ν = 1.

Kp vs Kc conversion

At 500 K, Kp = 1.25 × 10⁻² for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). Find Kc.

Δn_g = 2 − (1+3) = −2. Kp = Kc(RT)^{Δn_g} → Kc = Kp/(RT)^{Δn_g} = Kp × (RT)^2. RT = 8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ mol⁻¹ × 500 K = 4.157 kJ mol⁻¹ ≈ 4.157 × 10⁻² bar·L·mol⁻¹ when using appropriate units. Kc = 1.25 × 10⁻² × (0.08314 × 500)² = 1.25 × 10⁻² × 1727 = 21.6 mol⁻² L².

Trap: Δn_g counts only gas-phase stoichiometric coefficients. Solids and liquids are excluded.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

Derivation of ΔrG° = −RT ln K

StartΔrG = Σᵢ νᵢ μᵢ = Σᵢ νᵢ (μ°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ)
Separate standard and activity termsΔrG = ΔrG° + RT Σᵢ νᵢ ln aᵢ
Define QQ = Πᵢ aᵢ^{νᵢ} → Σᵢ νᵢ ln aᵢ = ln Q
Key relationΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q
At equilibrium: ΔrG = 0, Q = K0 = ΔrG° + RT ln K
Standard resultΔrG° = −RT ln K → K = exp(−ΔrG°/RT)
Direction formulaΔrG = RT ln(Q/K) (< 0 when Q < K → forward; > 0 when Q > K → reverse)

Practice Problems

1.At 700 K, K = 54.3 for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Find ΔrG°.

ΔrG° = −RT ln K = −8.314 × 700 × ln 54.3 = −5820 × 3.994 = −23.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

2.For the above reaction at Q = 200, find ΔrG and state the direction.

ΔrG = RT ln(Q/K) = 8.314 × 700 × ln(200/54.3) = 5820 × 1.302 = 7580 J ≈ +7.6 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔrG > 0 → reverse reaction favoured (HI decomposition).

3.Write the K expression for: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) ⇌ 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g).

Pure solids have activity 1: K = a_{CO₂}³/a_{CO}³ = (P_{CO₂}/P°)³ / (P_{CO}/P°)³ = (P_{CO₂}/P_{CO})³.

4.ΔrG° = +20 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Find K. Is the reaction feasible?

K = exp(−20000/8.314×298) = exp(−8.07) = 3.1 × 10⁻⁴. K ≪ 1 means products are not favoured at standard conditions. The reaction is thermodynamically unfeasible under standard conditions.

Part 29 Complete

PART 30 / 30Free Energies & Equilibriumvan’t Hoff Equation, Stability, and Phase Equilibrium

Part 30

van't Hoff Equation, Clapeyron Equation and Phase Equilibrium

Temperature dependence of equilibrium constants, Clausius–Clapeyron vapour pressure, the Clapeyron equation for any phase transition, and thermodynamic versus kinetic stability.

1

van't Hoff Equation — Differential Form

Exact derived result combining ΔrG° = −RT ln K with the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation

Differentiate ΔrG°/T = −R ln K with respect to T at constant pressure, using the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation [∂(ΔG°/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔH°/T²:

∂/∂T[−R ln K] = −ΔrH°/T²

−R (d ln K/dT) = −ΔrH°/T²

d ln K/dT = ΔrH°/(RT²)

van't Hoff differential equation

d(ln K)/dT = ΔrH°/(RT²)

Concept

Qualitative prediction

If ΔrH° > 0 (endothermic): d ln K/dT > 0 → K increases with T → product yield improves at higher T. If ΔrH° < 0 (exothermic): K decreases with T → Le Chatelier principle in quantitative form.
2

Integrated van't Hoff Equation

Assuming ΔrH° ≈ constant over the temperature range [T₁, T₂]:

∫_{K₁}^{K₂} d(ln K) = (ΔrH°/R) ∫_{T₁}^{T₂} dT/T²

ln K₂ − ln K₁ = (ΔrH°/R)[−1/T]_{T₁}^{T₂}

ln(K₂/K₁) = (ΔrH°/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)

= −(ΔrH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

Integrated van't Hoff equation

ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔrH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

Slope of ln K vs 1/T plot

slope = −ΔrH°/R
3

Clapeyron Equation for Phase Equilibrium

Exact derived result — no approximations needed

Two phases α and β coexist when μα = μβ. As T and P change along the coexistence line, the equality must be maintained: dμα = dμβ.

dμ = −S̄_m dT + V̄_m dP for each phase

Set dμα = dμβ:

−S̄_α dT + V̄_α dP = −S̄_β dT + V̄_β dP

(V̄_β − V̄_α) dP = (S̄_β − S̄_α) dT

Use ΔS_tr = ΔH_tr/T (at the transition temperature):

dP/dT = ΔS_tr/ΔV_tr = ΔH_tr/(T ΔV_tr)

Clapeyron equation

dP/dT = ΔH_tr / (T_tr ΔV_tr)

Concept

Sign analysis

For most solid–liquid transitions: ΔH_fus > 0 and ΔV_fus > 0 → dP/dT > 0 (positive slope). For water: ΔH_fus > 0 but ΔV_fus < 0 (ice is less dense) → dP/dT < 0 (negative slope). For all liquid–vapour transitions: ΔH_vap > 0 and ΔV_vap > 0 → dP/dT > 0.
4

Clausius–Clapeyron Approximation for Liquid–Vapour

Approximate result: valid when ideal-gas vapour and negligible liquid molar volume are assumed

For liquid–vapour equilibrium, ΔV_vap ≈ V_gas = RT/P (ideal gas), so:

dP/dT = ΔH_vap P/(RT²)

Divide both sides by P:

d(ln P)/dT = ΔH_vap/(RT²)

Integrate assuming ΔH_vap ≈ constant:

ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

Clausius–Clapeyron equation

ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

Slope of ln P vs 1/T

slope = −ΔH_vap/R

Concept

Trouton's rule connection

At the normal boiling point T_b, ΔS_vap = ΔH_vap/T_b ≈ 85 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for many non-polar liquids (Trouton's rule). This is an empirical pattern — deviations occur for hydrogen-bonded liquids (water: ΔS_vap ≈ 109 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) and small molecules with restricted motion.
5

Thermodynamic vs Kinetic Stability

A system is thermodynamically stable if it is at the global minimum of G (or at the phase with the lowest G_m at given T, P). A system is thermodynamically metastable if it is at a local G minimum. It is thermodynamically unstable if ΔG for any displacement is negative.

A catalyst or enzyme lowers the activation barrier but does NOT change G_reactants, G_products, ΔrG°, or K. Only temperature, pressure, or composition changes affect the equilibrium position.

ConditionΔrGΔrG°Direction
Q < K< 0 (spontaneous)independent of QForward
Q = K= 0 (equilibrium)independent of QNeither
Q > K> 0 (non-spontaneous)independent of QReverse
Q = 1, K > 1= ΔrG° < 0< 0Forward
Q = 1, K < 1= ΔrG° > 0> 0Reverse

Worked Examples

van't Hoff: K at a new temperature

At 300 K, K₁ = 4.0 for a reaction with ΔrH° = +20 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic). Find K₂ at 350 K.

ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔrH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) = −(20000/8.314)(1/350 − 1/300) = −2405 × (−4.762 × 10⁻⁴) = +1.145. K₂/K₁ = e^{1.145} = 3.14. K₂ = 4.0 × 3.14 = 12.6. Endothermic reaction: K increases with T ✓.

Trap: For endothermic reactions, ΔrH° > 0, so the term −ΔrH°(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) is positive when T₂ > T₁ (since 1/T₂ < 1/T₁). K increases with T for endothermic reactions.

Clausius–Clapeyron: vapour pressure at a new temperature

Water has P_vap = 12.3 mmHg at 15 °C and ΔH_vap = 44.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Find P_vap at 35 °C.

T₁ = 288 K, T₂ = 308 K. ln(P₂/P₁) = −(44000/8.314)(1/308 − 1/288) = −5293 × (−2.256 × 10⁻⁴) = +1.194. P₂ = 12.3 × e^{1.194} = 12.3 × 3.30 = 40.6 mmHg.

Trap: Use K (not °C) in the formula. T₁ = 288 K (not 15) and T₂ = 308 K (not 35).

Clapeyron equation — melting point vs pressure

Ice: ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔV_fus = −1.63 × 10⁻⁶ m³ mol⁻¹ at 273 K. Find dP/dT.

dP/dT = ΔH_fus/(T_m ΔV_fus) = 6010/(273 × (−1.63 × 10⁻⁶)) = 6010/(−4.449 × 10⁻⁴) = −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa K⁻¹ = −135 bar K⁻¹. To lower the melting point by 1 K, pressure must increase by 135 bar. This is the water anomaly (negative slope).

Trap: ΔV_fus must use the sign correctly. Water has ΔV_fus < 0 because ice is less dense than liquid water. This gives a negative Clapeyron slope — unique among common substances.

Thermodynamics vs kinetics — stability

For diamond → graphite at 298 K, ΔrG° = −2.9 kJ mol⁻¹. Comment on the stability of diamond.

ΔrG° < 0 means graphite is thermodynamically more stable than diamond at 298 K and 1 bar. However, the reaction is kinetically frozen: the activation barrier for rearranging the covalent lattice is enormous. Diamond is metastable — a local minimum in G separated by a huge kinetic barrier from the global minimum (graphite). Thermodynamics predicts direction; kinetics determines rate.

Trap: Never confuse thermodynamic stability (ΔrG° sign) with kinetic stability (activation barrier). Diamond is thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable for all practical purposes.

Complete Derivations

Step-by-step mathematical derivations

Each derivation below shows every intermediate step with stated assumptions, so that a student can follow the logic line by line.

Derivation 1

van't Hoff equation — complete derivation

Start from ΔrG° = −RT ln Kln K = −ΔrG°/(RT)
Gibbs–Helmholtz applied to ΔrG°[∂(ΔrG°/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔrH°/T²
Since ΔrG°/T = −R ln K[∂(−R ln K)/∂T]_P = −ΔrH°/T²
Simplifyd(ln K)/dT = ΔrH°/(RT²) [van't Hoff differential equation]
Integrate T₁ → T₂ (ΔrH° ≈ const)ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔrH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)
Plotln K vs 1/T gives a straight line with slope = −ΔrH°/R

Derivation 2

Clapeyron equation derivation

Two-phase equilibriumμ_α(T,P) = μ_β(T,P) along coexistence line
Along the coexistence linedμ_α = dμ_β
Expand−S̄_α dT + V̄_α dP = −S̄_β dT + V̄_β dP
Rearrange(V̄_β − V̄_α) dP = (S̄_β − S̄_α) dT
At transition temperatureΔS_tr = ΔH_tr/T_tr
Clapeyron equationdP/dT = ΔH_tr/(T_tr ΔV_tr)
Clausius–Clapeyron (l–v)Assume ΔV ≈ V_g = RT/P: d ln P/dT = ΔH_vap/(RT²)

Practice Problems

1.A plot of ln K vs 1/T has slope −4800 K. Find ΔrH°.

slope = −ΔrH°/R → ΔrH° = −slope × R = −(−4800) × 8.314 = +39.9 kJ mol⁻¹. Endothermic reaction.

2.For the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), K = 4.7 at 350 K and K = 0.13 at 300 K. Find ΔrH°.

ln(4.7/0.13) = −(ΔrH°/R)(1/350 − 1/300). 3.584 = −(ΔrH°/8.314)(−4.762×10⁻⁴). ΔrH° = 3.584×8.314/4.762×10⁻⁴ = 62.6 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic, consistent with dissociation).

3.The normal boiling point of benzene is 80.1 °C and ΔH_vap = 30.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the vapour pressure at 60 °C.

T₁ = 353.1 K (normal bp, P₁ = 1 atm), T₂ = 333 K. ln(P₂/1) = −(30800/8.314)(1/333 − 1/353.1) = −3705 × (1.700×10⁻⁴) = −0.630. P₂ = e^{−0.630} = 0.532 atm = 404 mmHg.

4.Why does the solid–liquid coexistence line for most substances have a very steep positive slope?

dP/dT = ΔH_fus/(T ΔV_fus). ΔV_fus is small (solid and liquid have similar densities) making dP/dT very large — enormous pressure change is required to shift T_m appreciably.
